COERCION OR CONCILIATION. Now lords and gents of birth and blood Restrain your fiery zeal: Powder and shot's not all we've got 7 A nation's woe to heal. IF If Ireland needs a friendly hand, A brother's honest shake, ..., . _ Let's hold it out with right good will, And not for Fashion's sake. .. 0, Ireland our brave working men .. Have forged no human chains; Despotic Power was never theirs, ; And runs not in their veins. -
i •

- Theirs is the soul that scorns to stoop To Insolence and Pride; 'Tis their demand that through the earth God's Justice shall preside. •In all thy depth of bitter woe - That never heart can tell, From Justice thy relief must come, And not from shot and shell. • 'Tis not from noble dukes and lords ; That Freedom ever comes; There is no love 'twixt clashing swords , Or peace in kettledrums. rt.= Content's a virtue strongly urged, By preachers duly fed; And force will be a remedy _ • When bayonets are bread. Let then official patriots curse And tyrants cry aloud; Let mighty dukes and lords coerce IMP The lightning in the cloud. Although a duke might make a law, Resistance to forbid, No duke with any ass's jaw Could do what Samson did. ---. 'Tis not the foot that crushed the flower,

2 Can ever make it grow; ' Tis not the grinding heel of Power Can cure a nations woe. 'Tis honest heartfelt sympathy That man to man unites, The Social Plan requires for all A brotherhood of rights. ....Daily News.

An Irishman, writing a sketch of his life, says he early an away from his father because he discovered he was only his uncle. When the King of Portugal was in England, Queen Victoria presented Sir Edwin Landseer to his Majesty as a painter whose works she had been collecting. "Ali, Sir Edwin, exclaimed the King, "delighted to make your acquaintance. I was always very fond of beasts." Artist, sketchhig tower not a hundred miles from Moo, to the party who keeps the keys of the said tower: "Are there any historical anecdotes about this old tower ?" Keeper: " Weel, sir, I hae been through every nook and cranny o't, but never came across ony in it." A bald-headed gentleman was recently importuned by some young ladies to present them with his photograph. He complied with the request, but instead of presenting them with a picture of his handsome features, sent a very striking view of the back of his head. The joke was duly enjoyed, but the projector was much surprised shortly after to see copies of the picture in the windows of a print shop. On inquiring of the attendant, he found to his horror the sharp photographer had pub- lished it. as "A remarkable picture of the moon." • A lady passenger by one of the West Highland stearpers bad unintentionally been annoying the man at the wheel by asking questions. At last he so far forgot himself as to tell her to "Go to Jericho." The lady was greatly shocked and insulted, complained to the captain, and in- sisted on an apology from the man. The captain politely promised to see to it. Having called the steersman, he told him that he must go to the cabin Where she was and make an apology. The man was/not convinced of his offence, but knew that he must obey orders, and so went off rather sulkily towards the cabin. Having reached the door, he stood there till the attention of the lady was directed to him, when he called out to her, "You need Xtot go," then turned and went on deck. Sven is FAME.—Thackeray once went to Oxford with the intention of delivering his lecture on " The English Bumourists" (subsequently world-famous) to the rising youth at Alma Mater, and as it was necessary to obtain the licenoe of the University authorities, he waited upon the Chancellor's resident deputy, who received him blandly. "Pray, what can Ido to serve you, sir?" in- quired the functionary. "My name is Thackeray." "So I see by this card." "I seek permission to lecture within the precincts." "Ah ! you are a lecturer. What subjects do you undertake—religious or political?" " Neither ; I am a literary man." "Have you written anything ?" " Yes ; lam the author of Vanity Fair." " I presume a Dissenter. Has that anything to do with John Bunyan's book ?" "Not exactly. I have also written Pendennis." "Never heard of those works, but no doubt they are proper books." "I have also con- tributed to Punch." "Punch! I have heard of that. Is It not a ribald publication?" THE PLACE OF CONVERSATION IN MANNERS.—PeopIe are generally more anxious to speak than to listen. They are frequently thinking of what they are going to say, rather than of, whan is being said; and even those who are most polite very often fancy it is sufficient if they seem to be attentive; and yet at the same time their eyes betray an absent mind, and show an impatient desire to continue their own train of thought. Another im- portant element is the art of saying the right word in the right place. When listening to the cares and troubles of others, it is scarcely gracious and certainly not com- forting, to give a long list of similar grievances. Nor is it polite, when a friend is shown a painting, sculpture, or other work of art, for him instantly to describe a similar thing, only more valuable, that he has seen else- where, or possibly has in his own possession. Several Instances might be given of saying the right word in the right place; but one is sufficient. For a host or hostess to introduce subjects with which they know their friends to be familiar is a delicate attention which may pass unnoticed at the time, but will have the good effect of making their guests feel at their ease and leave a pleasant recollection, as everyone likes to talk upon a, subject on ' -which he thinks he can talk well. Good humour, or the habit of being easily pleased, is essential to politeness ; but as there are often occasions when annoyances will arise, irritation may be concealed by a little attention to Art ineManners, and thus prevent the discomfort being felt by others. 66 mßs.,,—The history of THE ORIGIN OF "Mn." AND those everyday titles of Mr. and Mrs., which are now the common property of everyone, is not without interest, though in some a its steps it is a little obscure. In the earlier times of our history the ordinary man was simply William or John—that is to say, he had merely a Chris- tian name, without any kind of "handle" before it. or surname after it. Some means of distinguishing one John or one William' from another John or another William became necessary. Nicknames, derived from a man's trade, or from his dwelling-place, or from .some personal peculiarity,were tacked on their Christian names, and plain John became plain John Smith. As yet there were no "Misters" in the land. Some John Smith accu- mulated more wealth than the bulk of his fellows—be- came, perhaps, a landed proprietor, or an employer of hired labour. Then he began to be called in the Norman- French of the day, the " Maistre" of this place or of that, of these workmen or of those. In time the " Maistre," or " Maister," as it soon became, got tacked on before Ins name, and he became M..ister Smith and his wife was Maistress Smith. But gradually this sense of possession was lostosight ef, and the title was conferred upon any man who had attained social distinction of any kind, whether by mere possession of wealth, or by holding; some position of more or less consideration and import- ance. It is only within comparatively modern times that the term came to be considered an almost indispensable adjunct to everyone's name when mentioned in ordinary conversation or writing. Maistress Smith soon became Mistress Smith. Exactly how and when the term got corrupted cannot be said. Master Smith, however, re- mained Master Smith long after his wife became Mistress Smith.

Messrs. .Burgess Brothers, Wenona, 111., have just shipped seven Aberdeen-Angus cattle. Five are from the herd of Mr. O. C. Wallis. Bradley Hall, Wylam-on- Tyne. The other two were bred by Col. Goodman, Smeaton Manor. BUTTERINE.—The Staffordshire Chamber of Agricul- ture ho passed a resolution asking that the question of adulteration of butter should be made a special subject for discussion by the Central Chamber, "as at the pre- sent time it no doubt contributes largely to the general depression of.griculture." • The little Kerry cow, sent from Lord Roseber-y's farm at Mentmore to the dairy show at Islington, has now calved, and is giving 14 quarts of milk a day. Un- doubtedly this t'hardy little breed must come more into favour, especially when people begin to know how economical they are to keep. Six hunters lately sold by Mr. T. H. Hutchinson, Manor House, Catterick, have averaged £225 each. With the exception of two horses they were only light-weight hunters, thus showing that well-bred hunters that can perform can be sold at fairly good prices even in these denressed times of agriculture. Lord Falmouth and Sir William Williams have ex- changed for wee year the bulls, "Sir Michael" (1646) and "Duke of Flitton 17th" (1544). "Sir Michael" stood second to Mr. Perry's "Druid" (1317) at the Royal Show at York, was first at Kilburn, and first at Reading, and "Duke of Flitton 17th" was a first-prize yearling at the Royal at Reading, and first as a calf at Derby. Mr. Adams Earl, Shadeland Farm, La Fevette, Indiana, U.S., has purchased the noted Hereford bull, "The Grove 3rd," for £1,400. This animal was purchased by Mr. Culbertson at Mr. Turner's sale at The Leen for £B3O. Mr. Adams Earl is an enthusiastic supporter of the Here- ford breed, and has been using the famous Lord Wilton bulls Sir Bartle Frere and Romeo. The sire of The Grove 3rd, Horace, was sold when nine years old to Mr. F. Platt, Barnby Manor, for £5OO. The entries for the Paris Agricultural Show comprise 379 cattle, 92 sheep, 20 pigs, and 1,201 pens of poultry. The fat stock exhibition will be from February 27 to March 5. The entries include 377 cattle, 79 Tens of sheep (3 to the pen), and 14 large groups; 160 pigs, 1,308 .pens of live poultry, and 312 lots of dead poultry; 500 exhibits of cheese, and 380 of butter; 9,000 of agricul- tural produce, 200 of cider, 400 specimens of Algerian wine, 7,000 implements, and 20 collections of decorative plants' and flowers. The sale of the :Glencairn herd of Aberdeen-Angus cattle, the property of Mr. W. H. Whitridge, Baltimore, Md., was held at Chicago, when seventeen head of, bulls and heifers were sold under the hammer, at an average of £6l. A few minutes before the sale a telegram was received from Mr. Benton Garinger, Washington Court House, Oh., bidding £6O for each female in the cata- logue, but only four head went to Mr. Garinger at this • figure. The twelve head of females averaged £6B. Five bulls averaged £46. AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS ACT.—" Farmer George " asks: Can a farmer claim under the Agricultural Hold- ings (England) Act, 1883, compensation for grass seeds sown during the last year of his tenancy? I can find nothing relating to this in the Act, but it is clearly an unexhausted improvement.—lf grass seeds sown the last year of a tenancy are intended for "permanent pas- ture," it appears that "consent of the landlord is re- quired," but " seeds " sown in the usual rotation of crop- ping would undoubtedly be paid for by the landlord or incoming tenant in the ordinary course of valuations. Compensation for "seeds" sown the last years of a tenancy, if not specified in the Act, would be claimable as an improvement for which a tenant would be entitled to compensation under "custom." See section 57. THE " CONSERVATIVE " BRITISH FARM.—Here is an absurd statement from the Chicago Tribune :—" A recent traveller in England reports that fully one-half the wheat and other grain is cut with the sickle in many localities. The British farmer is exceedingly conservative, and is less disposed than his brethren on the Continent to adopt Yankee inventions and improvements." It would be interestines to learn where the "many localities" are in which the sickle is generally used. Perhaps the travel- ler did not know a sickle from a scythe. As to "Yankee inventions," the English farmer does not need to go to America for the best agricultural implements, though there are many good ones there as well as here, and some of them are used here. In what European country is the reaping machine more generally used than in England? A CO-OPERATIVE AGRICITVITRAL SOCrETY.—The 12th annual meeting of the Vale of Eden (Westmorland) Agricultural Society has been held at Appleby. Mr. Breaks was in the chair. The Secretary read the re- port, which showed a decrease in the receipts from the previous year. Manures sold amounted to 336 tons, against 342 last year, of the value of £2,201 13s. id.; feeding stuffs, 160 tons, of the value of £1,340 7s. 7d., against 189 tons, valued at £1,718 16s. 6d. Seeds showed a sale of £258 103. 10d., compared with £361 13s. ld. last year. There remained a balance of £4l 4s. Bd., which it was proposed to dispose of as follows :—lnterest on paid- up share capital at the rate of 4 per cent. per annum, £lB 10s., leaving a balance of £22 14s. Bd. A statement of accounts annexed to the report showed that the society's capital is £462 10s., with a reserve fund of £172 10s. 10d., and there are 159 members. HORgE WITHOUT BLINKERS.—A correspondent writes: —" About 14 years ago the firm I represented purchased ' for my driving a very well-bred Irish mare, unbroken, and three years old; in due course she was broken to harness, with blinkers, and I drove her with them for about four years. As she had a small head and a very wicked looking eye, I thought I should like to see her without blinkers. Taking every precaution, having a man to walk by her side with a leading rein, we put her to, svith the yard gates closed, in case of her bolting; but nothing of the sort occurred. After looking round at the wheels *once or twice, she went as quietly as with. ,the blinkers on, and I drove her for years after, some- times with them and sometimes without them. Being a high spirited mare, when drivine without blinkers she objected to the whip in your hand. I drove her alto- gether about nine years, in the country principally." BRITISH DAIRY FARMERS.—The British Dairy Farmers'. Association recently resolved to meet in Derbyshire in June next, for the purpose of discussing important topics and visiting 'different dairy farms and factories. In fur- therance of this proposal, a meeting was held at the Midland Hotel, Derby, on Tuesday afternoon, when Messrs. Gilbert Murray, Algernon Fawkes, Geo. Barham, E. C. Tisdall, and William C. Young (secretary), attended on behalf of the association, and several local societies were represented. After a brief conversation, it was re- solved to arrange a programme extending over four days—viz., June Bth, 9th, 10th, and 11th' Brailsford, Longford, Ashboume, Norbery, and Sudbury being among the places to be visited on the 9th and 10th. The other two days it was proposed to set apart for confer- ences at Derby, the headquarters. The following sub- jects were appointed for discussion :-1. The best sve- tern of cropping and storage on a dairy farm. 2. the utilisation of separated milk. 3. English cheese-making. 4. How to compete more successfully with the foreign butter-maker. 5. Selection and managemeat of dairy cattle. 6. Winter dairying. THE MARKS OF A GOOD MILKEIZ.-1. A good milker must be able to eat a great deal of food. Milk cannot be made without something to make it from. The cow does not secrete milk from the air, but from her blood, and her blood is supplied from the food she eats. To eat great deal a cow must have a strong jaw, and we may put this down as one of the marks of a good milker. A strong jaw does not necessarily require a big head, at least what is called a bull's head, large in the upper part, but a strong lower jaw with strong muscles to operate it. Any expansion of the head in other directions may be a detriment. 2. A good milker must digest a great deal of food. This requires an ample stomach or stomachs, for the cow has four. A large stomach is in- dicated externally by a large abdomen and great breadth between the hips, or great breadth of loins. A judge of cows will tell you that a cow should be wedge-shaped, tapering from abdomen to nose. 3. A good milker will have large milk veins—that is, large veins leading to the udder, under the belly. Those large veins indicate a large milker. 4. div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

The state of the weather during the past month has Prevented progress being made with some out-door I operations that force themselves upon us at this time of the year. Snow delayed the pruning of bush fruit trees, and the frost would not allow us to scrape the surface of the ground with the hoe, which we like to do previous to pruning, in order to clear the weeds before they are ; trampled, which we prefer to digging them in, as is usually done, not that we object to bury the weeds, but we have a great dislike to disturb the roots of the fruit trees. Since we adopted this plan, we have been free from caterpillars, which are so destructive to the leaves of Gooseberries especially; but we were quite uncon- scious that our treatment of the surface of the soil had anything to do with this immunity till a grower;of some hundreds of trees communicated his experience in one of the horticultural papers early last year. His crops had been frequently destroyed by caterpillars, and he was about to despair of carrying out his ambition of producing Gooseberries by the ton, when one day lie looked over the fence of one of his orchards, into what might be regarded as a neglected garden. There-he saw Gooseberry trees covered with leaves, which was more than he could boast of on his trees, separated only by a fence. The ground, he discovered, had not been dug for years, and, instead of hoeing the weeds and grass, they had been kept down by cutting them. This was, of course, the outcome of the owner's apparent neglect, but a lesson was taught, and the writer concluded that he had solved the great caterpillar difficulty, and he re- solved not to dig the ground between his bush fruit trees, but, nevertheless, keep it clear of weeds. It ap- pears that the moth finds the newly-dug ground a more suitable place to lay its eggs in, than in the hard surface, which will account for its presence when the soil is annually loosened. The caterpillar, the moment it , emerges from the chrysalis stage, requires a great amount of food, without which it will not long exist, and instinct, we suppose, directs the moth to lay its eggs where abundance of food is likely to be near at hand. If, therefore, we can only clear them from under the trees, there is no fear'of their travelling from their plaoes near by if food should be scarce there. ALLcrrmeisrrs.—Lordßrownlow has made arrangements to provide hundreds of cottagers with quarter-acre al- lotments at Tottenhoe. Lord Radnor has also deter- mined to give the allotment system a trial, and has ordered a large space of land at Folkstone to be let in allotments of from ten perches to half an acre, at from ' 9d. per perch. It is stated that there are upwards of 100 applicants. , THE FELONT GARDEN.—WALK EDGINGS (CONTINUED).— Having discussed the merits of -the usual subjects em- ployed for forming live edgings, we shall now proceed to deal with those in use for making what are termed dead edgings. Tiles are manufactured for this purpose, and are extensively used in front of houses of modern build. The best are the dark, hard-burnt Staffordshire tiles, as they are not affected by the weather. Their price is an objection, being over 6d. a yard if large quan- tities are not ordered. In the end we consider them the cheapest of all manufactured articles. They are neat and clean looking at all times--especially the plain ones, as the rain removes every particle of dirt that may lodge on them. This is not the ease if some of the variety of patterns are used. It would, however, be ex- ceedingly bad taste to introduce these or similar objects into the front of an old-fashioned cottage in the coun- try. Here we would prefer a combination of living and dead materials by first placing rough stones to 'indicate the outline, and plant between thorn at their base some of the diminutive creeping saxifrages and sedum& One or two species of Speedwell might also with advantage be used to complete this floral edging. THE GARENHOUSH—The agreeable change in the weather will allow air to be admitted into the green- house earlier in the day, and more freely than it has been safe to do for the past month. Cold currents of air must, however, not be allowed to rush through the house. When they prevail, it is better not to open the front ventilators, but to do all the airing at the top. When there Is likelihood of frost the house should be closed early, so as to husband some of the sun's heat, thereby requiring as little firing as possible. Watering is always best done early in the day at this time of the year, and the temperature of the water may be a little higher than the atmosphere of the houses. Succulent plants, such as Cacti and Crassulas, must be watered very sparingly for a month or two.

- - CRIMES OF VIOIENCS IN NOTTINIMAM.—On Saturday Frank Rowley, hawker, was indicted at Nottingham Assizes for wounding Marian Rose. In consequence of prisoner's loose habits, Rose's mother forbade her daughter continuing to keep company with him. Prisoner, after saving that sooner than any one else should have the girl he would "finish her," took her out for a walk, seized her unawares, and cut her throat two or three times with a razor. But for the interference of a soldier he would probably have killed her. The jury found him guilty of the full charge, but seir,ilee was deferred.—George Bremner was indicted for robbing Mr. Barber, engineer, of Leicester, of a gold watch an,l chain. The learn,d judge, commenting on other cases, expressed the opinion that for frequent offenders sentences must be made more scvere, light sentences only inducing others to crime.

' ATTEMPTED WIFE MURDER IN MANCHESTER. —On Saturday morning, about eight o'clock, a woman named Eliza Moss, the wife of John Moss, of the Masons' Arms beerbouse, Medlock-street. Holm, was conveyed to the Manchester Infirmary suffering from severe wounds about the neck, which had been inflicted by her husband. At an early hour P.C. Hallsworth heard Fereama of "Murder," and proceeded to the Masona' Arms. Moss and his wife were in Medlock-street in their nightdresses. Mrs. Moss was on the ground in the road, and her husband was stoop- ing over her with a razor in his band cutting her throat. The offloer, with assistance, dragged Moss aWIO7, wrested the razor out of his hand, and removed him to the bride- well in Park-place. MosaN daughter, a girl nine years old, had bravely endeavoured to prevent him cutting her mother's throat, but he stabbed her just above the bridge of the nose inflicting two seveze wounds between the eyes. Mr.. Moss had received a severe wound just below the ear, besides other injuries. Shortly before noon her depositions were taken by Mr. W. Armitage, ope of the oily justices. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEB
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEB

I "THE TRUE METHOD OF BIBLE STUDY." On Sunday evening the Rev. R. Pilcher, BA., dis- coursed in the Cairo-street Chapel, Warrington, on "The true method of bible study." The text was 2 Timothy, iii. c., $h and 17th verses. Elaviug briefly re-stated some of the opinions he expressed In! his sermon on the Sunday evening previous, a report of. which appeared in our hat issue, Mr. Pitcher remarked that it might be said " You do not look upon the bible as the word of God." Ha replied let them not use mere phrases to which they attached but vague meaning. If they meant that the collected religious literature of the Hebrew race. b-fore they lost th6ir Hebrew speech and began to write ' Greek, was word for word and in every detail to be taken as a message direct from God, the only share in it taken by the men being the writing down of the words, he cer- tainly did not believe the bible to be the word of God. God could not contradict himself either as to questions of fact or of morals. Yet contradictions in both respects could be pointed out in the Scriptures, and gave indeed whatever force they had to secularistic attacks upon Christianity. And, as he had pointed out, Christians had actually dropped some beliefs, as, for example, that in witchcraft, and that of anointing the sick with oil instead of sending for the doctor, a practice which the Roman Catholic Church re- tained under the form of extreme uection. Few instructed Chrietians would put on one dead level of value, moral, spiritual, or even literary, the cnrsing psalms and psalms that breathed the essence of religious trust ; the sometimes harroaing and shocking, and sometimes disgusting details of Leviticus, and the rich glowing spiritual loveliness of Isaiah ; the wnite heat of hate shown in the Apocalypse, and the pure loving morality set forth in the Sermon on the Mount, the. fable-kuotieg St. Jude, and the deep-seeing and soul-sear chiug St. John. Yet according to the theory which the phrase" Word of God " was generally made to express these -were eqaally valuable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, for perfecting the man of God in every good work. It seemed to him that the very statement carried with it its own rebuke. Attempts had been made to meet the fact of contradiction in scrip- ture by calling them successive manifestations of God. He should prefer to call them successive rises in spiritual insight en the part of men. But whether they said that the truth was only revealed in part or only seen in part, as in a glass darkly, as e.,t. Paul expressed it, the first unveiled to man was imperfect till the next part was unveiled, or the first part at which men caught a glimpse was imperfect till the next part came into view. In other words, the new revelation, or the new discovery made the old revelation or discovery at least more true and sometimes proved it untrue. Let him show by one example how the absence of that his- torical perception af the bible created contradictions where none really existed and "confounds the thoughts of men." In the old testament the prevailing idea of God is of strength. The first name of Him means force, as in Gab- riel the strong man or man of God. The second name in order of time, Jehovah, the living one, he who had life in himself, be who was the source of life, marked exactly the same advance in conception of divine things as the worship of Zeus, the kingly intelligence marked an advance amongst the heathen upon the worship of giants, that was the blind forces of nature. The time came when the Hebrew idea of God reached the high idea of holiness. He was the Holy One of Israel. Hence they had an historical development or progress from good to better, and a real evangelical pre- paration for Christ's teaching. It made the Lord's prayer possible. He asked them candidly to weigh the questions he was about to put, and answer them quietly in the shrine of their own hearts, which view of the bible was the more profitable for teaching; that which declared the mass of contradictions, tits., the " Word of God ;" or that which de- clared them to he the inevitable accompaniments of a series of efforts made by a most spiritually gifted race to see God more and more clearly and to serve Him with more steadfast love ? Which view of the bible was more profit- able for re„roof ? That which teaches that God ordered the Israelites to spoil the Egyptians, slaughter the Ca- naanitea, play fast and loose with A,syrians, dic., or that which sets those acts aside and condemns them as the natural mistakes and crimes of a savage race in a savage age; rats- tekee eqd. erinet!e, moreover, whiCh wrought their own punishment!. Wh:ch view was Mete proftLablt for correc- tion P Teat which accepted literally the imagery of this savage race and savage age and taught that there is to be a physical flame for spiritual offeeees ; an ininite torture for sins of finite man ; or that which taught they were con- cerned alone with the idea which underlies all this imagery, namely, that God did hate all wrong-doine and would by the solemn fire of discipline burn out the dross from their soula; a consuming fire which only the tears of sincere re- pentance could over quench.
TRIPLE EXECUTIoN AT CARLISLE

div.head: FOR THE PLUMPTON MURDER.
div.p: FOR THE PLUMPTON MURDER.

On Monday morning, Anthony Benjamin Budge, John Martin isaliam John White), and James Baker were executed in Carlisle Gaol for the murder of P.C. Byrnes, at Plumpton, on October 19th. The weather was cold and misty, but a very large crowd of people assembled in the vicinity of the gaol to see the black flag hoisted. The streets were blocked with people, an 4 many persons had taken up positions on tall buildings overlookiog the prison in the hope of see- ing the sentence of the law carried out. The High Sheriff (Mr. L. B. Dykes) prevented the gratifica- tion of this morbid curiosity by causing the scaffold to he erected in the old treadmill shed, close to the cells were the convicts were incarcerated, and the complete seclusion of the funeral procession was secured by the erection of a boarding to cover the short distance on the way to the scaffold, which was not already roofed in. Since their condemnation Budge and Martin, who belonged to the Roman Catholic faith, have re- ceived the constant ministrations of the Rev. Canon. Waterton; and Baker has been attended by the Rev. James Wilson, chaplain of the gaol. Rudge and Martin were inclined at first to reject the services of a spiritual adviser, as they considered it would be con- temptible for one of their type to turn pious at the eleventh hour. Canon Waterton, however, brought them to a proper appreciation of their position, and on Saturday both men received the Holy Communion after making sacramental confession. Baker was very attentive to the ministrations of the chaplain, and received the Holy Communion about half -au- hour before the execution. He took his last farewell of his father, mother, brother, ana sisters on Friday, and on the same day kludge received a final visit from his brother and his young nephew, who was christened after the condemned man, and whom he he had expressed a wish to see before he died. At a quarter before eight o'clock the prison bell itegan to toll, and Berry, the executioner, and his assistant commenced to prepare the men for death. The scaffold was a new substantial structure, with a cross- bar cap.tble of sustaining 16 tons. The floor was divided into two leaves, and the three men stood alongside one another close together. A few minutes before eight o'clock the condemned men, who had already been pinioned in their cells, were brought out and conducted to the place of execution. The distance that they traversed was short, and the grim engine of death was soon reached. Rudge and Martin were attended by Canon Waterton and Father Thompson, and the chaplain accompanied Baker. In low tones each minister offered the condemned the last conso- lation of religion. The other persons present at the execution were the High Sheriff, the Under Sheriff, three magistrates, representing the Visiting Com- mittee, two newspaper reporters, and the prison officials. When the men reached the seaffold, Martin was placed in the middle, with Rudge on his right hand and Baker on his left. While Berry and his assistant were adjusting the white caps the convicts engaged in prayer, repeating the words, "Lord, have mercy upon my soul." Baker also said with reference to the woman, with whom he bad lived, and to whom he had written on Sunday night, "Nellie, keep straight." He added, "I am an innocent man; but I forgive everybody. Lord have mercy upon my soul; Christ have mercy upon my soul." At eight o'clock the bolt was drawn, and the three men dropped through the trap. Drops of 4ft. 6ft., and 6ift. were allowed, and death was apparently instantaneous. Before death Martin told Canon Waterton to say that he admitted firing the shot which killed Byrnes; but that he did it without intention to murder, tut simply to disable the officer. Both Rudge and Martin declared that the "fourth man" who has not yet been arrested "had nothing to do witk it," and had merely joined them on the road. Inquests were held on the bodies by the city coroner (Mr. J. Hevreteon Brown). when the usual verdicts were returned.

Her Majesty's ship Diamond was re- ported in despatches just received to be at Bagga Island in the South Seas, and it was expected she would punish the natives for a shocking outrage and cannibalism. The object of the outrage was a trader named Childi, who had settled on the island a few months previously. A number of natives from several adjacent islands visited Bagga and called Childi out of his but. When he got outside, one of them strzek him on the head with a tomahawk. Childi put etp his hand to his head, when another native struck him on the wrist and broke it. A third struck him in the back with; a tomahawk, which felled him to the ground. The wretches then chopped off the man' S bead and lighted a fire on the spot. The body was then cooked, and tne murcligers made a hearty meal of it. The natives either took or 7estroyed everything belonging to their vic-.I rim. Cbildi had szttled in the island of Bagga because there were no natives there and there was flesh water. He was a trader. The natives returned to their islands after their revolting feast. Her M tjesty's ship Diamond came up soon after the occurrence, and the traders made the com- mander accpaainted with the facts. It was anticipated that the murderers would be punisho by the Diamond for the, .hocking crime. Toe natives of the island in question were, •Ir was said, showing an increased desire to attack white men: _ _

DEMONSTRATION OF LONDON UNEMPLOYED. RIOTOUS PROCEEDINGS. A demonstration of the unemployed of London, convened in connection with the London United Workmen's Commit- tee, waeche d in Trafalgar-square on Monday afternoon. By two o'clock the space round the Nelson Column and the fountains was three parts filled, and the opportunity was seized by some members of the Society of Social Democrats to address a portion of the crowd from the base of the Nel- son Column. Resolutions were declared to be adopted urg- ing the necessity for immediate steps tieing taken to allevi- ate the wide-spread distress, and Insisting that the metro- politan representatives should obstruct all business in the House of Commons until a bill was passed to authorise the Metropolitan Board of Works to undertake the erection of artisans' dwellings on vacant spaces, to ensure that workmen employed thereon should be paid the customary prices of labour, and favouring shorter hours of labour. One of the crowd, carrying a red flag, caused some excitement at this juncture by rushing acmes the roadway to the Grand Hotel, with a number of persons after him, but no disturb- ance followed. The Social Democrats addressed another meetine, and then the demonstration proper commenced by the holding of a series of meetings on improvised platforms in the centre of the square. Resolutions were adopted call- ing for the starting of useful public works in the metropo- lis and throughout the country, for the relief of the agri cultural industry, and demanding the appointment of a minister of commerce and agriculture. The crowd then began to disperse, but not before several persons standing on the edges of the fountain basins had overbalanced them- selves and fallen into the water, much to the amusement of the bystanders. A mob remained behind and smashed up the structures used as platforms, and threw pieces into the fountains. The Social Democrats marched off towards Cock- spur-street, headed by a man with a red flag; but the contingent soon dispersed. The rowdies who remained after smashing the platforms, thronged towards the Strand, and some rough horseelay followed, the pedestrians being roughly jostled, and several gentlemen haying their silk hats crashed. The police arrested two persons and sent for rein- forcements, and 100 men came down and partially dispersed the crowd. Subsequent to these proceedings a large crowd proceeded along Pall Mall, up St. James's-street, along Picca- dilly, Park-lane, and South Audley-street, smashing some windows in their progress. Stones were thrown at the Carlton-Club, where several windows were broken. In St. Jamee's-street the windows of the Conservative Club, Arthur's Club, and other buildings were partially wrecked by stones and ether missiles. Some shops were also at- tacked. The police appeared to be powerless, and whenever they interfered they were beaten off. The greatest damage was done in South Audley-street and North Audley-street. The immense mob rushed along the thoroughfare in a most menacing manner, and passed scarcely one house or shine without throwing stones or other missiles at the windows. They first attacked the shop of Mr. Archaad, jeweller, and a lot of roughs seized the watches and valuable articles of jewellery displayed in the shop. Between £3OO and £4OO worth of property was stolen. A little further on the win- dow of a btker's shop was entirely demolished, and the mob stele therefrom cakes and bread. Nearly every shopkeeper suffered more or leas. A London ccrrespondent says that the crowd had Pall Mall in its possession. It could have entered the clulas more easily than it took possession of the parap-d upon the stone balustrade in front of the Carlton and Reform. But after applauding the doctrine that work must be provided and delivering the other parts of the mes- sage- by the respective speakers "to those who live in luxury," the crowd melted away with three cheers for what was called the "social revolution." It was after this per- formance was ended and the crowds had moved away that the disorderly edit were committed which are meotianed elsewhere. On Tuesday morning people began to assemble in Trafal- gar-square at an early hour. By noon there were two or three thousand men scattered about. Rumours of probable disturbances quickly spread, and the West End tradeepeople at once took the alarm ; shutters were put up and other preparations made to meet the threatened danger. Hun- dreds of constables were on duty in Trafalgar-square, and strong detachments were posted at various strategical points shortly after two o'clock the news that the Prince of 1 Wales was holding a levee at St. James's Palace spread amongst the roughs, some 400 or 500 of whom at once marched from the square in the direction of the palace, until they found their progress barred by a strong body of police, who formed in line across the road near the Carlton Club. The mob, overawed by the resolute bearing of the policemen, and confused by the manceevree of two or three mounted inspectors, wavered, turned tail, and fled igne- minously. This was the only really serious incident of the day. By half-pact four o'clock Trafalgar-square was cleared, and further access to it prevented by a dr- don of police, and gradually all excitement died out. The following communication is from the Loctl Govern- ment Board:—" Mews. Burns, Champion, Hyndman, and Williams sought an interview yesterday morning with the President of the Local Government Board on the subject of the state of the unemployed, and with regard to the resolu- tions passed at the meeting held on Monday in Trafalgar- square." The following correspondence paseed :—(1) " Mr. Chamberlain is unable to recognise in Messrs. Burns, Champion, Hyndnaen, and Williams any claim to represent the workmen at present unemployed owing to the existing de- pression, and mast therefore decline to give them a personal interview. Mr. Chamberlain will be ready to receive any communication in writing, and to give it full consideration. London, Feb. 9. 1886." (2) "Messrs. Burns, Champion, Hyndmen, and Williams, called upon Mr. Chamberlain, in order that tLey migt4 be able to inform the public meetings of unemployed, whom they will address in the course of the I next few days, what Mr. Chamberlain, as President of the Local Board, intends to do in order to find work for the hun- dreds of thousands of starving men in London and other parts of the country, and to present the enclosed resolutions p,ssed yesterday by many thousands of unemployed men in Trafalgar-square. 'We may add that salutary pressure on the local authorities has entirely failed of effect, and the letters of 'hest, bodies to the Local Government Board re- main unanswered." (3) "Mr. Chamberlain has received the copy of the resolutions passed by a meeting in Trate'. gar-square. He does not think that the remedies proposed to this meeting by the Social Federition would be effectual, and he is unable, therefore, to promise any support to them. At the same time he is making independent inquiries into the extent and character of the distress, and all applications fretn local authorities in correspondence with the Local Government Board will receive immediate attention. In every case where the circumstances require it, and where they do not already poseess the power the Boards of Guar- dians will be at elm authorised to give outdoor relief when arrangements are made for a labour -test sufficient to pre- vent imposture. The question of public works is not one within the province of the Local Government Board.—Feb- rosary 9th, 1886." Mr. M. Kelly, the organising secretary of Monday's demonstration of unemployed workmen, says that no un- employed workmaat ,took part in the disturbances, which were deliberately planned beforehand by the Socialists. The Socialists had for weeks past made no secret of their intend tion to spoil their demonstration. Many tradesmen, on Taesday, estimated the extent of their losses, with a view of &aiming compensation. Messrs. Purvis and Bishop, jewellers, South Audley-street, aloes sustained damage to the extent of £5,000. It is believed that £20,000 will over the damage caused by the rioters. A number of men Were charged at several of the police Metr- opolitan on Monday. Tue s gerngedoodins the disturbances "n from jewellers' shops. In most instances remands were granted. laYawndithwibtheinsgtelnein A PANIC IN LONDON.—POLICE PRECAUTIONS. demonstration on Wednesday threw London into a state A rumour that the unemployed intended to make another of panic. The origin of the anxiety is said to have been the arrival of a message from Deptford that a band of rouges had set out towards London. Telegrams were at once sent i from Scotland Yard to the out police stations warning shop- keepers to close their premises, extra police officers were despatched to the chief thoroughfares, and as they went on duty they conveyed to tra iestnen a "general order' that they had better close their establishments. This was at one o'clock, up to which time business had been proceed- ing as usual. The police intimation caused so much ner- vousness that shops were slotted with remarkable rapidity, the remit, of eonrse, being that hundreds of people were soon hastening from the by-streets and courts into the main thoroughfares, and amongst them were many dangerous and mischievous persons. BY three O'clock thousands of people lined the main roads leading from London Bridge to the Elephant and Castle and along the Walworth reads. It was believed that the expected mob would rendezvous at the Elephant and Castle, and around this well-known house an immense mob collected and dis- cussed all kinds of wild rumours. The existence of the panic was visible along the entire relate from Clapham to Greenwich, and a computation was made that a length of more than thirty miles of shops had been closed against possible riot and pillage. As a matter of fact the Deptford mob never reached London, and while the Londoners were awaiting its arrival the people of Deptford and Greenwich were expecting the arrival of a body reported to be on the march from London to those places. In the course of the afternoon the alarm extended to the West End of London. It the Houses of Parliament the large gates were hastily closed, at Charing Cross Station the gates were closed and secured with heavy chains and large ptdlocks, and at the banks in South London the iron shutters were put up. On the part of the authorities measures were taken for guard- ing the bridges over the river, contingents of policemen were placed at various oetftrta in readiness for action, and ' troupe were detained in barracks to give assistance should it be necessary. On Wednesday the Home Secretary was in communica- tion with the authorities at Scotland Yard, where a number of witnesses were examined as tb the speeches on Monday, , and their statements were taken down for submieelon to the ' law officers of the Crown. It was stated on Wednesday night that warrants for the arrest of several Socialist leaders have been placed in the hands of Scotland Yard detectives. At a meeting of the Labourers' Amalgamated Union held on Wednesday, allusions were made to the conduct of the Social Democrats in inciting the scum of the Metropolis to pillage and plunder the shops of West ifnd tradesmen, and it was declared that the mob who did this work were not working-men. The Mansion House Committee for the relief of the unemployed on Wednesday passed a resolution re- cording its conviction that the acts of violence and crime committed on Monday were induced and oommitted by cer- tain lawless persons not connected with industry or with the working classes.

MURDEROUS ATTACK ON A CONSTABLE. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, a powerfully-built man named Michael Connor, who is well known to the police, was brought up and remanded on a charge of violently assaulting P.C. Hennessey, a memberof theborough police force, with intent to murder him. The as- sault was committed at Market Gate on Saturday night, and Chief Coittable Hunt, in detailing the circumstances, said that at 5-30 o'clock on Saturday evening, Constables Singleton and Hennessey were on duty at Market Gate, when prisoner and another man yet at large—named Michael Hennessey and. also well known—came up. The one not in custody said to Connor "Here's the 1)-- slops," meaning the constables, and prisoner said "Yes, that big headed b--; I would like to punch his b guts in." Singleton said to them that they did not want fly bother and asked them to go about their busi- ness. Prisoner and his companion went down Horsemarket-street, and when near the Griffin pri- soner dared the officers to come forward. They then went into a public-house on Town Hill, and Single- ton told them that they would be reported. At 6-10 the same evening prisoner and his companion re- turned to Market Gate. P.C. Hennessey was answering the inquiries of some persons regarding the time the next 'bus would leave when Michael Hennessey pushed against him, and at the same moment prisonerwas seen by two witnesses to take from out of his left coat sleeve a short poker, with which he struck Constable Hennessey a severe blow on the head. Prisoner and the other man ran away, and it was ascertained that they had gone to Manchester. Two constables were sent to Man- chester and at about two or three o'clock on Sunday morning, with the assistance of the Manchester police, Connor, who is known in Manchester as " Wallington Mick," was arrested in a brothel. He (Mr. Hunt) believed that prisoner had disabled one or two of the Manchester police, and that he had bit, one man through the thumb. He wasperfectly sat- isfied that the assault committed on the policeman was premeditated, and asked for a remand until the Ifollowing Monday in order that efforts might be masle to arrest the other man concerned. After formal evidence had been given prisoner was reman- ded accordingly. At the Borough Court, on Thursday morning, Michael Hennessey, the man who escaped, was brought up in custody and charged with taking part in the assault on the officer.—Mr. White (mag- istrates' clerk) : One prisoner was remanded on Monday on the same charge, and prisoner has been apprehended since.—P C. Hennessey said that pri- soner seized him by the le.. at tlie moment the other prisoner dealt him the blow on the head. The present prisoner appeared to him to be the most de- ternained and more inclined to do harm, both before and after the attack.—Mr. White: Dr. Starkey Smith says that but for the helmet the blow would probably have killed him.—Major Litton: It is evident it must have been a severe blow.—Prisoner said that he was entirely innocent of inflicting any harm on the officer. He never used violence, but was in drink He admitted being there, but denied OM he acted in concert with the other prisoner.— He was zenaanded until Monday next, when he will be brought up and charged in conjunction with Connor.

• BANK QUAY MISSION caATEL: On Sunday the Workingmen's Mission Chapel ! at Bank Quay, Warrington, was re-Opened after undergoing extensive alterations, collections to- wards the expense thus incurred being made after each service. Mr. E. Johnson, of Manchester, oc- cupied the pulpit at the morning and evening ser- vices, and the ROY. Howell Jones preached in the afternoon. There were good eongregations. Preach- ing in the morning Mr. Johnson took for his text the words "The way of transgressors is hard." He dealt very earnestly with his subject, especially addressing .his remarks to young med. If a youth, he said, began the right end up, as it were, was sober, industrious, and God-fearing, he would have an enlightened mind, a strong moral. fibre, and wonld be able to withstand temptation. If, on the contrary, the youth was a fool, could be taken by the collar and dragged into wickedness, and led a life of ;profligacy, he very often soon became a drivelling fellow creeping along the highway of life In its dark corners, finally to enter the grave he had dug for himself. Such indeed realised that the way of transgressors was hard. Mr. Johnson spoke of the physical as well as the moral effects of a pro- fligate living, and of the ruin and misery inflicted by a debauchee, not only on himself, but on his family and relatives. In asking for generous sup- port towards the fund for paying off the cost in- curred by the alterations Mr. Johnson remarked on the great improvement that had been effected, and mentioned that the teachers had already amongst themselves collected the sum of £l6 3s 6d. Anthems were sung by the choir at each service. The general appearance of the chapel has been completely changed. The old-fashioned seats and rostrum have been removed, and new benches and rostrum, made of the best-selected pitch pine, have been substi- tuted. In addition a new porch, facing Liverpool- road; has been erected, the entrance being at the side, with a large window facing Liverpool-road. ThEs floor is tiled with J. C. Edwards' Ruabon red tiles. Between the porch and vestibule swing doors with side lights and moulded panels are placed. The upper panels of doors and side lights are filled in with lead lights, and the appearance is very effec- tive. Behind the centre row of benches a screen is ! fixed 8 feet high, having moulded panels under- neath and upper panels glazed with fluted glass. The general arrangement of benches is with three rows of seats from vestibule to communion, with two aisles. Opposite the centre row is fixed the rostrum and communion, whilst on one side of the rostrum are placed the choir seats, which are slightly raised from the floor; on the other side benches are fixed. In front of each row of benches screens are fixed, the upper panels being filled in with diagonal V jointed tongued and ! grooved boards, whilst the lower panels are filled in with perpendicular V jointed boards. The benches are constructed in a substantial Mariner and the seats and seat backs are made with an easy slope and are very comfortable. Every provision is made for book boards and hat rails. The principal feature of the alteration is the new rostrum, a very satisfactory piece of workmanship. The front is divided into five compartments, or panels; at each end is one panel, and between these and the three centre panels wood columns are placed with small moulded and sunk panels on the front face. Each column is finished with moulded and sunk panel on front face, and with moulded base necking and cornice, which are fixed an the front and two sides of the rostrum. The two sides are constructed of small moulded panels filled with figured pitch pine. On the top of the rostrum a book rest is fixed with carved and moulded brackets. The communion in front of the rostrum is of pitch pine base, moulded and splayed with wrought iron standards worked to the architect's special design, and the whole is finished with a neat moulded walnut handrail. Important improvements have also been made in the:decotating of the interior of the building. The ceiling has a cream-coloured ground, and has been divided into panels with borders, and has also enrichments at each angle • the walls are painted a salmon tint, with a dado Of cinnamon colour, sur- mounted by a neat border pattern in colours. The plaster cornices and centre flowers have been re- lieved with blue, and along the two side walls a frieze about twelve inches deep has been worked; it gives a good finish to the decorations. At the East end of the chapel two panels have been formed on the wall above the dado, one bearing the text "Salvation is of the Lord," and the other "I will pay my vows unto the Lord now in the presence of all His people," worked on in gilt letters. The ,panels have ground work finished with stencil pat- tern, and all the windows have an ornamental bor- der running round inside the jambs. All the wood- work has been stained and varnished, and it in all respects does credit to those concerned. The joiners' work, kc., has been carried out by Mr. John Lloyd, of Wellfield-street, Warrington, and the painting and decorating by Mr. Wm. Wareing, of Academy-street, Warrington. The whole of work has been under the superintendence of Mr. Wm. Perry, architect, Sankey-street Chambers, Warrington.

PHILIPOPOLIS, SIINDAY.—The passage in the Imperial irade sanctioning the Turco Bulgarian agreement and rela- ting to the retrocession to Turkey of the villages in the Rhodope district has produced a painful impression here, the villages in question being close to Philipopolis and in- habited by Bulgarians as well as Mussulmans. ASlight disturbance has occurred at Eski Saghra owing to an at- tempt by the authorities to compel some military deserters to re-enter the army. ATe Deunt was sung in all the -churches throughout Eastern Rournelia this morning to celebrate the union of the province with Bulgaria. BELGRADE, MONDAY.—According to a statement made to the King by the Minister of War, the strength of the Servian army now under arms is 158,000 men, which figure com- Ptises the first and second class only. It is stated that the King will to-day sign a ukase ordering the mobilisation of the third class also, in which case the total strength would reach 210,000 men. ATHENS, MONDAY. Greet excitement prevails here in consequence of the receipt of a Constantinople telegram stating that the Turks, under pretext of searching for con- cealed arms and explosives on Greek vessels, have grossly insulted the Greek flag. SERVIAN WAR PREPARATIONS. BELGRADE, WEDNESDAY.—At a Council held this morn- ing under the presidency ef King Milan, the immediate purchase of fifty thousand rifles and twenty-five million cartridges was decided on. The King left at two o'clock this afternoon for Nisch. Two million francs were despa- tched to-day to the War Treasury at that place. ENGLAND'S A PTITII DE. CONSTANTINOPLE, TUESDAY.—Russia's principal objection to the Turco-Bulgarian arrangement has reference to the Personal position created by it for Prince Alexander, Russia being net so much opposed to the union between Bulgaria and Roumelia as to the Piince. The Porte has receivel information from tondon that ' Lord Rosebery will not change the policy pursued by Lord Salisbury in regard to the Balkan States, and that no coun- ter orders have been sent to the commander of the British Mediterranean squadron. The Ottoman Government continues its armaments. Great activity prevails in the arsenals, and Redifs are con- stantly arriving. THE PREPARATIONS FOR WAR IN THE EAST. . ATHENS, TERTRSDAY.-1 Royal decree will be issued to- morrow calling out two more classes of the naval reserve. It is stated that the Greek fleet is now at Vol°, and will re- turn to Salamis next week.

A Central News telegram, dated Paris, Thursday, states : —The French Gcvernrnent have advices to the effect that Bulgaria, in consequence of tne military preparations made by Servia, has no option but to mobolise her army im- mediately, in order to protect her frontier and to pteserve her integrity. FRANCE. THE PROPOSED FRENCH AMNESTY.—THE MURDER OF A PREFECT. PARIS, SATURDAY.—Thedeb.tte on M. Rochefort's bill for granting an amnesty to all political prisoners came on to- day in the Chamber of Deputies. M. de Freycinet declared that he could not agree to the proposal, and appealed to the Chamber to express by its votes its agreement with the views of the Government on the subject. The motion to proceed with the discussion was ultimately rejected by 347 votes against 116, and the bill was therefore lost. As individual, supposod to be the murderer of M. Bar- rivne, Prefect of the Lure. was arreetel yesterday, and con- fronted with some of the einployee of the Western Railway, who are said to have recognised him as the tnysterioue traveller who alighted from the train at the Mantes railway station on the evening of the murder. The Prefecture of Police confirms the arrcst. The mail is named Dubois, and it is stated that some time before the assassination Dubois expressed his intention of seeking revenge against the Prefect. Berg, now undergoing a term of imprisonment for being concerned in dieturbance at apolitical meeting, and by several resolu- :hens, evinced their determination not to grant to the Government the means to defray the current expenses of the State, the Rigsdag was to.day closed by the Government, and a provieional law will shortly b) decreed by the King. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. SWEARING IN OF THE LORD CHANCELLOR.—The House met at 40. Im anticipation of the ceremony of swearing in the new Lord Chancellor, several peeresses, among them Lady Herschel!, had been ushered into the ladies' gallery. Lord Herschel' arrived precisely at four, entering the House by the door to the left at the throne leading from the peers' ante-room, and at once taking his seat on the woolsack. He was then attired in his black robes and the ordinary Chancellor's wig. As soon as he was seated. Earl Granville rose and announced that her Majesty had been graciously pleased to create Sir Farrer Herschell. knight, a peer of the realm by the title of Baron Herschel', of the city of Durham, and to appoint him Lord Chancellor. —Lord Herschel' then retired below the bar, taking with him the seals of office, and shortly afterwards returned in his full robes of scarlet and ermine, being conducted by the Usher of the Black Rod and Garter King•at-Arms (Sir Albert Wood), the Hereditary Earl Marshall of England, the Duke of Bedford, Lord Monson. and Lord Sudeley, all attired in their State robes. After advancing to the throne, on the upper step of which, he knelt while laying his writ of summons on the royal chair, Lord Herschell retired with that document to the clerk's table, where the patent of office and the writ were read by Sir Richard Bethell, the reading clerk. Having next taken the oath of allegiance and subscribed to the peers' roll, the Lord Chancellor was conducted in due form, as on his entrance with the writ to the barons' bench, which is the third below the gangway to the left of the throne. Here he took his seat between Lord Monson and Lord Sudelev. This over the Lord Chan- cellor walked up the floor of the House, taking his seat for a moment on the bench immediately to the left of the woolsack, and then advanced to the woolsack, where, on taking his place as speaker of the House, he was at once congratulated by Lord Granville and Lord Barrington. as representing the two sides of the House, and subsequently by the other peers present.—At 4-15, on the motion of Earl Granville, the House adjourned to the 18th inst.

party was held in Newcastle on Sunday, when the following telegram was received from My. Parnell I strongly ad- vise the Irish electors of Newcastle to give waited support to Mr. Morley's candidature." The Irish party, who claim to be 2,000 strong in Newcastle, have previously strenu- ously opposed Mr. Morley.—Mr. John Morley addressed a crowded meeting on Monday night. Having twitted the Conservatives with firstabandoning and then again avowing a coercion policy for Ireland, he said the Liberals could net allow themselves to be dragged throngh the water- of bit- terness and affliction without an earnest effort to seek a better way. Further coercion might be possible, but the price would be too great. Parliament rendered impotent, Ireland honeycombed with secret societies, midnight drill- ings, passive resistance to taxes and rents, and money diverted from an open league to dynamite. We should be driven by the force of the opinion of this country and of the whole civilised world to try that policy of conciliation which the Government were asking us to try now. Would the electors of Newcastle sanction a policy of civil war? This was the only one which the Tories had to fall back upon. All tbis amply justified their expulsion from office , and the policy which might be expected from their succes- sors. Certain newspapers had urged Newcastle electors to extort from him the Ministry's plan. He was too new a Minister to respond precipitately to this invitation. But he would tell them what he was persuaded they would not do. They would net go to Parliament and say—" We have nothing to offer you except a policy of repression, restric- tion, and coercion." If the Tories called that panacea and patent medicine a policy, he did not believe the Govern- ment had one. There was not a member of the new Ad- ministration, from the highest to the humblest, who was not well aware that they were only beginning a very long and a very arduous journey; but the Prime Minister himself had told the country very plainly the lines on which he and his colleagues had undertaken their enormous task. They should not merely restore superficial order, but build up such a social state that order should be based upon the affections of the people of Ireland. The task was not be- yond the genius of English statesmanship. They would approach the task with consideration for every interest— that of the minority as well as the majority of the people, the landlord as well as the tenant. The day of half-measures was over, and the settlement must be final. MR. HENEAGE.—Mr. Heneage has issued an address to the electors of Grimsby in seeking re-election after accept- ing office as Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, with the charge of the interests of agriculture in which he says :—" I can assure the electors that whilst I desire to see Ireland peaceful and proeperous, I shall feel it my duty to maintain the supremacy of the Crown and the in- tegrity of the Empire," Mn. C. RUSSELL, Q.C.—A meeting in support of the can- didature of Mr. Scoble, Q.C., who is opposing Mr. Charles Russell, Q.O , the new Attorney-General. was held on Sat- urday evening in South Hackney. Mr. Scoble's address was interrupted by singing and shoutin.4, and finally the platform was stormed, and the proceedings closed in great uproar. SIR LYON PLAYFAIE.—Sir Lyon Plavfair, in his address to the electors of South Leeds on seeking re-election on appointment as Vice-President of the Council on Education states that it is unnecessary for him to enlarge upon the subject of education, as his views are well known to the constituency. MARJORIBANYS.—Mr. E. Marjoribanks, in his ad- dress to the electors of Berwickshire, states that her Majesty has appointed him Comptroller of the Household, and Mr. Gladstone has invited him to undertake in connec- tion with that office duties of a Whip to the Liberal party. He therefore appeals to tbe electors for a re- newal of the confidence which they placed in him in Decem- ber last. Mn. CYRIL FLOWER.—At a meeting of the Luton Conser- vative Association, on Saturday, it was decided not to eon- test the seat ageinst Mr. Cyril Flower, whio has been ap- pointed a Junior Lord of of the Treasury. UNOPPOSED RETURNS.—Sir William. Harcourt, the new Chancellor of the Exchequer, was on luesday re-elected for Derby, there being no' other candidate nominated. Mr. Mundella, the President of the Board of Trade, was also re- elected for the Brightside Division of Sheffield. Mr. Chamber- lain was re-elected for Birmingham, on Tuesday, without opposition. Mr. Childers WAS on Tuesday re-elected unop- posed for Edinburgh (Southern Division). Mr. Gladstone was re-elected on Wednesday for Midlothian. He as nominated by. Mr. John Cowan, and seconded by Mr. John Stewart, W.S. There being no other candidate, Mr. Glad- stone was declared to be duly elected. Mr. Trevelyan was returned unopposed for Hawick, on Wednesday.

div.p: THE STATE TiF IRELAND.

On Saturday, at Ltstowel Sessions. five persons were con- victed of riot and assaulting a bailiff at Bawnmore in Janu- ary last, three of them being sentenced to three weeks' im- prisonment, and the other two fined. Trig MocelmarEns.—An extensive raid for arms is re- ported to have taken place on Friday night at a place four miles from Listowel. county Kerry. A party of about 20 mooolighters, half of whom were armed with guns, visited a large number of houses and seized eight guns. They did not meet with any opposition, and they did not offer violence. They were all disguised. On Saturday, at the Liemore Quarter Sessions, Mr. St. John Grant, J.P., sought to eject a tenant for arrears of rent. The bailiff said he was afraid to go to the district to serve the ejectment notice, as a bailiff had been assaulted there before. The Judge stated that he had been informed that the district was a peaceable one, and therefore he had to decline the decree, as the notice had not been properly served. Addressing the Grand Jury at Fermoy Quarter Sessions on Saturday, the Recorder of Cork said the absence, of prosecutions at Quarter Sessions was not to be taken is a fair index that the country was in a state of content, tran- quility, and obedience to the law. It was his duty to con- gratulate them, but he did not think that any honest man could say that the present instance represented the state of the country. GALWAY arcrroN.—The polling for the election of a member for the borough of G alway, rendered necessary by the resignation of Mr.T. P. O'Connor. who had elected to sit for the Scotland Division of Liverpool, took place on Thursday. The result of the poll was as follows :—Captain O'Shea, 93,5; Mr. Lynch. 65. At the recent election the figures were :—O'Connor (N), 1,335; Hallett (C), 1(31; majority, 1.171. Ma. PARNELL.—A coirespondent, signing himself writes to the Pall Mall Gazette giving a genealogical .tree showing that Charles Stuart Parnell, M.P., has a common ancester with Earl Spencer, late Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, and of the Marquis of Hartington. At a meeting at Galway, on Tuesday evening, the Healy-Biggar faction gave way, and Mr. Lynch retired in favour of Captain O'Shea (Mr. Parnell's nominee) for the representation of Galway Borough. NORTH AONAGHAN ELnertox.--The result of the polling in this constituency on Wednesday was declared. on Thurs- day morning. The vacancy was caused by the retirement of Mr. Healy, who bad also been elected for South London- derry, and kas selected the latter constituency. The figures declared on Thursday morning were as follows:—O'Brien (P), 4,032; Hall (C), 2,534 ; majority, 1,498. At the general election the figures were :—T. M. Healy (P), 4,035 ; Sir J. Leslie (C), 2,686; majority, 1,370. STRONG SPEECH BY AN ULSTER M.P. -- Mr. Cobain, M.P., addressing an Orange meeting in Belfast, said the re- sponsible leaders of the Liberal party had deliberately placed themselves in a position in which Mr. Gladstone was the only instrument which was to register Mr. Parnell' seditious wishes. He called upon the people of Ulster to show to the people of England that the Loyalists of Ireland were determined to oppose Home Rule to the death, and that before it would be granted they would meet their foes man to man, and rifle to rifle, and prove to the world that t'ae warlike spirit of their ancestors still animates the Protest- ants of Ireland. MR. GLADSTONE ON THE PAPAL GIFT OF IRELAND TO ENGLAND.—W. Probvn-Nevins writes to The Times :—The enclosed letter from Mr. Gladstone, which I had his permis- sion to publish will probably interest many of your readers at the present time. The volume it refers to is a book called "Ireland and the Holy See and the Middle Ages," published a few years ago by Williams and Norgate. Mr. Gladstone conceives that the Papal gift of Ireland to England accounts in part for the present unhappy state of that country:— "Harley-street, March 3, 1879. My Dear Sir.—l have read your work with much interest, but I have Hot that close historical knowledge of the case which is necessary for the formation of a trustworthy judgement upon it. On one salient point, which you have argued with great ingenuity —namely, the donation of Adrian—l am not en the whole inclined to follow you. It is a question with me whether, as an abnormal and arbitrary proceeding, it did not vitiate, at the fountain head, the relation between English and Irish, and whether it has not been possibly the source of all the perversions by which that relation has been marked. England and Scotland had to fight out their battles, but they fought upon equal terms with the arms which Gad and nature gave them. So the feud worked itself out into unison and a complete harmony. But in Ireland the English fought with an unfair advantage in their hands; they had a kind of pseudo-religious mission, a mission with religious sanctions butetemporal motives. Ido not see how this could work well. Forgive my writing freely in answer to your invitation. You see lam much of an Irishman— perhaps more than you are.—Faithfully yours, W. E. ' GLADSTONE."

A CROWN OF GOLD OR A CORONET OF PEARLS is the privi- lege of few to have, but all cr.n rejoice in having their grey, white, or faded hair restored to its natural colour by ths use of Mrs. B. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer..—Advt. THE RAINFOIID ROICANCE.-14 t the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, judge, John Edwards, the defendant in the recent case known as the " Rainford Romance," was sued by Thomas Pennington, grocer, Peter-street, for £2 83, balance of account for groceries supplied.—Mr Swift appeared for the plaintiff, who for about ten months prior to April, 1881, bad a shoo at Rainford, near to where defendant lived with his supposed wife, Mrs. Westhead. He had gone through a form of mar- riage with her, believing her first husband to be dead. When the plaintiff gave up his shop defendant owed him £B, but the woman he lived with had reduced the amount to £2 Ss. Subsequently, defendant left Mrs Westhead and had not paid up the arrears. It was sought to recover from Ed- wards.—Mr. Swift, for plaintiff, submitted that defendant was liable, but Mr. Riley, who appeared for Edwards, ccm- tended that he had never given Mrs. Weethead permission to get things on credit.—His 11)nour gave a verdict for the plaintiff. A shipping smack s,nk in a gale on Monday, off Storno- way, and tix men on board were drowned. An officer of the Salvatioa Army who was severely injured during a recent disturbance at the entrance to the meeting hall, Paris, died on Saturday. The betrothal is announced of the Princess Marie Amaie d'Orl6tns, eldest daughter of the Comte de Paris, to the Duke of Bragauza, heir apparent to the Portuguese throne.

An explosion of gas occarred on Monday in a three-storey tenement in Johnstone, near Glasgow, seriously injur- ing five persons and causing considerable damage to property. READ R,.. THOMPSON it CO.'S SPEICILL CHRISTMAS OIFNR , let colamn of page 6.—.Advf. A telegram from the Viceroy of India states that Lient. O'Meara, who was wounded severely by dacoits near Pagan, on January 2, is doing well; as also are Simpson, Lloyd, Gwynne, and Carnegy. John Thurston, an agricultural labourer, was executed at Norwich, on Wednesday, for the murder of a fellow-work- man named Henry Springhall. Thurston confessed his , crime, which was prompted by avarice. ' HOME RULE.—A meeting of Englishmen and Scotchmen favourable to the establishment of an Web Parliament was held on Wednesday in the Westminster Palace Hotel, Lon- don, and a resolution was passed in favour of forming a British Home Rule Association to support the Irish people in their demand for self-government. FIGHTING INFECTION.—Dr. W. S. Saunders says :—" I have often limited infectious diseases to the room occupied by the sufferer by nailing a sheet saturated with dilute Condy's Fluid over the doorway." Caution :—Condy's Fluid bears the name of Condy and Mitchell at foolk of every label. Beware of worthless colourable imitations.—Adv. A SHOCKING CRIME.—A beerhouse keeper in White- chapel was indicted Oh Wednesday for tbe. murder of his wife by "setting her on fire" with a paraffin lamp. The jury found a verdict of manslaughter only, but the judge marked his sense of the enormity of the crime by sending the prisoner to penal servitude for ten years. GREAT FIRE IN GLASGOW.—On Saturday night, a fire occurred in the flour mills belonging to the Incorporation of Bakers, Glasgow. The once four-story mill was ren- dered a smouldering heap of ruins. Several firemen had some very narrow escapes. The mill was stocked with flour. I and the damage is estimated at between £25,000 and £30,000. Public Analysts have submitted CADBURY'S COCOA to-close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining anu nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— Advt. DEATH SENrENcs.—At Glamorganshire assizes, held at Cardiff, on Tuesday Tnomas Nash, labourer, was sentenced to death for the murder of his daughter, by pushing her over Swansea pier last December. At the same court a young man, named Laney, was sentenced to 18 months' imprison- ment for the manslaughter of his father, at Cardiff, on November lit. THE COTTON TRADE.—The operative cotton spinners in Oldham and the surrounding district have decided by an overwhelming majority not to accept the further reduction of 5 per cent. in wages proposed by the employers and recommended by the Operatives' Council. A ballot was taken on Saturday. and of the 2,733 members of the Asso- ciation who voted 2,541 declared against the reduction. WELSH FARMERS ON THE MOVE.—At a meeting of far- mers held at Penycae, Ruabon, it was resolved "That this meeting, feeling the present critical condition of agriculture in the Principality, strongly recommends the formation of a union of Welsh farmers, with a view of impressing upon the Legislature the necessity of a Land Bill for Wales." It was also decided to petition the landlords for a substantial reduction of rents. DEATH Or ME RECORDER OF LIVERPOOL—The death of the Recorder of Liverpool, Mr. John Bridge Aspinall, took place in London, on Saturday. Mr. Aspinall, who was in his 67th year, had been in failing health for some time, and his death was not altogether unexpected. He was the eldest son of the Rev. James Aspinall, M.A., rector of Althorpe, Lincolnshire, and was the brother of Mr. Clarke Aspinall, coroner of Liverpool. —Advt. 1 THR "CAT."—At Liverpool Assizes, en Wednesday, three young men, nam d Finnigan, Toner, and Cavanagh, were convicted of stealing a bag containing £BO from Mr. M. Huddleston in Smithdown-road, and using considerable violence towards him. Mr. Justice Day sentenced the pri- soners—Finnigan to nine. Cavanagh to twelve, and Toner to eighteen months in gaol, and also ordered them to receive respectively 15, 20, and 40 lashes with the "cat." ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE.—At Birmingham, OH Saturday, an old man named Meere, living in a court in Pershore-street, cut the throat of a middle-aged . woman, named Annie Jones, in the house of a neighbour where she lodged, and afterwards inflicted a fatal wound on himself. The woman lies in a precarious condition. Meere was a widower, and, notwithstanding his advanced age, being nearly 70, the crime is supposed to have been committed through jealousy. THE MURDER OF A CATTLE DEALER.—At the Glamor- ganshire Assizes, held in Cardiff on Wednesday, David Roberts, aged 30, a labourer, residing near Cowbridge, was canyicted of the murder of a cattle dealer named David Thomas, whom he also robbed of a large sum of money. He was sentenced to death. Roberts confessed to the crime, and exonerated his father, whe was also charged with the murder, father and son having been last seen in the com- pany of the murdered man Thomas. Irrarimsrma DISCOVEHY.—In the coarse of some exca- vations in King's Field, near Faversham, a collection of old coins and other valuable relics was discovered. Among the articles are two large gold pendants, one of which is set with garnets, two large silver brooches, also set with gar- nets ; a buckle set with three stones, a quantity of beads, , quartz, a ring, and a sword. Similar discoveries have been made in the same field on previous occasions during excavations. DEATH OF MIES WILLIM.—Miss WilliM, aunt of the late Bishop of Manchester, died on Saturday afternoon at Bishop's Court. Higher Broughton. She was born in the year 1789. and was consequently in her 97th year. Until a week age she had been in perfectly goad health, mentally and bodily, but without the slightest warning she was then seized with paralysis, and remained unconscious until her death. She was sister to the late Bishop's mother, and since Dr. Fraser's arrival in Manchester about 15 years ago she had resided at Bishop's Court. " ERNEST LINWOO D."
