COLLISION ow THE HIGHLAND RAILWAY.—AbOUI mid- night on Saturday, a Perth goods train collided with an Inverness goods train at Diva Station, on th,e El,ghland Railway. The Perth train had a snow plough and two engines attached. One of the drivers was hurled from his engine, and was picked up on the platform of tne station. He is not expected to recover. The driver of the Inverness train had his ant broken and his nose terribly cut. His fireman had his collar bone broken, while the other fireman was dangerously wounded on the head. There was a seri- ous destruction of plant.

CONGREGATIONALISM.—The year-book of the Congrega- tional denomination just issued shows the number of churches and mission stations in England and Wales is 4.218, against 4.181 in the statement of last year. Adding to this 166 stations reported by individual churches, but not included in county returns' there is a total given of 4,384, as against 4,347 list year. The number of sittings provided last year was 1,568,357. The total for this year is 1.582,409. In Scotland there are 103 churches, in Ireland 29, and in the islands of the British seas 12. The number of churches, branch churches, and missions in Great Britain, Ireland, and the islands of the British seas is 4,528. FOR ROUGH, RED, OR CHAPPED SHIN there is nothing equal to •. ANOTIIF,R STRIKE PROBABLE AT OLDILAY.—The mem- bers of the Oldham Operative Cotton Spinners and Twine& Association voted by ballot on Saturday in their several districts on the question of accepting another 5 per cent. redaction of wages proposed by the Masters' Association. The papers were counted the same night at the Spinners' Offices, Rock-street, when it was found there were only 192 in favour of the reduction and 2,541 against. Only 55 per cent. of the members voted. The month's notice given by the Mssters' Committee to the Operatives' Council expires to-day (Saturday), and if the employers are determined to carry out their proposition the operatives will have to re. ceive individual notice on the next pay day. EXECUTION OF TEE BARROW MURDEBER.--.00 Tuesday morning, Joseph Baines, fish hawker, who murdered his wife at Barrow on Christmas Day, by stabbing her several times in the breast with a large butchers' knife, was executed., within the walls of Lancaster Castle. The executioner— Berry, of Bradford—arrived from Carlisle on Monday after- noon, and attended to the necessary preparations. At a quarter to eight the bell of the Parish Church began to toll. Ten minutes afterward Baines was pinioned by Berry, and presently a procession entered the yard where the gallows was erected. Baines stood firmly whilst the noose was being :adjusted, and without any delay Berry completed his task. The drop fell as the gaol clock was striking eight. Death was instantanms. SAMMY WANDERERS V. COCKEIEDGE ROVERS.—Played on the ground of the former. After a close game the Rovers won by two tries to one disputed.
ADMISTIAW v. NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS.—This match was played on Satterday.and resulted in a drawn game, the for- mer ecering eight minor points to one.

WARRINGTON ROVERS T. PENKETH.—PIayed 012 Satur- day, on the ground of the latter, and resulted in a victory for the Rovers. Score :—Rovers : One goal, one try and three minor points, to one minor point. The tries were ob- tained by Allen, an the same player kicked the goal. • WARRINGTON ROVERS (2ND TEAM) T. LATCHFORD GYMNASIUM.—PIayeeI on the ground of the former, on Sat- urday, and resulted in a win for the Rovers by one try and five minor points to four minor points. •A disputed try was got by the Gymnasium, from which they kicked a goal under protest. The referee, however, refused to allow the try, 80 the Rovers won as above stated RUNOORN RECREATION 2ND T. TUERILOOK IST.—This match was played on the ground of the latter club on Sat- urday. The score at the finish was Tuebrook one goal one minor, Recreation two tries and five minors. The three-. quarters for Tuebrook played a splendid game. and for the visitors Carr, Abrams, Crompton, and PendleburV played well at back, and all the forwards played in good form.

FRODSHAM ROVERS V. CAMDEN SOAP WORKS (A. TRAM). —This match was played at Frodsham on Saturday, and an evenly-contested game ended in a victory for Frodsham by one try and seven minor points to three minor points. For Frodsham all the backs played a very nice game, their run- ning and passing being well done. The forwards played well to a man. For Runcorn, Tickle and Brazendala at back, and Hewitt and Christy forwards, played the best. The try for Frodsham was got by Darlington. Rogers' attempt at goal, though a good one, failed. LATCHFORD GYMNASIUM v. WARRINGTON ROVERS.— Played on the gronnd of the Rovers, and after a good game ended in a victory for Latchford by one goal and four minors to one try and three minors. The passing of Latchford was very good, especially the half backs. For the winners Newton (captain), Praeger, Parry, and Massey played well, as did A. Jones, Randalls, and Hand for the losers. Team : Latchford : Full back, Gardiner; three•quarters, Lake, Praeger, and Massey; half backs, Parry and Ashton; forwards, Newton (captain), Ayres, Dainteth, Cliffe, Locker, Dagnall, Hatton, Wilcox, and Sherratt _

RUNCORN SECOND TEAM v. EDGEHILL FIRST.—The re- turn fixture between these teams was played at Runcorn on Saturday, and although the day was cold a good number of persons gathered to see the second team play, who are be- coming strong .favourites with the Runcorn people, their smart running and loose play being much admired. After playing 60 minutes Runcorn won by one goal, two tries, eight minor points, to Edgehill one touchdown.Rafile, Antrobus, and Orme got the tries. The following were the teams :—Edgehill : Hilton, kack ; Deacon, Lamble, and S Lamble, three-quarter backs; A Lamble and Hall, half batks ; Barnes, Findlay, Blackburn, Ellison, Morley, Gaston, Bickerton, Haskeyne, and Strettle, forwards. Runcorn Second: Booth, back; H Cawley, W Riley, and T Davies. three-quarter backs; G Whittry and W Antrobus, half backs; J Gittins (captain), E Andrews, A Raflh, J Hoftland, T Cox, E Orme, J B Clarke, Snowball, and Dolan, for- wards.

RUNCORN RECREATION v. LEIGH (A TEam).—The above clubs met on Saturday to play off their fixture on the Re- creation ground, the visitors turning up with a short team, but found substitutes. Hayes started the leather, which was confined to neutral ground for a short time, when the Recreation forwards dribbled into the Leigh 25. Whinyates got a clear run in near the touch line, the place kick failing. On ckange of ends play was mostly in the Leigh quarters, the Recreation gettjng over the line several times. The points were, however, disputed. At call of time the home team were victors by one try, four minor points, to nil. Teams :—Recreation: T Charleston, back; Whinyates, Green. and James Clare, three-quarter hacks; H Pendlebury and W Woodward, half backs; G Yarwood, Pennington, Fox, Green, Hailwoo,l, Acton, Stubbs, Haves, and Bate, forwards. Leigh : D. Holt, back ; W. Wishlade, C. Rowland, and T. Pendlebury, three-quarter backs; H Tickle and S Taylor, half backs; F Prescott, H Corbett, J Murphy, J Bowden, J Darlington, J Maddock, J Graham, and P Hindley, forwards. SANKEY v. THELWALL.—This match was played on Saturday on the ground of the former. The visiting cap- tain won the toss, and J. Barton set the ball in motion about 3-30. Evans returned, but Jefferson got the bail, and was making tracks for the visitors' line when he was collared, and passed to Ash urst. The same player kicked into the visitors 26, and J. Barton following up succeeded in eluding the opposing backs, and scored a try. The same player took the place, but failed to improve upon it. After the drop out the visitors forwards rushed the ball into the home 25, The home team sent the leather back to the half way flag, when half time was called, the score being Sankey one try and one miner to Thelwall nil. After the interval the visitors' captain kicked off, and J. Barton returned, forcing Bate to kick the ball dead. After the drop out a scrimmage was formed, and the home forwards dribbled over the line, Highly completing the try. Jefferson kicked for the goal, but failed. Evans, for Thelwall, put in very strong runs, but was collared. Here the whistle sounded for time, leaving bankey the winners by two tries (Barton and Highly), two minors to nil. All the home team played well. W'rrarrEs v. SALFORD.—These teams met on Saturday, on ISaturday, on the ground of the latter, in the presence of a Ilarge number of spectators. At 3-30 Farrell started the ball for the visitors, and there being no return, the first scrim- mage ensued inside the home territory, but Slater eventu- ally relieved to the centre, and shortly afterwards the same player made a bid for goal, but a touchdown resulted. The home team had slightly the best of the game, and when half-time was called had scored two minor points to nil. Attiwell restarted for the home team, and the players from I the chemical town soon scored a touchdown, but this was 'neutralised when Jones, gained a try for Salford. Slater took the place kick, but failed, the score at the close being Salford one try and two minors to Widnes one minor. 'Teams :_Salford: J. Allen, back; V. J. Slater, C. Buxton, and A. N. Other, three-quarter backs; H. Clegg, A. Stott, H. Eagles, A. Attiwell, S. Williama, J. Shaw, J. P. Jones, J. Jackson, and H. Williamson, forwards. Widnes: A. Pen- nington, back; J. W. Smith, T. Barnes, and S. Bingham, three-qaarter backs; J. E. Farrell and T. Bidyard, half- backs ; A. Brown, T Fogg, J. Perrin, P. Corns, J. ,Goulden, J. Hardman, J. Gandy, J. Bingham, and Smith, forwards.

WAYERTREE v. ST. HELBNS. This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday before a large num- ber of spectators. The greund was very hard in cense- quence of the frost. A start was made by the Saints kick- leg off with the wind, and at the call ef half-time the score was :—St. Helens one try and two minors ; Wavertree two minors. On restarting the game became very fast, and Pen- nington, breaking away, passed to James, who secured another try for the Saints, which Has'an failed to improve upon. Shortly afterwards. M'Greachin, picking up in Wa- :eertree's 25, ran smartly into the Saints' territory, and wis- ing to P. Morton, the latter dropped a magnificent goal for the visitors. Wavertree were the victors by one goal and five minors to St. Helens two tries and three minors James, Finney, and Halton were best forward and Penning- ton behind for the home team. The ab3ve clubs meet again i in the first round of the West Lancashire and Border Towns I Challenge Cap. Teams :—St. Helens—T. Rogers, back; A. Tickle, H. Pennington, and W. Hasledon, three-quarter backs; E. Foreman and H. Varley, half-backs; T. Finney, , J. Halton, A.Borthwick, W. James. R. Twist, 1. Penning- , ton, J. Basnett, L. Kershaw, and W. Arnold, forwards. Wavertree—F. Hoyle, hack; T. Woodward, P. Morton, and S Gyte, three-quarter backs; A. M'Greachin and W. Peters, half-backs; T. Greenfield, G. Newton, G. Grierson, J. Morton. W. Baker, E. Bezant, J. M. Spedding, T. Single- ton, and W. Lawton Goodman, forwards. RUNCORN T. BLACYLEY.—Runcorn first team journeyed to Blacklev on Saturday to play the return match with a weakieam, being without lioffiand, Dean, Barnes, Johnson, and Joule. They nevertheless won by one goal, one try, and three minor points to three minor points. The frost had been very severe, and the ground was very hard. W Wright kicked off, and Key returned, when Lewis and Clarke dribbled to Blackley twenty-five. H Hughes here put in a splendid run, which was supplemented by another excellent dodgy run by Speakman, who ran in and secured toe first try, but the kick at goal failed. On the drop out Radford ran well down the field, but Lunt overhauled him and brought him down, and Wainwright brought the play to midfield. W Wright Broady, and ti Hughes kept up the attack, which ended in W Hughes securing a try, from which Lewis kicked a goal. During the second half the game was more even, nothing but minor points being regis- tered, Key for Blacisley and Woods for Runcorn having plenty of work, which they did well. Teams :—Runcorn: ' T Woods, back; Lunt, H C Speakman, and G Wainwright, three-quarter backs; H Hughes (captain) and II Andrews, half backs; W Wright, W H Broady, W Hughes, J Lewis. J Gatley, J Clarke, H Wright, W Dunbavand. and W Jenes, forwards. Blackley W Key, full back; R Smeth- urst, H Bailey, and J Ward, three-quarter back; Muirhead and Wilkinson, half backs; Ashton, Evanson, Hickey, Har- greaves, T Shaw, E Smethurst, White, Thom, and E Rad- 'Ord, forwards.

off their tie in the third round of the cup competition. At l the call of time the sc,re stood—Wigan 4 goals, Haydook 2. Wigan had three goals dtsa;lowed. Toe Wigan forwards Iplayed a good passing game, bat the backs hardly played up to form. Laing pbryed wtll in g eel. For Haydock IRalphs, Lowe, and Stirrup (back) played best. Haydock : Goal, Ralphs ; backs, Lowe atd Stirrup; half backs, ( Brown, Hughes, and Swain ; forwards, PornfrrA (cap. ' tam), Haseldsn, Ellis, Sha.p, and Kenyon. Umpire, Mr. Greenall. Mr. G. S. Lamont, of Liverpool, officiated as referee.

NEWTON COMMON RANGERS V. BILLINGE HORNETS (IsT.)—These two teams met for the first time on the ground of the latter on Saturday. Dale kicked off for the ; visitors up the incline, bat tbe home team were soon in pos- session of the leather and scored. Birchall added a second. The second half was very even but the home team proved Ivictorious by three goals to none. Dale, Newton, and Rigby i played well for the visitors. Teams—Hornets : U. Ashcroft, goal ; H. Williams (captain) and Waterworth, backs; Atherton, Boardman, and Bold. half-backs ; Birched', J. I Bid, W. T. Bold, James Ashton, and T. Atherton, for- wards. Rangers—T. Harrison, goal ; J. Dorrycott (cap- tain) and J. Worsley, backs ; Marsh, Newton, and ' Singleton, half-backs; T. Dale, R. Sephton, T. Waterman, A. Morris, and R. Rigby forwards. I WIGAN CuP TIE. —EA R LESTO WN WANDERERS T. GOL- BORNS —These teams met in the third round of the compe- tition for the Wigan and District Association Challenge Cup on the ground of the Wanderers, at Newton Common, on Saturday afternoon. The attendance of spectators was very large, and from the start to the finish the excitement was intense. There were one or two "fights" during the afternoon. For some minutes the visitors were represented by only ten men, but during that period they pressed the borne team. The turf was bard and slippery, but notwith- standing this a great amount of work was put in on both sides, and, after a well-fought though rough game, victory rested with the Golborne eleven by two goals to one. Teams :—Earlestown Wanderers: T. Champion. goal; H. Selby and J. Mather, backs; R. Johnson, J. Lowe, and W. Allison, half backs; T. Kirkham and A. Allen, right wing; T. Thompson, centre; J. Shaw and W. Shaw, left wing. Golborne : W. Jenkinson, goal; Clare and G. Clegg, backs; J. Clarke, J. Waddington, and W. Unsworth, half-backs; S. Morris and S. Cottam, right wing; J. Flynn, centre; T. Kay and J. Lowe, left wing. EARLESTOWN V. HAYDOCX (LATE TEMPERANCE).—The meeting of these clubs on the ground of the first-named, the 2vlesnes, Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon, excited some attention, hut owing to the oth-r attractions there was not very large attendance. There was a considerable number of spectators present, however, who were rewarded by witness- ing a hard-fought and evenly-contested game. Unfortu- nately the home club failed to muster its full strength, the absentees being Appleton (goal-keeper), Rich, Edison, Dag- nall (captain), and ogr4en. Their places were filled by second team men, but before half-time Roberts sustained a serious inja y, and during the whole of the second half, with the exception of a few minutes, the Earlestonians played only ten men, Roberts havieg retired. A hard-fought game resulted in a victory for Haydock by two goals to one. The following were the teams :—Earlestown: T. Failclough, goal; R. Green and J. Green. backs; J. Whalley, R. Bowker, and J. Duxbury, half-backs; Simms and Siddelev, left wing; T. Roberts, centre; Turner and liolcroft, right wing. Hay- dock : Taylor, goal; Hatton and Baines, full backs; Allen, Carter. and S. Harrison, half-backs; Blackley and G. Moran, right wing; M. Arnold, centre; P. Ttlist and J. Har- rison, left wing.

NOTES BY THE WAY. A grandly-contested game was the result of the meeting between England and Ireland at Dublin on Saturday, and it took the wearers of the Rose all their time to defeat their opponents by one try. rl,t by any means a decisive victory. The Irish team are to be congratulated upon the gallant fight they made of it.. _ _ .

-Batley managed to account for Halifax defeating them by two goals to one try. Widnes journeyed to Salford, but had to submit to defeat, though only by one try. Many of the principal matches were cancelled on account of the frost.

It is gratifying to know that the dispute between Scot- land and England has been settled, though conditionally. Scotland acknowledges the match in dispute a victory for England, on the consideration that an international board be now formed, to which all future disputes in international matches will be referred.

div.head: BRIDGE WATER NAVIGATION
div.p: THE BRIDGE WATER NAVIGATION
COMPANY, LIMITED.

The annual report of the directors of the above company shows the receipts for the past year t have been £292,708 OS 7d, and the expenditure £233.519 14s, leaving a net profit of £59,088 6i 7d. After the payment of interest on loans and bonds, which absorbed £9,698 3s, and increasing the river risks fund to £lO,OOO by the addition of £165 Is 3d, there remained a sum of £49,225 2s 4d, which, with a balance from last year of £3 480 5s lid and a transfer from the reserve funds of £13282 Gs flu, naade the amount avail- able for dividend £65,987 14s 01. The directors recom- mend that this amount shall be dealt with as follows :—The payment of a dividend of 5 per cent on the preference shares, £15,000; the payment of a dividend of 8 per cent on the ordinary shares, £28,000 (free of income tax); and the payment of a bonus on the ordinary shares at 4s per share (free of income tax), £20,000; leaving a balance of £2.987 14s 9d to be carried forward to next year. Interim dividends at the rate of 5 per cent per annum haying been paid, amounting to £7,500 on the pre- ference shares and £8,750 on the ordinary shares, the further sum of £7,500 en the preference, and £39.250 on the ordinary shares will he divided. The sum of £13,282 6s 6d, which is transterred from the re- serve fund for distribution, the report explains, is an amount I credited to tne revenue account hitherto apportioned to the reserve fund, which, in view of the sale of the undertaking to the Ship Canal Company, is not now required, and may therefore be distributed to the shaeeholders in the form of a bonus. Tae sum of £20,000 required to be deposited by the Ship Canal Company will, the directors state they are I informed, be paid in compliance with the provisions of the Act. A sum of £40.000, the balance of the purchase' price of lands bought from the company in 1872, had been paid to their account by the Cheshire Lices Committee, and this payment had enabled the directors to reduce their bonded debt by £3s.6oo—namely, from £200,000 to £164,400. A sum, £l3 954 12s Ild, had been expended in works for the improvement in the Mersey and Irwell N tvie,ation, in accor- dance with a reselution passed December 17, 1884. Of this sum £12.000 had been charged to capital, and £1,954 12s lid to maintenance, but for the present the works had been sus- pended. The repnrt adds that, in the Act for the con- struction of the Ship Canal, clauses had by agreement been inserted for the preservation of their interests, and the substance of the agreement had been communicated , to the shareholders in a circular letter dated September 4, 11885.

div.head: QUARTERLY RETURN OF BIRTHS AND DEATHS.
div.p: THE QUARTERLY RETURN OF BIRTHS AND DEATHS.

The quarterly return of births and deaths has just been issued, and it shows that low rates are the order of the day. The birth rate for the past quarter is taken at 31'9, whereas the mean of the ten previous corresponding periods is 337. The present rate is said to be the lowest for a fourth quarter since the year 1855. It is in the highest degree satisfactory to find that the death rate for the pest quarter is as low as 185, the mean of ten years being 203. This is the lewest December rate since registration a,as established in 1837. The death rate for the urban population is 19 7, and that of the rural popu- lation is said to be 16.7, the former being 2 4 and the letter 0 9 below the average of ten years. Measles slightly passed the average rate, but whooping cough agreed closely with it. Scarlet fever was a little under one-third the average rate, and °Vet forms of fever happened at one-half the aver- age rate. Small-pox happened, or was tatal, at the rate of one-third of the average of ten years. The mean temperatureeof the air, as recorded at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich. was 42-5 in the past quarter, and was thus one degree below the average of 114 years, taking corresponding periods in all cases. The rain measured 737 inches in the three months, or 737 tons per acre; and this is reported as being a quarter of an inch under the average of 70 years. The marriage rate is still very low, namely, 143 for the past September quarter, or nearly 1 per 1,000 under the maan of ten years. The Registrar General states that only on three occasions in nearly fifty years has so low a rate been regarded for the third quarter of the year. It is reported that 49,598 emigrants embarked in the past quarter, including 27,981 English, 4,471 Scotch, and 8,058 Irish, English and Irish emigration aaving declined as com- pared with the fourth quarter of 1884, and that of Scotch people having increased. div.head: E EXAMLN ER. SATURDAY, FEBRUARY la, 1886
div.p: E EXAMLN ER. SATURDAY, FEBRUARY la, 1886

MR. JOHN MORLEY, the new Chief Secre- tary for Ireland, is just now the observed of all observers, from the fact that heghas some- what unexpectedly been called to an exceed- ingly difficult post at an exceedingly difficult time. Since he first entered Parliament— some three years ago—he has made progress in political estimation, as the finances of the country were at one time said to do—by leaps and bounds;. and yet it strikes people as extraordinary that a politician who has never previously held office of any kind, should not only be admitted to the Cabinet, but asked to take a post which, 4t this junc- ture, must be regarded as of the first impor- tance. It is extraordinary; but the answer is that Mr. JOHN MORLEY is an extraordinary man. If he has not been, until recently, prominently before the public, he has not been without influence upon public men and public affairs. As a writer, he has long been looked up to by men to whom the people are in the habit of looking up. If he has not before been in office, he has been in power : if he has not before been in the Cabinet, he has had a good deal to do with shaping Cabinet Councils. . Mr. GLADSTONE has long recog- nised his power and his worth, and having decided to make yet another attempt to, bring peace to Ireland, he knows tltat, he cannot have a more able and resolute, and at the same time a more observant and sympathetic lieutenant than the new Irish Secretary. Mr. MORLEY'S views on Ireland have not been de- termined by regard for the Irish vote; they are the outcome of years of study_of thelrish ques- tion. His has been as the Voice of one cry- in.g in the wilderness. Now he is being heard in populous places. There are few men who write for the press who, looking 'back upon leading articles written years ago, do not feel that they have at times changed somewhat on particular questions with the change of events. Mr. MORLEY is one of the few who, so far as Ireland is concerned, can afford to have what he wrote years ago compared wit!,-1 what he is saying to-day. The " Pall Mall Gazette," of which Mr. MORLEY WS at one time editor, has just issued an "extra," giving quotations from his leaders ; and those who compare passages

div.p: written half a dozen years ago with tha speech which he delivered in Newcastle late as Monday last will be struck with the_ clearness, consistency, and the firm grasp ot the subject which they everywhere reveal. The new Irish Secretary is not a doctrinaire who is going to Ireland believing he holds in his hand an instantaneous cure for all the ills of the body politic. He knows that Ireland is, to use his own words, "the tomb of political reputations ;" and he " cannot understand how anybody can be very san- guine about Ireland except for perorating ptir- poses at Westminster.' This was said before he became a member of Parliament. but it expresses the opinion he still holds, for he never hesita,es to admit the enormous difficulties which beset the Irish problem however it is approached. But, what then .• Are we to turn aside—are we to shirk the problem because it is a difficult one? He Will have none of that. He thinks, to vary a well' known couplet : 'Tis better to have tried and failed, Than never to have tried at all.

Speaking during his election campaign three years since, Mr. MORLEY said :- "There had been too much nursing and coddling in Ireland, and they had much better give her a chance of doing things for her- self." The Irish Secretor.), is amongst those who believe that power alone can teach re- sponsibility, and that the duty of the British Parliament is, by experiment upon experi- ment, to find out the safest and best way of letting the Irish people govern themselves. The present system of government is bad; it is admitted to be bad by politicians of all shades. The other day Lord COWPER, who preceded Lord SPENCER as Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, went so far as to say it was " a hateful system." Mr MORLEY takes the same view; he is going to Ireland as an ofic,r under the system, but we may, be quite sure that it is with the object of seeing its evils and its weaknesses, to the end that he may aid in putting something better in its place. The Tories believe that this should be done, but they are not the men to do it. They can express themselves through Lord CARNARVON as feeling that it is desirable.to " extricate ourselves from the miserable habit of exceptional legislation ;" but with them, as events have shown, it is one thing to desire and another to do. When% difficulties arise they have nothing better to fall back upon than the habit which they admit is miserable—in other words; coercion. Mr. MoRLsY regards coercion as a bad weapon, as a weapon to be thrown. aside because it has so oiten failed: This is not because he would be slack in dealing with disorder, but because he thinks that the • ordinary law, rigorously applied where there is need for it, is likely to be sufficient, pro- vided it is accompanied with obviously honest efforts to remedy the wrongs of a nation. Writing on the occasion of the arrest of Mr- PA iiNELL, he said—"lf great social disorder has spread over a counLry, from whatever cause, every Government, exactly because it is a Government, is bound to do its utmost to restore order temporarily even while it is re- moving the more permanent causes which have made disorder national and justifiable. This is not the language of a man who , would fear to strike if striking became neces- sary; but rather of one who regards striking so "a miserable habit," and would seek to put down disturbance by removing the causes of discontent. Concluding his speech at New- castle, on Monday, Mr. MORLEY said :

There will be,.or ought to be, no violence. I, at any rate, am not going to forget that I have written.i a hundred times—a thousand times—that justice - is the sovereign and supreme virtue in all relations, . whether between.man and man or State and State. (Cheers.) That justice, the commonwealth, the - strength of the realm, will be the guiding star of. our policy. I hope, and I believe, that when .that. policy is explained with chapter and verse it will have the support of the people of this country.. I believe they will give to it a fair and a patient consideration.. I believe that the attempts to kindle • the fires-of race prejudice, of religious bigotry, and to fill the land. with political panic—l believe that the attempt,. however assiduously fomented-will fail, because I hare faith, which history has-taught me—l have faith in the courage and the judgment of the people-of this land. (Cheers.) These are the words of a just and brave man who is wishful to do well for his kind. With such a Chief Secretary as Mr. JoHN MORLEY,. and with such a Prime Minister as Mr. GLAD— STONE., we may still hope to see the dawn of a: better day for Ireland.

THE demonstration of the unemployed, im London, on Monday, terminating as it did: in a riotous attack upon West -end clubs anl shops, will have served the questionable end; of the Social Democratic Federation in bring- ing their doctrines into prominent notice: When people are hungry and angry, they are not in the best frame of mind for reasoning upon economic laws, and the socialists,, knowing this, took advantage of the situationi to advocate force as a remedy. They werr not the prime movers in the demonstration,; I and it is not too much to assert that if, thky had kept off the scene the large crowd,w.ould have probably dispersed. But when.spe.akars like Mr. BURNS and Mr. HYNDMAN asl .. a mob to "look at the clubs,"and talk about " sacking bakers' shops,"they nee Al nin be surprised if a riot. ensues. After the miscthief had been done, these worthies- did, however, affect to express regret at " what ha 3 oc- curred in St. Jam'es's and 't)iccadilly," Force, it was suegested, would have to be resorted to ; but " the leaders of: the Social: Demo- rats were not the men to call upon unarmed men to run risks of collisions,with•pollice and soldiery." lionsense off. this kind is under- stood to mean that the Social Democrats are preparing :For the Revolution abet which. they so frequently talk.; but in this instance ite is not unlikely that th.e• leadc-rs were anariouS4. rather to escape the consepaereces of their,- • violent speeches. Nothing, asit seems to us, can, be more reprehensible that for educat:ed man, like Mr. HYNDMAN and Mr: BURNS to incite thoughtless and ignorant workmen to break. the law, they themselves :keeping in the.: backgreound whilst the mischief is being' done. But these Socialist leaders wilL, find', that they cannot so eaei,ily escape responsi- bilhy. ; and they may possibly take another ,- view of the situation if they come to be, locked up along with some of their victims-. We have every sympathy with tile unem- ployed, and trust everything will be done that can be. done to mitigate thu evils of their situation. It is a pity that they should be made the prey of political intriguers— whether social Democrats or Fair Traders, for between rickety stools of this kind they are sure to come to the ground. The Fair Traders, it is true, did not preach Revolu- tion, but they certainly did not mend matters by trying to turn the demonstration to their , account. There is a large body of men in the metropolis who are out of work, and who cannot get work, and there can be no ques- tion that those who have means would help them—once assured that hinds provided will not be abused. "FAIR Trade," the organ of the Protec- tionists, has been vainly attempting to take Colonel MCCORQUODALE to task because he Pertinently referred to the Americans as be- mg unable, on account of Protection, to Compete with the English in ship-building. Re is now told to look out. "There is," we are informed, "a movement going on in the States which bids fair to remove all difficul- ties, and with the aid of subsidies such as .those which are paid to steamers by Eng- land for carrying the mails, we may in a very short time behold the American mercantile marine resuming its old position in the Atlantic trade." Fair Trade is always just ' going to do something ; it never gets it done. But how absurd to suppose that the f traction which is paid for carrying the mails is going to revolutionise the shipping trade Of the United States l "The aid of sub- sidies" may, of course, mean something 111°re ; but we do not suppose Brother Jonathan is such a fool as to take a new departure in ship-building at the very mo- 'pent when freights are at a very low point, and when profits are nil Capital cannot be made to flow uphill, not even with a Fair Trade push-behind in the shape of a subsidy. Let it be assumed, however, I Or the sake of argument, that a subsidy IS ! .desirable in the *interest of the American shiPping trade, what is the inference? If F.dir Traders at home have any idea of con- sistncy they would require the English , Government to protect English shipping ! merchants by topping the Yankees with a Still higher subsidy. Thus, if the Governments Were sufficiently foolish, there would bea war of i ,subsidies which would result, not in mprov- Pig the shipping trade of either country, but In taxing the millions of both countries in Order to enrich the comparatively few who are interested in the shipping trade. Money apent in that way would be worse than thrown away, for the coddling of trade would cause builders to rely upon the Stare rather than upon their skill, industry and energy. The end of the matter would be that we should have worse ships at a higher price, whilst England and America would be poorer to the extent of their subsidies. All this is plain ienough to all but the Fair Trader, who some- now cannot see an inch before his nose.

RESTORATION OF FARNWORTH PARISH CHUacH.—As our readers are well aware, there is a scheme on foot for the extensive restoration of the ancient edifice, Farnworth Pariah Church • and it is pleasing to record that the appeal for donations is having a generous response. The estimate for carrying out the work is £1,680, but it is probable that the total cost will be £2,000. Already £l.OOO has been re- ceived. Amongst the subscribers are the Legh estate office, which contributes £250; Mr. Tipping, Bold Hall, £100; King's College, Cambridge, £5O; J. T. Swain and T. Ban- ner Newton, of Liverpool, each £2O; Mr. Turton, Liver- pool, £25 ; J. Banner Newton; £2O; Mrs. Beck, £3O; Rev. George Bond, £3O. There are also a unesber of smaller do- nations. Each of the churchwardens have contributed £25. The Bishop of Liverpool has promised £2O. It is expected that £350 will be required for an organ, and towards this Mr. Riding has given £5O. Mr. T. Moss Horsfall has offered a stained glass window for the east end of the , church, which is equal to a donation of £250. BURNED TO DEATH , AT Winerss.—On Monday evening Win. Henry Atkinson, seven years of age, who lives with his parents at 13, Beement-street, was burned to death. The boy, his sister, aged five years, and another child were left in the house whilst the mother went to visit her parents in John-street, a few hundred yards distant. Immediately she had departed, the boy commenced to play, with the are, and quickly his clothing was in flames. 'His agonised screams brought in a boy' named Lee, who resides in the next house. He ran immediately to Dr. McDonnell's sur- gery, and Mr. Richards was quickly on the spot and applied remedies. Aul. the boy's clothing with the exception of the wrist bands and neck band of the shirt were burned from his body, and his chest was fearfully iajured. He died the same night. On Wednesday Mr. W. T. Husband held the in- quest at the Maintop Hotel, Mersev-road. It appeared that the mother was only absent from the house ten minutes, and that she had been engaeed ministering to a sick child at her mother's house. A verdict of "Accidental death " was recorded. Nottniwiow DIVISION LIBERAL COUNCIL.—A Meeting of the Liberal Council for the Northwich Division takes place to-day at Northwich. Runcorn possesses 97 representa- tives. The following resolutiom will he submitted for ap- proval :—" That this meeting of the General Council of the Liberal Association representative of the Northwich Divi- sion. congratulates the Right Hon. William Ewan Glad- stone on his return to the high position of Prime Miuiste. of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, exr presses its iniabated and unlimited confidence in him as th- leader of the Liberal party, and entertains tin fullest asssee TanCe that he will introduce a measure which, while main- taining the union between the two countries asd the integ- rity of the empire, will meet all reasonable demands of on- fellow subjects in Ireland." A second resolution to ber proposed reads " That this meeting of the General Council of the Liberal Association for the Northwich Parliamentary Division places on record its satisfaction at the result of the recent election in the return of a Liberal member with such a large majority, a result which has vindicated the passing of the Franchise and Redistribution Acts, and is a just recognition of the Liberal principles held in this part of Cheshire." CONCERT AT WIDNES.—A concert under the auspices of the Wesleyan Gospel Temperance Society, which has its home in Oakland-street School, took place on Tuesday even- ing. Tee room was crowded with an appreciative audience, and the chair was occupied by Mr. W. W. Gossage. The programme consisted of sslections from Handel's Messiah. , elozert's twelfth Mass, and the Cantata Belshazzar, which were rendered by a choir of about 40 voices, ably assistsd by a string band. The choir performed its work in a style which reflected credit upon themselves and upon Mr. W. Whitby, the conductor. The items calling for special mention were " And the glory of the Lord," Gloria," and "Magnify, glorify." Miss Daintith sang " Froas out homes " and " Fading away " with care and intelligent of Runcorn, cep. tributed " Taphtewle,csitateihonor,dap,d Miss Wright, and "The old arm chair" with pathos and power, and she secured much applause. The (wet Lovely piece " was given by Miss Jones and Miss i Wright The recitative. "Comfort ye my people " was contributed by Mr. Holford, of Runcorn, with considerable success. A clarionette solo by Mr. Ryan was well, re- : ceived, and Messrs. F. H. and A. D. Whitby were recallsd for the pianoforte duet "Canary birds." Mr. A. D. Whitby aleo skilfully executed a pianoforte solo entitled "Sabbath eveni•tig chimes." Mr. J. Helper sang the recitation " Be. hold I tell von a mystery and the air The trumpet shall sound." A capital programme was brought to a close y the Hallelujah Chorus.—A vote of thanks was accorded re Mr. Gossage, on the tuition of Mr. W. Hartland, sscon- ,.ded by the Rev. R. Burden ; and a similar complitatot was r paid to the vocalists and conductor.

WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART SCHOOLS.—Mitjar Hill, of ;the Royal Engineers, has this week conducted the annual in- spection -of the Widnes Science and Art Schnol. -.The, ap- paratus and registers were examined, and rheAnspector expressed. his entire satisfaction with the arrangements made by the committee for carrying on the ulass,s. Williams and oeveral other boys Were t 2 wlaying in Coolmondeley-street on Thuredav afternoon, the 4th inst. Green, 24, Bridge- street, Warrington. Price 6d.—Advt. - THE NEW HIGI SHERIFF OF LANCASHIRE.—It 15 believed that Sir A. B. Walker, Bart., has been se-, lected by her Majesty.the gueen as the High Sheriff of Lancashire for the next year, in succession to Mr. James Williamson, of the Ityelands, Skerton, near Lancaster. Sir Andrew, it is understood,' will begin. his duties as High Sheriff at the spring assizes. • ALMANAC SHOW AT CROFT. On Saturday, the first annual almanac show was held at the house of Mr. Isaac Ilaines, the Horse Shoe Inn Croft, when there was the large number Of 154 entries, which consisted of some fine specimens of almanacs, which had been tastefully arranged round the large baga- telle room. The judges were Messrs. F. W. Ball. T. Battersby, and J. *Roberts. Several prizes were awarded. THE HOME IRON TRADE.—There is no improve- merit in the English iron. -market. Pig-iron is as , dull as ever, and fears are expressed that the con- I tinuedlarge 'output will make matters still worse.) The Glasgow warrant market has been rather more active this week, but the tone is very dull, with a general impression that prices will probably go lower, as iron can be bought from some makers at under the market price of warrants. Closing quo- tations of warrants on Wednesday were 398 5d cash and 39s 6d a month with buyers, sellers asking a halfpenny a ton more.—lron. • AN AFFECTED WARRINGTONIA.N.—At -the St: Helens Town Hall on Friday,Martin' Lyon, who said he came from Warrington, a big fellow, was charged with • drunkenness, and When in the doCk he commenced to cry like a child, wiping his .eyes with a scarf he had, round his neck. The Chairman: You don't want us to believe that you are crying for this, do you? (Prisoner continued to cry.) I think we ought to give you ss. extra for this cry- ing. If you are so much affected don't get drunk again,that is all. You must pay ss. and costs, orgo for seven days, Prisoner was then retxoved. DEATH FROM BURNING AT CA.DISHE.A.DOD Wednesday, at the Railway Inn, Cadishead, an in- quest was held by Mr. F. Price. on the body of Emily Warburton, aged four years and eight months, whose parents reside at No. 3, Warburton Buildings, Cadishead. The evidence showed that -the mother, *after lighting the fire on Sunday morning, went to the pump for some water. In 'the meantime the child came down stairs, and got on the fender. The night dress caught fire, and the child was burned in a frightful manner, death ensuing on the, Tilesda,y 'morning. The jury brought in a verdict of "Acci- dental death." - , THE SHIP CANAL.—Opposition is to be offered in the House of Commons to the bill promoted by the Manchester Ship Canal Company with the view of enabling that body to pay to• the shareholders in- terest out of capital. Unless this power be conferred it will, the promoters say, be almost impossible to carry out the scheme from which so nany practical' advantages are expected to. result. In this connec- tion it may also be • mentioned that the Corporation of Salford are applying for Parliamentsry sanction to subscribe £250,000 towards the company's autho- rised cfipithl. of £10,000;000. It is not thought that the opposition to .the payment Of •interest, out of capital has much chance of being successful. . A PRESTON.BROOK MILK DISPUTE.—At the Liver-. pool County Court, on Tuesday, 'before his Hontiitr, Judge 'Thompson, the case of Basnett v.' Warbtirton was heard. It was an action brought by' Daniel Basnett, farmer, Preston Brook, against Peter War- burton, milk dealer, of Liverpool, to recover the sum of £lO 16s Hid, -alleged balance of account due to him. The plaintiff Was represented by Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor, Warrington, and Mr. Woodburn, barrister, instructed by Mr. Harold Lumb, solicitor, Liverpool, appeared for the defendant. The defence was a set .off and counter claim for overcharges in plaintiff's milk accounts rendered to defendant, amounting to upwards of £3O. When the case was called on for hearing an arrangement was come to' between the parties. The jury, were discharged and judgment was entered for the defendant on the claim; and for £l5, without costs, on the counter claim. ' A. BRIDEGROOM'S' RECEPTION IN CHESHIRE.— ReDently an appeal •waB mhde to a London magis- trate by a prepessessing young woman,' who com- plained that herbusband, had deserted her the day after their'wedding on the, extraordinary plea that .he.ha,d been.drUgge.d and then taken' to the church to be married. Natually the girl's story excited much commiseration, and it is also perfectly true. The drugged bridegroom is a native of Cuddingtoin, Cheshire. Lately he 'became acquainted with ,11 'young woman living at a country house as a lady's ; maid. He made love to her, they became engaged, and when he left for London the neighbours under- stood it was for the purpose of being married, lie has just returned to Cheshire, but his romantic story preceded him, and his reception was very lively. Several attempts have been made to duck him in a pond. The village has become very hot for him, the feminine residents being especially desirous of an interview. A FAITHLESS BRIDEGROOM.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, before Lieutenant-Colonel W. W. Pilkington and Alderman Harrison, Sarah Ann Jackson, a young woman living at 11, York-* street, St. Helens, sought to have an affiliation order made upon Charles Fishwick, of Oswestry. Mr. T. Garner (from the office of Messrs. J. 0. and W. Swift) appeared for the applicant, and Mr. 11. L. Riley defended.—Mr. Garner stated that plaintiff lived as domestic servant with defendant's parents

COUNTY FOOTBALL PLAYERS IN RUNCORN.—Messrs. H. C. Speakman (three quarter), W. Hughes, and J. Lewis, of the Runcorn team, are chosen to play to-day with Cheshire against Yorkshire. WIDNES C.E.T S.—A meeting of the members took place on Thursday night in Waterloo-road School. The Rev. C. Rumfitt presided, and an excellent programme of songs, recitatione, &c., was gone through. HALTON BURIAL BOARD. —At a meeting of this Board, on Tuesday, a letter was read from the Home Department ap- proving of the site of the proposed cemetery, and its con- struction will shortly be commeraceltl. ST. PAUL'S CHURCH INSTITUTE, WIDNES —,The Rev. J. Wright Williams, vicar, has been appointed president of this society for the ensuing year; vice-presidents: The Rev. A. A. P. Hamilton Wilson and C. Rumfitt, Mr. H. Wade Deacon and tne churchwardens. • Mr. W. Lowe is secretary, and Mr. T. Hughes, treasurer. RUNCORN STARR-BOVirEN:TT BUILDING SOCIETY.—An ap• propriation in connection with the ttrst seciety took place on Monday evening, in Mr. Handlev's (the secretary's office). Mr. F. L. Scott presided, and Mr. John Darlineon, who is employed at the Weston Ceemical Works, was thel successful member. He is entitled to the loan of £2OO free of interest. The next appropriation takes place on the Bth March. SOUP DINNERS AT RUNCORN.—Last week end the com- mittee of the Runcorn Y.M.C.A. continued, their good work of providing the poor people of the town witn sub- stantial soup dinners. The response, however, to their appeal for support has not been by any means encouraging. and the work cannot be carried on unless more aid is forth- coming. Yesterday 200 poor persons were provided with soup and bread at the expense of Mr. F. A. Lake, presi- dent of the Y.M.C.A. The distribution, as usual, took plece at the Mersey Mission-room. WIDNES DRAMATIC SOCIETY.—This recently-formed so- ciety has more than fulfilled the hopes and anticipa• ions of its founders, and now numbers nearly 100 membere. Many of the members are poeßessed of histrionic abilities of no mean order, and they netke their first essey in public on Friday and Saturday evenings 'next week, with Byron's capital comedy " Our boys." Professional talent will have no place in the performance, but the cast is nevertheless a strong one. Already between 200 and 300 seats have been reserved. Further particulars will be found in our adver- tisement columns. GAME TRESPASS NEAR WIDNES.—At the Woolton Petty Sessions, on Friday, Thomas Wright. labourer, Crontomaud Richard Beswick, joiner, Ditton, were summoned by Peter Saint, gamekeeper in the employment of the Earl of Sef- ton, for having trespass,d on land belonging to Lord Sefton while illegally in pursuit of game. About a week ago-the complainant encountered the two defendants, in company with another mau who had since left the elistrict, and on the latter he found a hare which had just been killed. Su- perintendent Barker said that Wright was well-known as, a poacher. The Bench imposed a fine of 40s and costs on each defendant. THEFT BY A WIDNES SCHOOL BOY —At Widnes Police Court, on Monday; James Sinmyt. 13 years of age. whoee parents reside in Appleton Village, was charged with steal- ing a coat, the property of John Rigby, 10 years of awe, of Irwell Brow. The two boys attended the Appleton school en Thursday, the 28th January, and Rigby placed his coat in the cloakroom. At the conclueion of school in the after- noon the coat could not be found. On Saturday last the prisoner went to Mrs Jameson, pawnbroker, Ann-street West, stated that his name was James Smith, ;hat he lived at 4, Pleasant-street, and that his mother had sent him to pledge the coat for 3s 6d, as she wanted money to pay the rent. Mrs Jameson ultimately lent 2e 6.1 on the article, and the prisoner was apprehended by the police.—The pri- soner who denied that he hat stolen the coat, was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod. A RUNCORN BOIT OWNER FlNED.—Richard Abel, Twat owner, was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions on Mon- day, charged with keeping a trap without a license—Mr. Abel pleaded guilty.—Mr. Heal prosecuted on behalf of the Inland Revenue authorities, and stated that on the 4,t) December Mr. Speechley, an officer of the Inland Revenue, saw the defendant.and his wife in a carriage driving. A declaration was sent to Mr. Abel by post on the same day, and after waiting some time, Mr. Speechley called for an ex- planation. Mr. Abel said they had had the carriage for some time, but they had only used it for a mouth" No license was paid for, and the declaration was not returned. Mr. Abel had. stated to Mr. Heal that he had only used the trap for electoral purposes. This was not true, as there was no election on the 4th December.—Mr. Aid said he only got the trap in December, and as he bad not owned a con- veyance before, he was qeite ignorant that a license was re- quired.—A fine of 40e and costs, Os 01, was imposed. ROSBERY FROM A RUNCORN BUILDER.—Robert Peacock, described as a loafer, was brought before Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. J. Handley, at Runmwn Police Court on Saturday, charged with stealing One plane, two screwdrivere, two chisels, and three bits, value 17e, from the shop of Mr. Hy. White, builder, Greenwav-road, Runcorn, and belonging to Thomas Bradshaw and Israel Heyes. Heyes and Bradshaw left the tools safe on the evening of the 4th inst. Next morning they were missed. Subsequently Police-clmk Wal. lace found that the tools bad been sold to Mrs. Rooney, Regent-street, for is; and apprehended Peacock—John Morrieslandlord of the Commercial Hotel, Bridge-street, stated that about ten o'clock on the night in question prisoner said "You would laugh if you saw me going up High-street to linutsford to-rnorrowf'--The Bench committed the prisoner , for a month, and Mrs. Rooney was told she had had a very narrow escape from being charged with acting as a pawn- broker without a license, and she was warned to be more cautious in future. THE ATLAS CHEMICAL COMPANY, LiMITED.—The 11th annual ordinary general meeting of this company was held' in the large room of the Central Hotel, Widnes, on Tues- day, the chairman of the company, Alderman Thos. Cook, J.P., ex-mayor of St. Helens, presiding. There was a full attendance of directors, and a large body of shareholders was present. In moving the adoption of the directors' re- port and accounts, the chairman said the market had been very unfavourable, the prices of some chemical products being lower at present than they had been known before The directors had given great attention to economy in manufacturing, they had, therefore, been able to reduce the liabilities of the company and ta make an important addi- tion to the reserve fund, and they believed that by careful manufacture they would not only succeed in meeting the markets but be able to lay before the next meetings balance sheet which would be satisfactoi yto the shareholders. The retiring directors, Mr. P. Bancroft and Mr. R. Cook, were unanimously re-elected, and Messrs. Stead, Taylor, and Stead were re-appointed auditors to the company. VEGETARIAN LECTURE AT WIDNES.-0O Monday even- ing, a large audience -assembled in the Malins Temperance Mil to hear Mr. Chapman, of the Vegetarian Society. Manchester, deliver a lecture on vegetarian cookery. The chair was occupied by Mr. E. Passev, who delivered a short address, as did also Mr. George, the secretary of the War- rington branch of the Vegetarian Society. The lecture was held under the auspices of the Hope of Appleton Ledge, 1.0.G.T., the choir' of which opened the proceedings by sing- ing "The World's Jubilee" in good style. The subject ef the lecture was, " How to make a Christmas pudding with- out suet ; and steak and onions without meat ;" and Mr. Chapman had intended to cook the pudding kefore the eyes of the audience, but an insufficient gas supply caused that portion of the proceedings to be abandoned. The lecturer apologised for the disappointment, and as a solatium he cooked some apple fritters, and distributed them to the peo- ple. The subject of vegetables versus flesh meat diets was handled in a first-rate manner. A vote of thanks was passed to the speakers and chairman, on the motion of Mr. T. Ray, seconded by Mr. S. Owens, at the close of the meeting. . . .

THE RUNCORN SOAP COMPANY. The twentieth annual ordinary general meeting of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, Limited, took place os Wednesday morning, at the Law Association Rooms, Liver- pool. Mr. A. P. Fletcher, the chairman of the directorate, presiding. The report ef the directors for the past year, which was taken as read, showed that the gross profits (in- cluding transfer fees) amounted to £21,090 4s 7d, from which must be deducted office expenses, salaries, commis- sions, rates, income tax, audit, atc., £3,635 88 lid ; and bank commissions and balance of trade-discounts, £487 4s, or a total of £4,122 12e 11d, leaving the profits at £l6 967 Hs Bd. The balance from last year aninueted to £5,278 16, 3d ; less directors's fees, £l,OOO ; total, £4,278 16s 3d; leaving an available balance of £21,246 Is 11d. it was pro- posed to appropriate this as follows :—lnterim dividend of lOs per skare paid in August. Z 6,000 ; preposed dividend of 13e pr share, £7,800 ; amount to be written off nitrous I towers and was plant, £2,205 7s 4d; and balance carried forward, £5,241 Os 7d; total, £21,246 7s 11d. During the past year there had been a steady decline in alkalies, clos- ing with prices lower than ever recorded, with the excep- tion of bleaching powder, which, although perticipating to some extent in the depression, had been maintaioed at a remunerative figure, owing to the agreement among manu- facturers to reduce the productioe, and had contributed to the foregoing statement. The gas works at Runcorn and Weston, :deo the towers erected for econornisine nittate of soda, had given very satisfactory results, and it was pro- posed to write off £2.205 Is 4d, liquidating the balance of the original costs. Taking all things into account the directors did not think that a dividend of 5 per cent. could be considered unsatisfactory. Besides this they hut a balance to carry forward, and nal written off the balance of the original cost of the nitrous towers arid gasworks. Tali LONDON POpONING MYSTERY.—Further investiga- tion of the London poisoning mystery has resulted in the arrest of Mrs. Bartlett, widow of the deceased. On Thurs- day, the Rev. Dyson, Wesleyan minister, gave evidence at consicerable length. He admitted having bought chloro- form for Mrs. Bartlett, and having made a false statPrnant to a chemist who supplied him with the drug. Mrs. .13,irt... lett had not given him satisfactory explanations as to what, bad become of the chloroform, and bad on one occasion stiA to him tbat if he did not incriminate.her she would not in- Criminate him. It bad not been arranged that she should become his wife, but he had expectations of that char- acter.

At the meeting of the Widnes Local Huard, on Tuesday, the report of the Medical Officer of Health (Dr. Cooper) for 1885 was submitted. It stated that "during this year the number of deaths registered in the township of Widnes was 449, and calculating on a population of 27,000 persons to the middle of 1885, this gives a death rate of 18.62 per thousand of population, as against 22.18 per thousand, the death rate for 1884: Zyrnotics : The deaths from the seven principal zymotic diseases numbered only 25., or 092 per thousand, showing a still greater decrease on the previ- ous year, when the fatal cases of zymotic diseases num- bered 124, or 4'67 per thousand. Those for 1885 were as follows :--f-Scarlatina, 2; measles, 2; whooping cough, 1; diphtheria, 1; diarrhoea, 13; typhus fever, 1 ; typhoid fever, 5; total, 25. SALE OF A. CHURCH LIVING—By 9ublic auction the ad- vowson of St. Catherine's, Liverpool, was sold on Thu-.day at the Law Association-rooms. Bidding commenced at £lOO, and the advowson was knocked down at £1,150, the pur- chaser being Mr. H. D. Horsfell, the builder and patron of St Aenfs's, Ullet-road, and sen of Mr. florsfall, the builder of St. Margaret's, Prince's-road. The right of next presen- tation to the living thus passes into the hands of a gentle- man whose desire will be to make a complete transformation in the service of the church, and who will very probably secure an opportunity of carrying out his views by coming to some arrangement by which the present incumbent wilt quit Liverpool. RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR ST. HELENS —About Ave o'clock on Thursday afternoon, while a coal train was pro- ceeding along the Rainford single-line eection of the Lon- don and North-Western Railway, the draw-bar of one of the waggons broke, six trucks left the line and were upset, and twenty or thirty tons of coal were strewn about in all directions. It appears that the train was comnosed of thirty-five waggons, principally coal, coming from Sk el., intsridAle to Widnes. When it reached Rookery Station, , running at a high rate of speed, the tyre of the twenty-fifth waggon suddenlybroke, and it and the following fire wag- gons kit the rails and were overturned. One waggon was placed on the line aeain, but the other tee. with large masses of coal, were thrown into the adjoining field. The line was completely blocked. As son as possible, Mr. Poole, district traffic inspec.or, went to the scene of the accident with a gang of syerey or eighty men and the cranes. Fires were made, and the men sat to i work, but it was late in the night before the line was cleared. i In the meantime, traffic was worked by a train running from R:itiford Junction to the block, and another train taking the passengers, who had to walk past the debris to St. Helens. IL special train was then run to Widnes, but the passengers for Liverpool and Manchester joined the ordinary trains at St. Helens. It was half-past ten o'clock before the men were able to get the line in working order and return to St. Helens.

A Local, SLINDER CASE.—At the Liverpool Assizes on Monday a local action for slander, Critchley v. Brownbill, was heard. The plaintiff is the wife of an agricultural labourer, residing at Sutton, St. Helens, and the action was brought against the defendant, who had accused her of having committed adultery with another man. The defend- ant lodged with plaintiff and her husband, and was related to them by marriage. The alleged slander was uttered m the presence of the husband of the plaintiff and the wife of the man who is accused of having committed the adultery, and in consequence of this Critchley had left his wife.—Mr. Walton, who appeared for the plaintiff, said that the plain- tiff did not ask for vindictive damages, but only sought to clear her character. After evidence had been called for the plaintiff, Mr. Shea said that he had just been instructed, and asked that the case might be adjourned. The defendant denied having uttered the slander.—Mr. Walton pointed, out that the case was actually closed, the defendant not !laving put in an appearance.—iiis Lordship declined to ad- journ the case, and directed the jury to find for the plain- tiff with nominal damages, as it could not be said that any !pedal damages had been sustained by the plaintiff.—The jury then awarded £l5 damages to the plaintiff.—lt is stated that the action was not expected to be reached as soon as it was, and the counsel originally instructed by the defend- ant (not Mr. Shea) had, without informing the solicitor, Lone over to Manchester to hold a brief at the sitting of the Palatine Chancery Court. He had not returned when the action was called, and the judge expressed his sympathy with the defendant in the unfortunate position in which he was placed.

WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB. A special general meeting of the members of this club was held at the White Bull Inn, Horseinarket-stree.t, on Wednesday evening, when the chair was occupied by Mr. John Marsh. There was a good attendance of members. —The hon. sec. (Mr. John L. Stelfox) read a letter that had been received from Mr. J. Barclay, M.P.. in reply to a resolution passed at a committee meeting of the club, thank- ing that gentleman for his recent action on the agricultural question in moving an amendment to the Address. It was dated January 28, 1888, and WAS as follows :—'4 I thank the committee of the Warrington Farmers' Club very cordially for the resolution you were good enough to send me approv- ing of my action in the House of Comtnons on the Agricul- tural question on Monday last. It is a great encouragement to find the farmers throughout the country taking an active interest in Parliament proceedings affecting them, especi- ally in the face of the apathy, not to use a stronger term, of their representatives. Farmers may feel assured that un• less they bestir themselves they will get no redrese, and if they act with determination that they will soon find their wants attended to. If many Liberal (why?) members had not wilfully absented themselves the Government would have been -defeated on my amendment, and in coneequence any succeeding Government would have been bound to deal with the agricultural question. It will not be long before there is another general election, and farmers by the division of Monday night, have had the opportunity of learning who are their friends and opponents. As to a bill embodying agricultural reform I intend to introduce a measure dealing with the sub- ject, but I would respectfully advise farmers not to commit themselves to any bill. I have made proposals in my measure [applicable generally to Scotland] but unwilling candidates and opponents will find objections in the details of any bill and so find an excuse for not supporting it. Be&des, there may be other and better means of carrying on what is wanted than I propose. Tile farmers ought to I agree on what. is wanted and leave to Parliament the beet means of giving effect Co their wishes. According to my views the farmers want (1) a fair rent fixed by an impartial and competent authority [the best authority or means is a matter for discussion, possibly the best would be arbiters, or rather umpires, selected by the representacive local govern- ment boards about to be constituted]; (2) freedom of calti- vation and security of tenure, either at a fixed rent or periodically revised by the same authorities; t 3) free sale of the tenants' interest in his holding (compensation is un- satisfactory) ; the value of the amount can- not be ascertained with certainty, and the ex- pense in the the case of small holdings is at least very formidable. It is no use getting any one of these wants without the other. What was his security of tenure if the landlord could arbitwily raise the rent, and you cannot have security unless you have right to sell the improved value of the holding when you have to leave it, by death or I otherwise. Nothing less than the three requirements will benefit farmers, and time and trouble spent in trying for less is wasted. These principles must he applied to exist- ing laws. Our Ecotch farmers under existing laws are being ruined, and they are becoming desperate. At the next [general election there will probably be not a single land- lord returned for the north of Scotland. Engliela farmers and labourers are beginning to follow the example. I have no hope in this Parliament of any agricultural reform, and the great satisfaction is it will probably not last long. The best course for such a club as yours is to take up a decided position, and adop: principles which all farmers can under- stand and recognise would be for their benefit. The Farmers' Alliance has paltered with the subject, endeavouring to conciliate both parties. Tne consequence is that the asso- ciation is hated by the landlords, and it has not secured the confidence or support of the farmers. I hope you will ex- cuse my offering you this advice. lam anxious to effect the reforms I have indicated. Great progress has been made. Little objection and no argument were offered to my propo- sitions in the base on Monday last. The feeling in the country is strong enough to make the land representatives cautions. The next step is to make them complaisant, and if the farmers would only be still bolder and more deter- mined, that step is not far off."—lt was resolved to record the receipt of the letter on the minutes.—lt was stated that a member of the club, Mr. Davies, of Bollington, had written to Mr. Brooks, M.P. for the Altrincham Division, regarding his vote on the same subject, and the reply of that gentleman was read. In it Mr. Brooks said that he had voted against the amendment because he did not think that the interests of farme‘s would Lave been advanced thereby ; it was, be said, a measure brought for- ward in the interests of party, and not of farmers. It was not a proposal binding upon the House, but simply an amendment to the Address.—Mr. JaaN MARSH, the presi- dent, then read an able paper on " Manures," for which he received the cordial thanks of the club.---A discussion fol- lowed the reading of the paper.—There was no other busi- ness.
ORIENTAL PALACE BAZAAR. On Thursday afternoon, the Mayor of Warrington 'Alderman Harrison) opened a bazaar in the Drill
Hall, WaiTington, in aid of the Catholic schools of

the town. Of bazaars, as of many other things, it can truly be said that the old order has given place to the new. A few years since all that was required for a bazaar were a fairly capacious room and stalls

unadorned, except with the multifarious wares with which they were stocked. But the promoters of a bazaar of any pretensions who neglected scenic and other accessories would now be regarded as retrogressive in their methods. The Catholics of Warrington in this their first bazaar have not laid

themselves open to any charge of this kind, for on the present occasion the design of the bazaar is both novel and effective. It is that of an "Oriental Palace Bazaar," and the work of arrangement and decoration in connection with it has been executed by Mr. G. M. Bridges, of Lynn. This work has been done so skilfully that the Drill Hall presents a very lively representation of an eastern bazaar. To add to the impression at the end of the hall, opposite the door, an orches- tra is arranged amidst several lofty arching pillars, and the room is hung with Chinese lanterns. The dresses of the ladies who have charge of the stalls, many of which have something of the oriental fashion about them, also adds to the effect. The stalls which are eight in number are aranged in various parts of the room. The League Hall stall and that of Mrs. Price flank each side of the main entrance, and then on either side of the hall are the stalls of Mrs. and Miss Cavanagh; Mrs. Fox and Mrs. Taylor; Mrs. Hind and Mrs. Unsworth ; Mrs. and Misses Dolan; Mrs. and the Misses Fleming (refreshments) ; and of the confraternity and chil- dren of Mary. There is a more than usually large dis- play of articles, many of which are of great value. In the centre of the room is exhibited the splendid gift of Mr. E. Connor, Sankey-street, which consists of a very valuable tandem drac, completely equipped in every respect. Amongst ''the more notable ar- ticles on the various stalls were a large musical box, models of churches and other buildings, oil paint- ings. portraits of local priests and dignitaries of the church , and a number of very beautiful work-tables, and screens. The orchestra is occupied by Mr. T. J. Down's large and well-trained band of local instru- mentalists, which rendered in an admirable manner numerous selections of music. At the time of the opening of the bazaar there was a numerous attend- ance. Amongst those present, in addition to the Mayor and Mayoress were the Right Rev. Abbot O'Gorman (President General of the English Bene- dictines), Fathers, Sumner, Murphy, Brown, Fish- wick, Snow, Cummins, 3lorrall, Rigby, Dolan, Beauvoisin, B. Murphy (all 0.5.8.), and Fathers Thompson and Lennon; Alderman Webster, Mrs. Broadbent, Miss Atkinson, Mrs. John White, Dr. and Mrs. Fox, Mrs. Reynolds, Councillor and Mrs. J. Pierpoint, Councillor and Mrs. Francomb, Councillor and Mrs. Fleming, Mr. E. Connor, Mr. R. I. Wynne Jones, &c. Mr. Dewhurst, the trageslian, was also present, and after the opening ceremony gave in a powerful manner a recitation, for which he was warmly applauded. The Rev. Father BROWN said it was his pleasing duty to ask their worthy Mayor if he would kindly declare the bazaar open. He might tell them that it was at very great inconvenience, and he was afraid almost at a personal risk, that the Mayor was amongst them at all that day, for he had been and was still suffering from a very severe cold. (Hear, hear.) The Mayor, however, said he was deter- mined to come and declare their bazaar open, and this showed the interest he took in all good works got up in their town. (Applause.) They had had many examples of that on the different occasions on which the Mayor had BO kindly consented to preside at the various festivities got up In the town, and again on that occasion he had been glad to come amongst them to declare the bazaar open. (Applause.) The MAYOR, on rising to declare the bazaar epee, was greeted with applause. He said: Ladies and gentlemen,— Bazaars and sales of work have become such a necessity of the time, that we can hardly glance either at a metropolitan or provincial newspaper without seeing some announcement either of bazaars that have been held or that are about to be held in aid of some philanthropic work, such as the building of churches and schools, homes for the sick and needy, irc., and I don't regard it as a reproach to Warring- ton that we have also had a good many during the last year or twg, and for the most part very successful ones too; and I think l may say with which almost every religious denomi- nation in the town has been distinctly connected except one, for my memory does not enable me to recollect that the Catholic portion of the community have ever had a bazaar in Warrington. That fact alone will, I hope, stimu- late us all, of every religious creed in the town, to come forward and help to make this bazaar a pre-eminently suc- cessful one, for I think I need hardly say that the object which has called it into existence is one of the highest that can engage the attention and excite the Christian sympa- thies of mankind, the education, both temporal and spiritual, of these who will in a few short years become the men and women of our own, as well as of other towns. (Applause.) The Catholics of Warrington are doing a great work, for they require school accommodation for 1,200 children, whilst a new infant school is urgently required, and extensive alterations to meet the growing necessities of the time. And when we consider, what I hope shall be for- given for saying, that the Catholics of Warrington are the very poorest of all religious bodies in the town, the well- to-do portion, very few in number, must have made great personal sacrifices to have accomplished so much among themselves for the good of mankind. (Applause.) I think I need hardly tell anyone I see before the now in this room teat instruction and educetioa are an imperative necessity of the age ; and there is a great differ- ence between instruction and education, let me say, yet they are indispensable to each other. You may teach a person to read and write, and to communicate his thoughts to his fellow man, and this may be called instruction but what avails it if they are unfit to judge between the books containing error anel those containing truth ? Instruction may provide the means of putting into practice that which is taught by education, but it can never take the place of education. (Hear, hear.) The first developes in us the knowledge of our duties, but education gives us the capac- ity of achieving them, and the two combined really mean education based on religious tuition, t'ne education of moral feeling, duty and principle. The foundation of our national sorrows lies in a diseased moral condition of the people, and education, based on religious teaching, and properly in- terpreted, is the readiest means of veining access to the moral netare of the class3s it is so desirable to elevate. It will give to the mind more correct apprehensions of Providence, and enlarge the boundaries of their moral being, while it ennobles, and digni- fies, and makes them of worth to themselves. Though there are people to be found who say they don't think it necessity that the working.man should be educated inasmuch as it will not cause him to do his work more effi- ciently and that in some respects the ignorant is more desirable than the educated working-man, because education mades men feel above their position, and renders them dis- contented, I venture to say the very opposite is the truth, as is proved every day, by the thousands of well-educated people that leave England for distant lands, and are conten- ted to labour at any occupation, no matter bow humble it may be. Therefore, I venture to say that such objections may be relegated to the limbo of exploded fallacies. The best educated men, if they are sober, capable and indus- trious, are always the best paid, because they work with more intelligence than the ignorant, uneducated man, end it is important and gratifying to know that the Church of England and the Catholics stand on the same platform, shoulder to shoulder, in condemnation of any system of national education not combined with religious teaching of some kind. (Applause.) The MAYOR then declared the bazaar open. The Right Rev. Dr. O'Goaeoese proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor for having opened the bazaar. He (Dr. O'Gorman) had roily been in the town a couple of hours, and yet in that time he had been able to ascertain that their Mayor was always ready to do any work when the benefit of the poor and needy was concerned, and he could see from the generous sacrifice that the Mayor had made to be there that day he was ready to do anything in that line. (Ap- plause.) Councillor FLEMING seconded the proposal last made, and the vote of thanks was accorded with acclamation. The Rev, Father FM:MICK then moved a vote of thanks to the ladies and others who had given their services in con- nection with the bazaar. That, he said, was the first bazaar the Catholics had held in Warrington, and it had been looked forward to with great interest by themselves, and also by many belonging to other denominations. Many who did not belong to their denomination had come forward generously and given them their aid in every way, and they had no idea at all till they begun to azrange for that bazaar that they had so many friends out of their own denomina- tion, and they felt grateful to them. (Hear, hear.) They had, he continued, been obliged to raise new schools, and now had a considerable debt to wipe off. They had had to build a new infant school which alone cost £5OO, and they had also had to make alterations to their other schools, so too meth money could not be raised for them. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Father Fishwick then referred to Mr. Connor's handsome gift of the drag, to the services of Mr. Downes and his band, and to Mr. Dewhurst's offer to recite at the opening of the bazaar. He concluded by again mov- ing a vote of thanks to the persons referred to. Dr. Fox seconded the proposal, which was also accorded with acclamation.

Prisoner was wearing a nre, suit of clothes, the same he was wearing in eeurt.—en°,_ prisoner, who pleaded not guilty, was remanded until rr' day.
