div.head: SHOCKING NEGLECT OF A CHILD.
div.p: SHOCKING NEGLECT OF A CHILD.

At Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, Harriet and James McKean, man and wife, were charged with neglect- ing to provide their child, aged five months, with food and medical aid.—Mr. Shearer, relieving officer, appeared to prosecute. and said that he visited the hease of prisoner's on the previous Friday and found there three children. The house was in a dirty condition and the children were cry- ing. In the front place there was no furnitisre at all, and in the kitchen there were two chairs and an old table. Up- stairs there was only a small bed. The child had been ex- amined by the doctor, who would say in what state he found it. Its weight was 71b3. 3z3., and it was almost like a skeleton; although, when bern it was a very fine child.—Mr. liarboarne, relieving officer, said that the female prisoner came to the office at the Workhouse, and asked admission for herself and three children. She said that her husband had turned her out, and that he was in the habit of drinking and keeping bad company. She also said that her husband earned /13 a week and gave her 303 each week, and that she and the children had had nothing to eat for three days. He gave her an order for admission 'to the House. The seine night he went to her house in I Warbarton-street and found no one there. Next morning hiwattention was called to the child at the Workhouse, as it was very thin and emaciated, and almost like a skeleton. The husband came and took the two children away, and the female prisoner took her discharge the seine day. In the even- ing he and Mr. Shearer visited the house and found it to be almost destitute of furniture and in a dirty condition. There was some bread on the table.—Margaret Bibby, Warburton- street, said that she sew the female prisoner frequently. She (Mrs. McKean) liked a drop of drink, the same as any other woman. (Laughter.) She had seen the child, and it was very dirty.—Another woman said that she had seen Mrs. McKean drunk several times, with the baby with her. —Dr. Spinks, surgeon at the Workhouse, said that he had examined the child, and it seemed to be generally healthy, but was very thin; it was apparently only suffering from starvation.—A woman who was called as a witness said that the child was a " beautiful, fat" baby when born. The male prisoner was a "good one," and earned plenty of money. He took drink, but he always saw that there was plenty of food in the house, and she had seen him give his wife 303 or 355, and also bring home a beautiful leg of mut- ton, a piece of bacen, and other things.—Alderman Pica- mere: Do you think she is a jealous woman ?—Witneas Yes, she is very jealous, and that is what has caused all the bother. The woman she is jealous of is as innocent as a little baby that never saw daylight. (Laughter.)—P.C. Bowen said that he arrested the female prisoner on Satur- day afternoon. There was meat on the table, and he re- marked that there seemed to be plenty to eat. She said " Yes, he generally brings in all the meat to the house." In reply to a question, she said that the previous week her husband gave her 303, and that he generally gave her 303 or 3:55. He earned from £2 to a 103 a week. Witness arrested the male prisoner that morning. He said that he plenty of money, and had taken hadfood giinyteon thief: house.wife The rooms of the honse, witness added, were in a filthy state. The female pri- soner said that she had always looked after her baby as well as she could. She added that she had found out that her husband had something to do with another woman by hearing him talk in his sleep.—Mr. Fairclongh Heve you seen him with this woman? Prisoner: I have

seen him round the corner where she lives; they have seen each other, and I have seen them* stare very much at each other. (Laughter.)—Chief Constable Hunt : Do you know anyone who has seen them together ? Prisoner : No, sir.—The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. White) : What did he say in his sleep? Prisoner : He was telling her to meet him in the market. He said "Margaret Higgins" and 1 that is the same person. Every Wednesday he does not come home for his dinner.—Alderman Pickmere : Are you , sure you were not dreaming yourself ? Prisoner : I was ' not.—Alderman Davies: He would says' Dear Margaret " you know, and not "Margaret Higgins," so yea must be mistaken. (Laughter.)—The male prisoner said that he was quite innocent in the matter. He worked from six o'clock in the morning until ten at night, and gave his wire plenty of money. When he went home he found her drunk and carrying on.-Mr. Baird ough : Do your children ever com- plain of want of food ?--Prisoner : Yes, I have had to find it them during the week. She has over 30s every week from me. --A gentleman in court, who had had dealings with McKean, gave him a good character. Be had several times sold him furniture.—The Bench said that the husband appeared to have given his wife sufficient money, and he did not seem to be as much to blame as her! The female prisoner would go to gaol for threi, months, and the husband would be dis- charged. '

LINSEED LOZENGES, solidified linseed tea, laxative and de. muicent, 6d; postage 2d. Kay, Brothers, Stock Port, and all Chemists.—Advt. A SINGULAR OTRUSIGHT.—/i singular oversight arising out of the la-3t municipal contests for St. Helens, was re- ferred to at the County Court, on Wednesday afternoon, before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, judge. Mr. Malkin, solici- tor, made an application on behalf of Mr. R. G. Brook, one of the candidates, to allow that gentleman to pay a certain sem of money which unfortunately be had left out of his list of expenses at the last municipal election. They were left out by forgetfulness, and he asked his Honour for per- mission to reinstate the amount. He wished to be fair and pay the amount owing.—Mr. H. L. Riley said he appeared for the claimant and had entered the action in the County Court against the candidate, but the sum had been paid into court. The money had been taken out of the court by his (Mr. Riley's) clerk, but before it was banded over to the claimant they wished to have his Honour's consent. The candidate's expenses did not exceed the estimate. His Honour said he saw no reason for not allowing the ex- pense to be paid, and he accordingly made the order asked for.

div.head: FXAMINER. SATURDAY, FEBRUART 13, 1886.
div.p: THE FXAMINER. SATURDAY, FEBRUART 13, 1886.

EARLESTOWN. ANTI VAccutsToas SITIEHONED.—During the present week summonses have been served upon three members of the Earlestowu branch of the National Anti-Crimpulsory Vacci- nation Society who have failed to carry out orders of the magistrates to have their children vaccinated. William Whitley Owen, pork butcher, Bridge-street, has been sum- moned in three casei ; James Parrott, of 42, Sankey-street; and James Gritnshaw, of 177. Legh-street, have each been summoned in one case. The summonses will be heard at the
next Newton Petty Sessions. APPRIMIINSION OF DESIIRTBR£3. P.C. Parker,
stationed at Wiuwiek, on Saturday mornimg apprehended three soldiers named Wm. Lewis, James Leyland, .and Wm.

Johnson, privates in the South Lancashire Regiment sta- tioned at Orford Barracks, on a charge of desertion. The men were going in the direction of St. Helens, and when asked for their pass they admitted they lyid cone, and said they had got out of the barracks, their obj,-ct being to see some of their friends. They were brought up at the Occa- sional Court-house, Warrington, on Saturday, when they

were sent back to the barracks. Gone) TEMPLART.—The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Template was hell on Mon- day night, under the presidency of Bre. George E. Warbur- ton, W.C.T. Reports of several lodge committees were sub- mitted and considered, after which the advisability of pro- curing a banner for the lodge was discussed. A committee was appointed to consider the matter, and report to the next meeting. The W. Sec. (80. George Clarke), then road circulars with regard to the District Council meeting, the Weeleyan and Congregational Bands of Hope. The even- ing's programme was" Scraps, Facts, and Tit-bits," and a large number of interesting and instructive selections from the Watchword, the Juvenile Templar, and other periodicals by Brothers George Clarke, E. Newman, T. Gorse, J. Bar- nard, E. C. Matthews, and others. The session, was a very pleasant one. PROPOSED RAGORD SCHOOL FOR EARLESTOWN. —Daring the past week or two steps have been taken for the forma- tion of a ragged school, by which children of all denomi- nations, whose religious training is at present neglected, will have a chance of attending an evening service each Sunday. The proposal originated from Mr. G. Dring, the town mis- sionary, and to carry on the movement a committee of two , persons from each of the Nonconformist Sunday schools was formed as follows :—The Revs. J. Kent (Wesleyan), F. N. Shimmin (Primitive Methodist), W. C, Taylor (Bap- tist), and J. Allatt (Congregational).; Mr. G. F. Avelino land Mrs. Street (Baptist), Mr. J. Woods and Miss Thomp- son (Primitive Methodist), Mr. Graham and Miss Newman (Wesleyan). and Mr. Ashton and Miss Birks (Congrega- tional). The services are intended to be held in the old Primitive Methodist Sunday School, Legh-street. Mr. C. Ashton has been appointed treasurer. Gosenen Messrosee—Under the auspices of the Eerles- town Gospel Mission, whose services are acid each Sunday in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, Mr. Irving, of Liver- pool. gave a public lecture entitled " Alcohol, or the modern evil," in that building on Saturday evening. There was a fair attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr. Joseph Cordingly. The lecturer, in the course of an hastructive address, referred to the expressed opinions of medical and other gentlemen on the subject of alcohol, and urged the less they had to do with it the better people would be. He maintained that it was an injury and an evil to society, and quoted nnmerous instances of its injurious effects. tiering the evening a selection of songs, recithions, dm., was given by Meseis, George Warburton, A. Warbuiten, John Taylor, Horridge, Miss Pickett, Master Pickett, Miss Jane Bancroft, and Miss Jane Eechue. On the following day (Sunday) Mr. Irving preached two special sermons in aid of the Mission funds. 'Here were large attendances. and Mr. Irving's remarks were listened to with great attention. The collections realised a fair amount. EXTRAORDINARY ROBBERY AT NEWTON. —At the Newton Town Hall on Friday, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, Richard Walsh, a young man, described as a groom from Warrington, was charged with stealing a horse clipping machine and a clothes brush, the property of Dr. J. W. Watkins, of Newton. About half-past four on Thursday, as Oliver Beresford, groom to Dr. Watkins, was entering the stable yard he saw the prisoner coming out of the saddle- room, and the latter asked if the docter wanted a groom. Beresford replied in the affirmative, and the prisoner then said, " Oh, I've had a look round the yard, it appears rough, and I don't think I'll ask for the place. I have come from Warrington, and am going back again." He then went away, but two hours afterwards Beresford missed a horse-clipping machine and a clothes brash. He gave in- formation to P.S. Cummins, and the prisoner was apprehen- ded at half-past eleven o'clock the same night, at a lodging- house in Ashton, in bed, with the stolen articles under his pillow. He had else in his possession a pair of carriage reins, which he admitted having stolen from the posting establishment of Mr. Edward Connor, of Warrington. The prisoner was remanded to the Newton Patty Sess;ons. CONGRSIILTIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL.—The CongTega • tiocal School-room, Crow-lane, was crowded on Wednesday evening, when an unusually enjoyable entertainment was given under the auspices of the Band of Hope. The chair was occupied by Mr. B. B. Glover, and among the gentlemen present were the Rev. James Allatt, resideet minister. The principal feature of the proceedings was the performance of the Liverpool Handbell Ringers, whose selections were brilliantly executed, and acknowledged by prolonged ap- plause. The pieces were "Auld Lang Syne," "The Hunts- man's chorus," "Blue bells of Scotland,"" Men of Har- lech," "Wedl may the keel row," and •‘ Village chimes," varied with a pleasing selection on " Fairy bells " by Mr. P. H. Ingram. An excellently arranged programme of songs, recitations, duets, pianoforte solos, Jac., was also gone through, among those taking part being Miss Bothwell, Miss Owen, Miss E. Jones, Miss G. Allatt, Miss Glover, the Misses Tait, Miss M. Sudworth, Miss Daisy , Holmes; and Messrs. R. H. Jones, C. Thompson, A. !Caldwell, B. and C. Corlett, and R. Horridge. The enter- tainment throughout was of a very enjoyable character, and concluded with the singing of the National Anthem. CROW LANE larriorm SCHOOL.—In aid of the funds of St. Mary's Catholic Church, Crow-lane, a musical and dramatic entertainment was given in St. Mary's Catholic Hall on Monday evening by the members of the St. Mary's Catholic Glee and Dramatic Society. The hall was crowded by an appreciative audience, who manifested the greatest enthusiasm The choir, under the able leadership of Mr. John Banks, efficiently sung the glee "Awake oelian Lyre," and Mr. John Gibbons followed with " Ebren on the Rhine." He was enthusiastically recalled, and he gave "Under the old flag." Mr. Banks afterwards apologised for the non-appearance of Mrs. Ashcroft through a severe cold, and he was warmly applauded for his render- ing of "The sweet little island of green." Along with Miss Kate Holland, he also took part in the amusing duets "Why don't you leave off smoking ? " and "Matrimonial life," both of which were highly appreciated. "Jack's yarn" was finely sung by Mr. T, Kenny, and that gentleman also appeared to advantage in his rendering of " Midshipmite." Messrs. Wilkinson, Kenny, and Banks effectively gave tbe trio " A little farm well till'd," which' created considerable amusement. An Interesting piece en- titled I love but three," was excellently rendered by Miss Kate Holland, and an invisible chorus enhanced the de- light of the hearers. Mr. Banks brought the first portion of the programme to a close by amusing songs entitled "Grandfather Shoreham" and Dr. Bolus." The fame entitled "The village lawyer " kept the audience in roars of laughter. Each of the characters was well sustained, the performers being Mr. Banks, Mr. J. Fitzgerald, Mr. T. Fenny, Mr. P. Brown, Mr. J. Gibbons, Miss K. Holland, and Miss Ashcroft. During the evening the Rev. Father Lennon cordially thanked the audience for their attendance, and alluded at mere length to the subject of free education, a proposal whioh he condemned. COURSINth—THE CHAMPION STAKES WeN BY Mn. STONE. —Mr. Thomas Stone, of Newton Park, was the fortunate winner of Champion Stakes first prizes of 111,000 at the Kempton Park Champion Coursing Meeting on Saturday. The event was for 64 all-aged greyhounds, and Mr. Stone entered Phcebus, a dog belonging Mr. Pilkington, another great courser, as his nomination. The early etnges of the course were run on Thursday and Friday, the concluding rounds taking place on the following day. Phcebus cleverly defeated its opponents on the two first days, and for the concluding day's coursing the ground was in capital order. A more representative and influential company was never seen at Kempton Pars coursing meeting. The com- mencement was made with the filth round of the Champion Stakes, the first slip being that 'between Mr. Hibbert's Gay City and Mr. Thompson's Arawa. Odds of 3to 1 were laid on the former ; and in a magnificent course he defeated Arawa most decisively. Phcebus was favourite at 7 to 4 against Mr. Rink's Northern Star, but although the general impression was in his favour, the judge gave the first run as an undecided. In the second spin, however, he displayed his vast superiority most decisively, and fortunately the course was a shott one, or he would have been heavily handicapped for the tinaL Amidst tremendous excitement Gay City and Phcebus were then pat into the slips for the deciding course, odds of 13 to 8 being laid on the first- named ; but the friends of the non-favonrite were extremely confident, and a large amount of speculation resulted. A better course for deciding an important prize was seldom witnessed, both greyhounds doing their utmost, but P6aahus was just superior in all the essential points, and eventually he won very cleverly. The victory of Phoebus was received with the greatest amount of enthusiasm—indeed the cheer- ing was immense when the white flag was hoisted and the splendid victory announced. Although the winner was not one of the ,leading favourites at the outset, he was still backed to win a good stake, while public bickers were not unmind- ful of the favourable manner in which he was drawn for his early courses.
LIBERAL CLUB DISCUSSION. " IRISH GRIEVANCES."

I "Irish Grievances" again-formed the subject of discus- ' . mon at the weekly meeting in connection with the debating class esta.blished at the Earlestown and District Liberal Club, Fairclough-street, on Thursday evening. The same topic was discussed last week, but so great an interest was excited that it was decided to postpone the debate. At its resumption on Thursday evening, there was again a good attendance, and in the absence of Mr. W. D. Bardis, who had been announced to preside, Mr. M. P. Campbell, the n!wly.appointed secretary and registration agent to the Liberal Association of Newton Division, occupied the chair. Among these present were Messrs. John Clarke, Henry Way- well, C. Kelly, L. F. Foulkes, James Rutter, and Mr. T. Morris (secretary). The Chairman gave an instructive address on the subject, remarking that it seemed to him we were now on the eve of a crisis which, he thought, the greater number of people did not fully realise. We had been tha conquerors of Ireland four times in the past, and he thought this country must '

now adopt one or other of four courses. The first was the establishment of Ireland Sean independent country; 2nd, the establishment of an independent Parliament in Ireland, with power to legislate over exclusively Irish questions, but controlled by guarantees from interfering in Imperial questions and from exceeding certain points in the matters on which it had to legislate ; thirdly, the establishment of some kind of local government for Irelarel, not by a Parlia- ment, but possessing many of the attributes of Parliament; fourthly, doing nothing at all; and, he might add, fifthly. re-enacting the Crimes Act, and taking up Lord Spencer's work at the point at which he dropped it. The people were waiting anxiously to know the course the present Govern- ment would adopt, but he thought the Prime Minister would take the wisest and most just course—that he would avoid the filth mode; be was too great a man to take the fourth, and he thought Mr. Gladstone would not take the third, but would take either the first or the second course. He urged that three things required to be remedied in Ireland, the laws. some obnoxious custom., and the antagonisms of religion, so called. He commented on the various proposals urged to remedy the evils, and after remarking that he thought we had the present physicians in power able to effect a cure, concluded by expressing the hope they would have an interesting and profitable discussion. (Applause.) Mr. James Rutter then resumed the debate. He criticised the remarks of Mr. Morris. Mr. McEvoy, and others at the previous meeting, and went on to say that his paper last week brought the Irish grievances down to the year 1714, or the year when George I. became King. He quickly glanced at the subsequent differences with the Irish people, their struggles, commented at soma length on the restric- tions placed upen Irish trade and commerce, and alluded in condemnatory terms to the laws imposed on the Catholics. Following a reference to the famines in Ireland, and the corruption which had prevailed at the Irish court, he concluded by saying it was often said that when Ireland had its own Parliament the people were worse off than they were now, and though there might be some truth in that the times were now different, and people had greatly improved privileges. He hoped the time was not far distant when there would again assemble another Parliament on College Green in lieu of the one of which they were most unjustly deprived at the commencement of the present century. (Applause.) Mr. Thomas Walsh, as an Irishman, thanked Mr. Rutter for the manner in which he had referred to Irish grievances, and said if Englishmen generally would try justice for a change, instead of so many doses of drastic coercion in re- gard to Ireland it would be more effectual, and might heal the wound which had been so long open. He held that If Ireland was independent and a protective tax imposed it would be quite justified in order to keep out the "shoddy " of Lancashire, the plated goods of Birmingham, and the cutlery of Sheffield until the Irish manufactures had been properly started. England feared Ireland as a prosperous mercantile rival and that was why so many restrictions had been placed on Irish manufactures in the past. He thought he saw the dawn of the period when that question would be speedily settled by justice be- lag granted to the Irish race.—Mr. Lewis T. Foulke ad- mitted that Ireland had greatly suffered from famines in the past, and said Euglishrnea generally had been too cred- ulous in regard to Irish sufferings. He commented upon the reluctance of the Irish leaders in condemning the fear- ful outrages which had occurred, and he thought Mr. Par- nell and the other leaders lacked courage of which they ought to have been ashamed. He believed both political parties were anxious for the Irish question to be settled on a basis that would shelve it beyond the range of pelitics, and he urged that Mr. Gladstone would do what he considered beet for Ireland and the benefit of this country. (Applause.) Mr. Thomas Morris said there was no doubt Ireland had suffered under its grievances. but Englishmen had had many of the grievances, which, as lead been pointed out, occurred in the dark ages. He did not think the Irish people had treated the efforts of the Liberal leaders to give them jus- tice in the spirit they ought to have done, and in that respect they had a justifiable complaint against Ireland. He pointed out that there was a Land Act in force in Ireland far better than anything of the kind in England, and concluded by remarking that he hoped they were approaching a new era in which Irelaed would secure compensation for the injus- tices and grievances under which she bad suffered. (Ap- plause.)—The debate was continued by others.

that the population of Widnes is not likely to go clean out with the birth rate at 500 per I,ooo.—Mr. Dutton : Its the gas, sir.—Dr. O'Keeffe explained that the high death rate was in consequence of the large number of deaths amongst children up to five years of age. Deduct these from the deaths the rate was something under 8 per 1,000. Widnes still continued to be one of the healthiest towns in Eng- land.—Mr. Handley : What is the reason of the high death rate amongst children under one year ?—Dr. O'Keeffe said a great many died immediately after they were born. He would not attribute the cause to anything. He did not like to impute motives—(,laughter)—to the opposite sex.— Mr. Dutton: That's through the gas Mr. Handley.—Dr. O'Keeffe : No; they have not been attended by any mem- ber of the medical profession.

div.head: ACCIDENT XOSPITAL.
div.p: THE ACCIDENT XOSPITAL.

Mr. Carey said he had made inqc.by into the cause of SO many persons who were injured in the lowa being sent to the infirmaries in Livrpool rather then to the accident hos- pital at Widnes; and he found that the shilling a day the patients had to pay deterred them from using the hospital. He therefore proposed that the Health Committee be re- quested to inquire into the whole sobject and advise the Board whether the shilling charge could not b. abolished.— Mr Gasket! seconded the motion. His opinion was that in- jured persons were sent to Liverpool solely en account of that shilling a day charge. It brought in about £2O or £3O a year; and it seemed to him that it would be wise to abolish the charge and conduct the hospital on the same basis as the infirmaries in Liverpool. He would have it supported from the rates entirely for the benefit of the rate- payers.—A short conversation took place upon the holding of the Next spring fair, and it was decided that the subject should be decided at the nest meeting.—The minutes were then passed also the motion with regard to the hospital.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.
On tbe motion of Mr. ilanTire;', accounts amounting to 3,734 188 id were passed for payment.
THB FARE LIBRARY.

The General Purposes Committee recommended that about ,ilOO be expended upon books—that temporary shelved be provided in the Board-room for the books—and that the room be open three evenings each week, from five to eight o'clock, for the purpose of lending books, subject to such rules as the committee may arrange.—Mr. Carey moved, and Mr. Handley seconded the adoption of this minute.—Mr. Dutton said it would be a good plan if they ' could utilia-3 something of this sort at each end of the town. It would be a great benefit to the parties who would never otherwise avail themselves of the opportunity of read- ing books.—Mr. Heves. How many ends are there to the town 7—Mr. Dutton: Two—(laughter)—one at West Bank and the other at Simm's Cross.—Mr. Taylor suzgested tha the hours should be five to nine.—Dr. O'Keeffe asked whether the £lOO was to come from the honoutable member for Northwich, or from the rates.—Mr. Sadler said if some efficient system of lending the books was not arranged, he was quite sure all the books would not come back.—Mr. Dutton: Ton will have to form a Library Committee.— Mr. Carey said the General Purposes Committee were tem- porarily appointed a Library Committee for the purpose of starting the library on a small scale as soon as mi4ht be. The books the committee would choose for the £lOO would. he presumed, be of a comparatively light and entertaining character. In the lending of books they should take the same precautions for getting the books returned as they did in Runcorn, St. Helens, and so on, where, he understood, that no one could take a book out without a recommendation signed by One or more responsible householders. The Llik they proposed to spend was to be obtained from the rates. They did not propose to spend the £l.OO that Mr. Brunner kindly offered at present. The Chairman declared the minutes passed.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of Widnes Local Board was keld on Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Carey, Wright, Dutton, Heyes, Taylor, Gaskell, jun., Houghton, T. Handley, Husband, J. T. Allen (clerk), I. Carr (gas engireer), W. Higginson (surveyor).

div.head: TUB INPSCTIOITS DISBASPS HOSPITAL.
div.p: TUB INPSCTIOITS DISBASPS HOSPITAL.

The Clerk read a letter dated the 22nd ult, from the Local Government Board, in which it stated that the Board had considered the report made by Mr. Terry, with reference to the application of the I.c.cal Board for sanction to borrow £4,000 for the purpose of providing a hospital. The Board directed him to state that they were advised that the pavilion which was designated a small-pox ward on the plans was too close to that marked fever ward, and that the former ward should be placed at least ten feet further in a northerly direction from the latter, so as to afford an intervening space of at least 40 feet. The plans were returned so that they might be amended. The Board understood that the Local Board only proposed at present to construct part of the kospital at an estimated cost of £2,000. It was very desirable that the whole of the buildings should, if possible, be erected at the outset. It would be found that a contract for the whole of the buildings could be let on more advan- tageous terms than if the works were split up, and the Board suggested, therefore, that on the ground of economy as well as that of convenience, the work should be preferably carried out as a whole. If, however, the Local Board still proposed not to expend £2,600 on the scheme at present the Board would be prepared to grant them, 'sanction to the borrowing of that amount provided the plans were modified in the manner indicated in the present communication.— Dr O'Keeffe asked the Surveyor whether he could remove the small-pox ward so as to meet the wishes of the Local government Board. In regard to the carrying out of the entire scheme, he considered that inasmuch as they were, comparatively, and had been for a long time, completely free from infectious disease, he thought the portion pro- posed to be erected at present by the Local Board would meet the requirements of the township for many years to ootne.—The Surveyor replied that the ward could be arranged as suggested. —lt was unanimously de- cided that the Surveyor alter the plans as snip gested that the Clerk reply to the Local Govern- ment Board that the proposed buildings were quite suffi- cient,

div.head: TRH WATER SUPPLTO--14XPECTED DEFICIENCY.
div.p: TRH WATER SUPPLTO--14XPECTED DEFICIENCY.

The engineers' report to the Gas and Water Committee oontained the fellowing:—" Stock's Well—l beg to direct your attention to the gradually failing supply of water at this station, and request that the qlestion of lowering the pumps or some other scheme which will enable us to work the engines at their full capacity, should receive your early consideratlen. This decreased yield, together with the con- stant Increasing consumption, is at present being met by incessant pumping at Netherley' but unless a better supply is •obtained from Stock's Well, difficulty will soon begin to be experienced in meeting the demand. Sulphate Plant —This plant continues to work satisfactorily, and I now submit certificate for the sum of £292 7s BJ, being the amount due to the contractors. Thirty-one tons of sulphate have been sold during the past month. The rainfall for the month has been :—Gas yard guage 2 805 inches, Pex Hill guage 2.470 inches, mean 2.637 inches. Water in stock January 2Tth, 1886, 4,731,349 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 16.98 candles.—Mr. Gaskell moved, and Mr. Wright seconded the adoption of the minut,s.—Mr. Dutton asked why the illu- minating power of the gas was less this mßnth than it had been for the past twelve months.—Mr. Gaskell replied that the illuminating power was supposed to be 17 candles. Of course they could not always attain the exact power, and with this single exception during the 12 months the power had been above 17 candles.—ln reply to Mr. Dutton, Mr. Gaskell explained that the water at Stock's Well rose to the same level, but the yield was not so great. After pumping for some time the water sank too low for the pumps to act upon it, and they had to wait until it rose again.—The I minutes were passed.

THE ASSISTANT ENGINEER. Mr. Gaskell stated that there were 62 applications for this post, and on his suggestion, seconded by Mr. Houghton, It was decided to leave the appointment in the hands of the Gas Committee.

div.head: NEW STREETS.
div.p: NEW STREETS.

The Surveyor reported to the Highway Committee that Messrs. Sayce and Handle completed the reconstruction of the main sewer near to Messrs. Golding, Davies, and Co.'s works on the sth inst. In order to give employment to the unemployed, it was decided to give instructions- to Mr. D. Hirst to at once proceed with the excavation at Crow Wood. Mr. W. Leadbetter having called the attention of the committee to the unsanitary condition of Yiaduct-street, it was recommended that the street be made under the previ- sions of the Public Health Acts.—Mr. Carey moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Dutton asked for the infor- mation of the public whether the streets the Board decided should be made twelve months ago bad been made or the work commenced P—Mr. Creey said the committee had pro- ceeded with these streets as rapidly as circumstances would permit. Notice had been given in almost every case, but in many cases the time had not expired. Of course, the notices would be acted upon when the time came.

div.head: INFANT MORTALITY AND ITS carsE.
div.p: INFANT MORTALITY AND ITS carsE.

The Medical Officer of Health had reported to the Health Committee that during January there were 116 births equal to a rate of 50 61 per 1,000, and 52 deaths, equal to a rate of 23.11 per 1,000. There were 20 deaths amongst children under one year, ard seven between one and five years. Two deaths have occurred by zymotic disease. The medical officer, surveyor, and inspector had been instructed to I ex- amine and report upon the drainage of back premises in Anne-street, and if necessary to serve notices to abate nuis- ances.—Mr. W. Hartland protested against the proposed slaughter-house, in Oakland-street. —The Surveyor also re- ported against the site selected.—lt was therefore recom- mended that the site be not approved. There had been no patient in the hospital since 31st December. It was repor- ted that the receipts at the market for the month amounted to £29 lOs 10.1, being an increase of £ll 14s lid as com- pared with January, 1885. It was resolved that if the usual fair were to be held the Highway Committee be re- quested to remove the slag and macadam from the market ground.—Mr. Heves moved and Mr. Husband seconded the passing of the minutes.—The Chairman : It seems to me

div.p: ASHTON.

Tali ROBBERY AT PARK-LANE.-At the Liverpool Assizes on Tuesday Samuel Hill (36), collier, for breaking arid entering the shop of the Park-lane Co-operative Store. Ashton-in-Makerfield, on the 23rd Jinuary, and stealing a shirt, a pair of stockings, and £lB Os, was senteneed to 18 months' imprisonment.

div.p: PIZI4.SCOT.

EIRRYICB OP SONG.-0a Sunday afternoon, the Wesleyan Chapel was fairly well filled, when a service of song, en- titled "Rag and Tag," was rendered by the choir, under the conductorship of Mr. W. Mercer. Mr. Ames presided at the organ, and the Rev. John Shipham gave the connective readings. A collection was made towards defraying the cost of prizes to the Sunday school scholars. Comcsrwr v WHISTON.—The Whiston Brass Band gave a grand vocal and instrumental performance in the National School on Saturday evening, when they secured the services of the following distinguished artistes : Miss Dora Powell (Mostyn), Madam Wiseman (St. Helens), Mr. A. , Maynjer (Liverpool), and Mr. J. Graham. Mies Quick was the accompanist. The Brass Band, under Mr. J. Corns, played selections at intervals in the programme. Captain H. R. D'A. Willis occupied the chair. CONCBRT AT PRBSCOT. A grand miscellaneous concert I was given in the libel:mar schoolroom, on Tuesday even- ins, under the auspices of the recently established reading- room. The committee secured the services of the following ladies and gentlemen :—Miss Stead, Miss M. Harris, Mrs Flint, Mrs A. J. Shaw, Mr. D. Goldswortb, Mr. J. Dearden, Mr. S. H. Ames, and Miss Harris as accompanist. The Rev. James Johnstone presided. The several items of the pro- gramme were well received, Mr. Ames'receiving hearty en- cores to which he had to respond twice. The proceeds were devoted to the reading-room fund, and it is a pleasure to have to record the appreciation of this institution which already numbers over 40 members.

HUYTON. C.E.T.S. (HurroN BRANCH).—Oct Monday evenirig an entertainment was given in the infant school, consisting of Bungs and readings by the Misses Blezard, Miss M. Terry, Messrs. G. E. Jowett, lit. C. Davis, J. Roberts, and H. S. Daine. The vicar, the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, occupied the chair, and a personal experience address was given by Mr. William Lamble at the close of the meeting, which was well attended. TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION.—The Huyton Park school was well filled on Tuesday evening, it having been announced that Mr. Saape, of Liverpool, would address the usual meeting. Mr. E. S. Eccles presided, and, after a piano solo by Miss Cecil, Mr. Snape gave a powerfal temperance address, dealing with the enormous expenditure in intoxica- ting drink, and the evil consequences arising therefrom. A solo was rendered by Mr. P. Capper, and the proceedings closed. IitrYTON QIZIARRY WELSH BAND OP HOPE TREA.T.-0/1 Wednesday afternoon the members of the above, together with adult friends, numbering altogether 170, sat down to a well appointed tea, catered by Mrs. Griffiths, of Huyton, in the Rose Cottage room. The good things were served by Mr. and Mrs. Ellis, Mr. J. Edwards, and several other friends, the pastor, the Rev. J. Roberts, giving every assis- tance. After tea an adjournment was made ta the Welsh Chapel, where an excellent entertainment was provided, the pastor in the chair, and the children were rewarded with prizes of books for successful competition in reciting, &a. A distribution of oranges was made at the close.

div.p: • GOLBORNE•

TnE GAS SUPPLY.—Another Public meeting of gas con- sumers was held at Golborne on Friday night, when it was stated that the gas company had decided to reduce the price to small consumers from 4s 7d to 43 21 per 1,000 feet, less 5 per cent. discount if paid within twenty-one days, as against a penny in the shilling previously allowed.—The Chairman (Mr. John Davis, manufacturer), stated that the discount really amounted to about 3d per 1,000 feet, but as the company only now undertook to supply 17. candle gas, as against 20, consumers were actually worse off than be- fore.—The meeting resolved to form itself into a Gas and Water Consumers' Association, and appointed a commit- tee to make all necessary inquiries, and report to a further meeting. THU LIBBIZALS OF GOLBORNI3.—DaIing the past week the Golborne Liberals have been making active preparations for leaving the old Associations Rooms in Heath-street, and entering their new premises, which are centrally situated in High-street. The latter, consisting of a large newly-built house and shop, have just been internally decorated, and are admirably suited for the purpose for which Mr. W. Mit- chell has generously placed them, rent free, at the disposal of the committee. After making ample provision for the resident caretaker, there are four commodious rooms for the use of the association, the floors of which have been covered with linoleum and other imitable matting. In addition to the usual bagatelle, reading, and smoking rooms, provision will be made for supplyiug light refreshments to members of the club and travellers, the want of which has long been felt in the nekbbourhood. Considerable expense has been incurred in furnishing and fitting, up the premises, to meet which a subscription list was op4ned en Monday evening, when upwards of £lO was raised amongst the committee assembled. At the Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, Mary M‘Gavna (23), servant, pleaded guilty to the charge of having, at Sutton, on or about the 15th December, being then delivered of a 'certain male child, unlawfully, by a certain secret disposition of the dead body of the said child, endeavoured to conceal the birth thereof. A certain minister residing in a remote district of the Highlands was sent for to christen the child of a shepherd in one ree the loneliest glens of his parish. He set out, but, on reaching a burn which he had to cross about half-way on his journey, found it swollen, and the road impassable. However, the father, who was already informed of this event, was waiting on the other side, and had brought the baby with him. Preliminaries having been discussed, he waded out as far as he could into the stream, and held out the child at arm's length, while the minister, standing on the other side, splashed water with both hands and with all his might, stopping at intervals to roar out above the rushing of the waters," Flee he gotten ony yet ?" div.head: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CONFERENCE
div.p: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CONFERENCE

AT ST. HELENS. A conference of the members of the Primitive Methodist connection in the St. Helens, Warrington, and Earlestown Circuits was opened in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Westfield- street, St. Helens, on Monday afternoon. The object was stated to be "to consider the best means of promoting the Work of I God among us as a community, and to adopt means by'which Each of us may to the greatest possible ex- tent, receive of His fullness, edify one another, and win souls for Christ." There was a very fair atten- dance, notwithstanding the unfavourable character of the weather. The proceedings were conducted by the Rev. John Picks well, resident minister, and among those present were the Rev. J. Calvert (Warrington), Rev. F. N. Shimmin (liarles- town), and Mr. T. Clarke (Earlestown), who attended as a deputation.—After devotional exercises and the reading of a portion of scripture, the Rev. J. Pickwell heartily welcomed the friends who had attended that conference, and he was anxious they should all have a part in considering the best means how they might promote the work of God amongst them as a community. He had no doubt they had all many times offered up the prayer "0 Lord, revive thy work," and he felt sure they had need to offer it again that after- 1 noon. There appeared to him a great necessity for a re- vival of the work of the Lord. They had had revivals in ! the past, and they might took at the past as a guarantee 1 • i that they would have them again under similar conditions. One very important means of promoting a revival of the I work of God among them would be personal service and self sacrifice to the work. They could not all work in the same way, nor was it necessary they should. There was a variety of work in connectiou with religion, and they had , each to find out the exact kind of work for which they were i suited, and then heartily and earnestly do it.—The Rev. J. Calvert (of Warrington) alluding to the remarks of Mr. Fickwell on personal consecration, said the work of God i must first begin within them, and then it was sure to spread. 1 Notwithstanding that we lived in a Christian coun:ry and ; boasted of our enlightenment and privileges there was a i great amount of darkness, and Mr. z,purgeon's ideas of 1 Christianity at the present by was very dark. Christianity i was not making that progress it ought to do. lhey should i • not shut their eyes to that fact. He strongly supported Mr. i Pickwell on personal consecration to the work of God, and : urged that they should all show an every day religion : which should so shine about them as would lead others to ; seek the Saviour. He was very much in favour of society i class meetings, and he strongly urged the great importance : of class leaders visiting their uiern4rs and absentees. i In that respect he thought a great deal more 1 good might be done by means of their claeees 1 than was at present done. div.p: showing a complete self-surrender of Himself to God, in the next place absolute obedience to the will of God and then untiring sacrifice in the discharge of their duties towards God. He advocated a close and sincere communion with God in prayer and' spirit, and urged there was a danger when they got too indifferent about the prospects and positions of others. He alluded to the lessons taught to others by a good example, and spoke of the influence they exerted amongst their families, friends, and neighbours by their every-day lives.—Mrs. Bedgegood, of Lowton, in a few re- marks spoke of her early connection with the cause of Primitive Methodism in St. Helens, and said that after forty- five years connection with it she held a position as Sunday school teacher, and she hoped she could continue to do so as long as she lived.—The afternoon meeting then concluded with singing and prayer. A number of the friends then adjourned to the school- room in Kirkland-street, where they partook of a substantial tea. The Conference was continued in the chapel in the evening, when the Rev. John Pickwell, resident minister, , again presided, and he was supported by the gentlemen pre- viously mentioned. After a brief address from the rev. , Chairman, Mr. T. Clarke (Farlestown) gave an excellent ad- dress. an personal holiness. in which he urged that they ! could do nothing of permanent good without the help of God, and in seeking to promote His glory and kingdom they should seek to be endued with powers from on high. The reason why the early pioneers of Methodism had such a great success in their labours was that they were endued with that power of which he had spoken_ He exhorted them all to try and attain that height of Christian perfec- tion which characterised the early Methodists, so that they might succeed not only from the pulpit but in private con- versation and mixing up wills the masses, in persuading men and women to flee from the wrath to come. He ad- 4 vised a more brotherly unity amongst the individual mesa- I bers and leaders, and they should in a spiritual manner try ! to reconcile any offended brother and sister. They could ; not expect to get on unless they had peace and unity amongst them, and if they so worked it was quite possible that success would attend their efforts.—The Chairman, in calling upon the Rev. F. N. Shimmin to speak on the subject" Our relation in regard to our young people," said they were very anxious to secure the children on their sides.—The Rev. F. N. Slvmmin, in a careful and earnest address, said children at an early age manitested a force of , individuality, and at an early period showed they had tier- i tain preferences and the power of decerrniulng between right and wrong, while they clung tenaciously to views they had early formed. He referred to the tact that the early pioneers of their church had to grapple with adult characters ad- dicted to dog racing, pigeon flyino., gambling, and other pursuits, but the times had altered, and the question was being asked bow they could reach the masses. He main- tained it was possible to reach the masses through the children and rising generation, and quoted the opinions of Edwards, a great American revivalist, and Baxter, the writer of the " Saints' test" as to the value and importance of the early training of children to the means ot grace and , a devotion to Christ. He remarked that if he neglected his ! own children's salvation and conversion he would be a hypocrite—a professional parson. He appealed to them strongly to look after the children from the hour when they' were born; to train them up in the way they should go, and if they succeeded in doing that he was sure they would have a larger increase, and there would be many more Christians than there were at present —Several local speakers followed, in which the points of the addresses were briefly alluded to; and thanks were accorded to the deputation for their kindness in attending the conference.

div.p: OUP LONDON LETTER.
• LONDON, THITRSDA.Y.

For three days interest in politics has been obscured by the riots in London. They began on Monday, growing unexpectedly out of a meeting of the unemployed held in Trafalgar Square. There are, unhappily too many unemployed in London, but it is certain Ttiat had these poor men been left to themselves they would have been satisfied, as many other crowds meeting in Trafalgar Square have been, V) make their plaint and then quietly dis- perse. But there is a little body of notoriety-hunters n London who call themselves Socialists, and who would reform the world. They took the opportunity vf the gathering of the unemployed to bring them- selves to the front. jt was they who led the throng westward to break windows and wreek shops. There is always prominent on th3se occasions a section of the population whose condition of non-employment Is chronic. These are the• roughs and loafers who haunt the thoroighfares, snatch purses from un- protected women, and knock down and rob unwary passengers. There is one company of this brigade of "the unemployed" who have taken possession of a street in Clerkenwell, and will not permit anyone to pass throagh wearing a top hat. That is a comparatively minor eccentricity, and the place ' and the humour of its inhabitants being well known it is only occasionally that an innocent stranger walking along the street finds himself set upon, his hat beaten over his eyes, or knocked off and used as a football, so playful are the unemployed that lounge about the corners of our streets. The damage done to property on Monday by the mob that sloped slowly towards the west is very Considerable, and the anxious inquiry of suffering tradesmen as to who is to pay has not yet been satisfactorily answered. But the humours of the mob, their fierce, ~,,saulu3 on .hons, and their reck- less destruction of things that were of no use to them—sponge baths for example—sink into insigni- ficance in contemplation of the conduct of the police. The cry of "Where were the police!" is a familiar one to the British housekeeper; but never since the Metropolitan police were incorporated was there such on exhibition of incompetency as has been displayed through these riots. Sir Edmund Henderson seems to have utterly lost his head. One story in explanation of the total disappearance of the police relates how a considerable body was ordered to concentrate in Pall Mall, but that in the excitement of the moment the order was transmitted, arranging for ren- dezvous in the Mall, a quiet spot far remote from the scenes of outrage. However this be, what is certain is that only here and there was to be seen an alarmed policeman forlornly gazing upon the seething throng.

But; the shortcomings of the police were active as well as passive. On Monday they abandoned the streets to the mob. On Wednesday, awaking to a condition of extraordinary energy, they went run- ning through all the streets of south London pro- claiming the advance of a mob from Greenwich, and hysterically commanding shopkeepers to run up their shutters. The injunction was accepted with alacrity, and never before was beheld such a scene in the borough in the neighbourhood of the Elephant and Castle and down the great highways that lead through Brixton and Clapham to the south. , After . ten minutes fearful excitement every shop was closed, whilst carpenters hastily summoned were barricading the windows of public-houses which did not possess shutters. Hare again it is incred- ible that with all the appliances of organisation, telegraph and telephone, the police should have been hoaxed by the myth of the advancing mob from Greenwich.

There are many stories of adventure and narrow escapes of individuals. But the funniest I have heard relates to the Earl of Dunraven. His lord- ship, as eVeryone knows, is a principal leader of the Fair Trade movement, which combined with the Socialists to form the dangerous element of the crowd. Lord Dunraven, standing in 'Pall Mall, watched the Passage of his friends without the slightest apjoiehension regarding his personal safety. Before he was aware of it, he had become the object of concentrated attention by the Fair Traders at so much a day and a quart of beer. He was not only dressed in broad cloth and wore a hat, but looked upon the crowd through gold-rimmed pince-nez. Suddenly the noble lord, attacked from behind, had his hat struck off, he himself being hustled from Fair Trader to Socialist, and from Socialist to the unemployed of the street corner. His hat was kicked hither and thither, and his lord- ship was glad to escape in a passing cab with, it is to be hoped, quite new views on the subject of Fair Trade.

Mr. Beecher reports to a friend in London a . curious accident that has befallen him. Some weeks ago he stated in the course of a sermon tlmt righteousness was the central theme of the Gospel, and that as far as he recollected the word religion was not in the Bible. It is marvellous that so -shrewd a man and experienced a preacher should have let himself into a trap like this. He had scarcely left the pulpit when one of the elders, hurrying into the vestry, told him that the word religion was to be found in the Epistle of St. James. Mr. Beecher, conscious of what would befall him, for the New York papers give a digest of his sermons every Monday, took occasion at the even- ing service to recant and admit his error. But this did not save him. The very next morning letters began to arrive correcting his statement. They increased the next day, and went on day after day as the news spread over the vast area of the -United States. At the date of Mr. Beecher's, letter the wave had reached lowa, "and" Mr. Beecher adds, "I suppose it will spread to California. I did not know that so many people read the Bible." Mr. Beecher's studies having been extended he is now ready to take responsibility for the statement that the word religion occurs five times in the New Testament and not once in the Old.

Lord Savernake, whose latest exploit in the way of punching a policeman's head reminded the world once more of his existence, has gone out of town for a short time to recruit his energies, mentally and physically. But he will be back with the flowers in the early spring, and once more we shall see him in his remarkable costume with broad seams jutting out from his coat in all directions, and buttons so big that upon emergency they would serve for plates at a luncheon party. The noble lord's highest model of sartorial taste is the coachman of earlier days. I suppose no one could give him serener pleasure than to mistake him for one of the swell 'busdrivers who drive four-in-hands between Brixton, Clapham, and the city for the convenience and distinc- tion of city clerks and merchants. It is not very long ago .that Lord Savernake got married. The object of his affection was Miss Dolly Tester, of the Empire Theatre, Leicester-square. If Lord Saver- nake d i does not n the meantime get his head broken in some brawl with cabm en i or police, he will be . Marquis of Ailesbury, sit n the House of Lords and make laws for us. .Should Dolly Tester also survive she will be Marchioness of Ailesbury, .oan scarcely be refused the entree at Court, and will I sit in the House of Lords when the Queen opens 'Parliament, whilst the noble Marquis will strut about in scarlet robe slashed with ermine.

Sir Arthur Sullivan, it is said, is going to be mar- ried. He met his fate on his last journey across the Atlantic on other business bent. The lady is a Cali- fornian, her name Sybil Sanderson. California is a happy hunting ground for English would-be hus- bands. It not infrequently happens that travellers who leave home without matrimonial intention are sometimes trapped at San Francisco. Thus it was ' with Sir Sydney Waterlow, who went forth on a journey without the remotest matrimonial inten- tion. Ile arrived in San Francisco a free man and left it enslaved to a pretty young widow. . It was at San Francisco, too, that Sir Thomas Heslceth's io.urney round the world came to an abrupt conclu- sion. He came, he saw Miss Sharon, she conquered, I
id Sir Thomas got no further round the world than [e Golden Gate.

In London just now there is a curious state of dugs, which indicates perhaps even better than Le ruins of South Audley-street and Pall Mall, the ;neral distress, and the extent of the prevalent pression. Strangely enough the illustration is he found, not in the case of an abundance of ;rsons seeking employment, but of employers who •'t command the services they need. The is that of domestic servants. Dapper ioms, pompous responsible looking butlers, cobs- footmen with their hair full of powder, are a •in the market. They can he had in any .atity, and at almost any price. The wages of )ks and parlour maids have this winter gone up by twenty per cent. The explanation is unfor- ately quite obvious. Ever so many people have to "put down their establishments." The swell

THE PENNY 'BUS.

Sir,—l am a great admirer of the pluck which produced and the cnergy which has maintained the successful venture known as the Penny 'Bus, and in the hope that it will continue to des.rve its popularity, I venture to make toe following remarks. First of all, it is extremely desirable that care should be taken to pre.,&•mt cats from sleeping ,in the busses at night, or that thNstrasv with which the 1 floors of the busses are covered, shoJd be free from the o lour which is peculiar to the feline race of the male sex. Further, that if ladies are allowed to bring dogs into the huszes on days during which the atmosphere is humid awl the streets consequently muddy, the said dogs should not be allowed to •• sit" in their dirty coats on the cuiuioned seats, provided for their betters. I give these hint., which are the result of my personal experience, in , toe hope and belief that in future my enjoyment of so cheap a boon as a penny ride may not be marred in the way in- dicated.—Yours, PUBLICOLA.

div.head: EDDISBURY DIVISION.
div.p: THE EDDISBURY DIVISION.

Sir,—lt is not likely that Mr. litrell will aeain come for- ward to contest this Division, but in respect to Mr. Tomkin- son, his chance of success has not, in the opinion of a great many Liberal electors, been enhanced by his conduct in respect to Mr. Irwell ; in fact I consider that Mr. Torckin- sou has in this instance played into the hands of the Tories. I lierefore wish to mike a suggestion—and I do so with a 1 sariousness—viz, that Mr. C. Reynolds, J.P., of F,odsharn, be requested to come forward as the Liberal candldate for this Division. I consider him to be a gentleman to whom the Radical and Liberal electors of Eddisbury would be able to give their united votes. No doubt Mr. Tomkinson would mike a good representative of diluted Liberalism, but Mr. Irwell has weaned a great many of us from tkat kind of stuff. We want a candidate who is not fettered by veseted or domestic ties, one who will pledge himself to sup- port a popular measure without fear of a frown, or courting the smiles of my lord so-and-so. Is Mr. Tomkinson prepared to do this? I doubt it.—l remain, yours, Frodshaii, Feb. llth, 1886. PLEBEIAN.

Mr. Crawford said he married Miss Virginia Smith in ' 1831, the lady being many years his junior. He then pro- ceeded to give evidence which supported the above state- ment of his chimed. The Attorney-General pointed out that the evidence was against the lady, but not against Sir Charles, and he should ask for the present to postpone the cross-examina- tion. The Judge said that per se it was not evidence against Sir Charles. The cross-examination was postponed. Ann Jameison, parlournaaid at Mr. Crawford's house since January, 1882, was called to prove that early in 1832, when they were in town prior to Mr. Crawford's arrival, Mrs Crawford went out immediately after dinner, and did not return the next morning till half-past seven. Witness also spoke to freqaent visits of Sir Charles Dilke to Mr Craw- ford's house in 1883. By the Attorney-General: She knew Mrs Crawford was a relative of Sir Charles. Witness showed Sir Charles into the room where visitors were ordinarily received. He usually staved about half an hour She did not attach any impor- tance to the visite. She recollected no visit in Sydney- place, but should say there were more than five visits when they were in Young-street. Mrs Crawford told witness to tell the petitioner all she knew about Sir Charles Dilkee That was on the 17th July. She told Mr. Crawford about Captain Foster's visits, which began in 1881. Witness took a letter to the post from her mistress to Captain Foster as late as July, 1885. Some were addressed to a chile in London, and some to Ireland. Wit- ness never posted a letter from Mrs. Crawford to Sir Charles Duke. George Ball was called to prove that 'Mrs. Crawford did not sleep at the house of Mrs. Harrison during the month of February, 1883. , This concluded the case for the petitioner, and the court adjourned for luncheon. After the adjournment for luncheon, the Attorney-General submitted that there was no case for the co-respondent to ans wen His Lordship said the statement of Mrs. Crawford could not be evidence against the co-respondent. The Attorney-General then commented on the evidence of the girl Jamieson as showing the visits were of a nature from which' an inference of impropriety could not well be drawn. They had, he continued, °cone to the conclusion to leave the case as it stood, and they did not think it necessary to call Sir Charles, for a man in his high position to be questioned as to indiscretions in the course of his life- time. He suggested there might have been strong desire to fix the guilt of a third person on Sir Charles. Sir Henry James added that Sir Charles Dilke had placed himself in their hands, and they took the responsibility of not calling him. , Mr. Inderwick said he could not object to Sir Charles , Dilke being struck out of the petition. Mr. Lockwood said he did not propose to address the court on behalf of the co-respondent. Mr. Justice Butt, in giving judgment, said that respondent had been guilty of adultery with the co-respondent, and at Ithe same time to dismiss the case as against the co-respon- dent was a state of things which at first sight did not look quite reasonable; but when it came to be considered there wae nothing, unsound. The admiesions of guilt made to her husband by the respondent were clear, distinct, and circum- stantial, and must be accepted as true, because respondent did not go into the witness box and retract or deny them. Therefore he was compelled to come to the conclusion that adultery was committed, and to grant the relief the peti- tioner craved for, but against Sir Charles Dilke there was no evidence worthy of the name. Nothing could be clearer than the examination upon this subject, viz., that an unsworn statement of a person in the position of Mrs Craw- ford was not entitled to be received or even considered in a court of justice as against the person with whom she was alleged to have committed adultery. In common fairness respondents admissions ought not to be for one moment weighed against Sir Charles Dilke, the case against whom he therefore dismissed with costs.
CRITIC

SOCIAL EQUALITY. Sir,—l suppose " Jaques " was in an hypercritical humour when he played off so much upon my prefix' " capitalist" t,) "landlord," seeing that the real meaning of my query was contained in the following words :--" Both ' (that is the landlord and capitalist) "extract a luxurious living from the poor." Where, then, is the distinction, so far as results are concerned, in connection with the poor ? This may be "very elementary," but "Jaques " has not re- plied to it I affirm, without fear of successful contradic- tion, that there is no difference between the two parties, in that their wealth is taken from the labours of others ; and both are "monopolists," too, in this possession of power to command labour for their own aggrandisement. There is this redeeming feature on the part of the capi- talist, he is a co-worker with his fellows—his assistants. He is what Carlyle designates a "captain of industry," just as the manager of a co-operative industry is. Only the latter has his salary fixed for him, while the former fixes it himself by claiming all the profits arising from trade. But what does the capitalist give to his fellow-men in return for the enormous heaps of labour-formed wealth which is found in his possession? What has he ever done to justify his practice of absorbing so much of the produce of his assistants? Why should the few be unjustly allowed to absorb more than their just share of the wealth which is• only produced by the united labours of all engaged in its productiths and distribution?

" Jiques " goes on to say that "if a man creates his own fortune, he takes nothing from anybody else." " If," "aye, there's the rub ;" that little word 'qualifies " Jaques' " whole case, and I ask him to produce such an extraordinary re- sult of " the great natural law of evolution." The fore- going queries may be" very elementary " indeed, neverthe- ltss I have never yet been satisfactorily answered by either capitalists or their followers. Perhaps I may be more " ex- acting " in these matters than "Jaques " appears to imagine.

In order that your readers may not mistake the spirit of this controversy between " Jaques " and myself, I wish it to be clearly uederstood that I do not quarrel with either the landlord or the capitalist as itidividuals—not even as landlord or capitalist—but I regard the present laws and conditions, which admit of such unfair inequalities, as being subversive of the highest and best interests of the human family. No doubt if "Jaques" and myself—as- suming he is not a capitalist—were to exchange our psi.. tions with both the parties under review, we should, to all lut:ints and purposes, do as they do. Therefore, while we disagree with these inequalities amongst us, we do not con- demn persons of "distinction and fortune." Mv reply to "Jaques" en communism I will pen next week, as I object to write long letters for the press. W. H. CHA.PMAN.
February 11, 1886.

BEGGING AT LILAIM.—A.t LyITU:II Police Court, on Wednesday, Margaret Matthews, a well-known character from Altrincham. was broight up before Mr. Dewhurst, on a charge of begging. She had frequently been convicted of similar offences, and was now sent to prison for seven days.

Sir,—Perhaps you will allow me to inform your corres- pondent" Ignorant "that the phrase "three acres and a COW " ists fir ot pptts hr Mr. PrAriPrio Fr.. See. Allotments and Small Holdings Association, ttc.," to the system adopted by Lard Tollemache in Cheshire, and, I be- lieve, at Helminghatn, in Suffolk, namely, of allowing farm labourers the privilege of hiring three acres of land etch, adj'Aning their cottages, and of keeping a cow and other stock. In a footnot, (page 20, Three Acres and a Cow) he says :—" The words originally placed at the head of this description of what its estimable originator describes as part of u 8 lie's work,' bave:been popularly adopted as sum mink up the general idea of those who aim at establishing. through- out the country a system of allotments and small holdings. Quoted derisively by the Chancellor of the Exch=quer. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, and promptly disavowed by him in that sense, the expression three acres and a cow' has passed into a saying alternately.weful to advocates and op- panents of the aims of the author."—Thanking, you in anti- cipation for your space, I an, yours faithfully, St. Helens, Feb. Well, I Oust nothing like this will ever take place in proud England, but rather that the landlords will take a stitch in time and ease their tenants' difficultiee, which they have to meet, by reducing their rents. Another grievance which working-men have to bear that our fathers escaped, is the heavy cost of educating their children. Now, I yield to no man in being a friend for edu- cating the children. In fact lam strongly in favour of compulsory education, but when I find that I had but two. pence per week paid for my education, and no books to buy for me and went through the 'same kind of education as is now taught in the sixth standard, I cannot help but ask my- self the question, how is it that this should be so? In the days of my youth, there was nothing like the amount of Gevernment grants for education that there are now. Irt at are Government grants given for if it is not to ease the poor on account of being compelled to send their children to school? Evidently, the time has come for Free Education. Well, I will leave this subject, in the hope that men wl 0 are able to write to the papers on it will do so because it is a question that requires men with more ability than I possees.—l remain, yours respectfuily,_

div.head: MR JuillN DiutiLEY, MP.
div.p: MR JuillN DiutiLEY, MP.

• "Men of the Time" gives the followink account ! of ;the new Chief Secretary for Ireland:— Mr. John : Morley, M.P., is the eldest son of the late Mr. Jonathan Morley, of Blackburn, Lanc'ashire, where hemas born in December, 1838; was educated at Cheltenham College and at Lincoln College, Oxford, were he graduated B.A. in 1858, and M.A. in 1874. He was called to the bar at Lincoln's Inn in 1559. He was for some years editor of the Literary Gazette, the title of which was subsequently altered to the Parthenon. MeMorley was editor of the Fortnightly Review, from 1867 to October, 1882. He was also editor of the Pall Mall Gazette from May, 1880, till August, 1883. Ile unsuccessfully contested the borough of Blackburn in 1869, in the Liberal inter- est, and the City of Westminster in 1880; but in Feb.;lBB3, at a bye-election, he was returned as an advanced Liberal by the borough of Newcastle-upon- Tyne, defeating This Conservative opponent, Mr. Gainsford Bruce, by a majority of 2,256 (9,443 votes against 7,188.) Mr. Morley presided over the great Conference of Liberals held at Leeds in October, 1883. His works are—" Edmund Burke, a His- toriCal Study," 1867;. "Critical Miscellanies'" 1871, 2nd series, 1877; "Voltaire," 1872; "On Com- p.romise,'' 1874 ; " Rousseau," 1876 ; " Diderot and _

he Encyclopredists," 2 vols., 1878; 'Life of Richard Cobden," 1881. Mr. Morley is an honorary L.L.D. of the University of Glasgow. The " Pall 'Mall- Gazette" (" extra '! number) says: —Mr. John Morley, the new Chief Secretary for Ire- land, is`the first editor in this country who has ever been made a Cabinet Minister. He has held no in- termediate office between the editorship of the "Pall Mall Gazette" and the distinguished official position which places in his hand the government of Ireland. It is an instance of rapid promotion un- paralleled in our time. Awl, yet so universal is the recognition of the.eminent ability of Mr:Morley that the fitness of the e.Vpointinent has, hardly been seriously questioned even by his most vehement political opponents. Whether the result will justify the high hope with which the nominatiOn.has been hailed on all sides is a point, of course, on which no one can speak with confidence. In the passages (quoted from Mr. Morley's leaders) there are sen- tences of political counsel which might have been written by Burke, and predictions of • impending disaster which have been only too fatally fulfilled by events. They remind us that Mr. Morley's reluc- tance to resort to coercion was no mere fanatical devotion to Constitutional pedantry, but *as due' rather to a profound conviction of the enormous magnitude of the social revolution in Ireland. He wrote- from Dublin, September .3, 18.82:—" If I thought Ireland a tough problent beforej think it much mOre.to Since I've seen it closer ,And he will probably find it tougher still when he approaches it in his Official capacity. But he at least Will not under-estimate the gravity of his task or recoil from those measures of organic change which alone offer even a ,possibility of securing the re-settlement of Ireland: On Wednesday morning 'Lord Aberdeen, the new Irish Viceroy, and Mr. John Morley, Chief Secretary, anived in Dublin, having crossed the Channel to- gether in the mail steamer Ulster, They were sworn in before the Lord Justices at a special meet- ing of the Privy Council. Subsequently the new Lords Juatices were sworn to govern in the Viceroy's labsence. Lord Aberdeen returned immediately to England to make preparations for his public entry into Dublin. Mr. John Morley, returned to New- dastle„havittg to fight for his seat. He was first re- turned .to Parliament. from Newcastle at the by- election in 1883, consequent upon the death of Mr. Ashton Mike. On Thursday night Mr. 'John Morley addressed a meeting of the electors of Newcastle. , He said that all _he had heard in the few hours he 'had been in
Dublin confirmed him in his views with regard to Ireland which he had held' for the last five or six

years; but he was not so "rapid" as his predecessor (Mr. W. H. Smith), and he had not learnt so much during his visit as would justify him in saying that night, "here is our Irish policy." It was a most unreasonable thing to demand of him that he should at the present moment bring, before them a bill for the reconstruction of government in Ire- land. He held, however, that separation would be a disgrace to England and a disaster to Ireland. Nor would he ever be a party to placing the minority' and the property of the minority at the mercy of the majority in Ireland. If the majority should be Inclined to deal lawlessly with them none would stand up more strongly than he for order, equal rights, and justice. Any measure the Government ultimately framed would be submitted to the full blaze of public criticism, and the empire could not be disintegrated without the people knowing. and having the opportunity of preventing it.--On the motion of Mr. Burt, M.P., a vote pledging the meet- ing to support Mr. Morley was carried with great enthusiasm, and with only one dissentient. • THE ELECTION- YESTERDAY. LIBERAL VICTORY. Yesterday whilst the polling was going on Mr. Morley addressed a meeting of workmen outside the gates of the Armstrong Works. He felt, he said, that amongst the Elswick men were his staunchest supporters. They stood by him in 1883 and 1885, and he believed they would stand by him in 188 G. He had been chosen to fill a post of great responsi- bility, and to which were attached what the world thought great dignities, but he assured them they were not losing a friend because receiving an offi- cial. He should always be glad to do anything for the great industrial classes of this country. therefore he called upon workmen to make a sacrifice to-day for him and the Liberal party, and go the poll. (Cheers.) 1 o

The polling proceeded quietly all day, and at four clock less than half of the thirty thousand eled- tors had recorded their votes a state of things which the Conservatives considered to be in their favour. The counting took place immediately after the close of the poll, and the result was as follows John Morley (L) C. F. Hammond (C)
Liberal majority 2,721 Mr, Morley's majority at the general election was 629 only, the Irish electors voting against him at the bidding of Mr. Parnell.

Edelsten and Sons, .E 1 13s. ; Monks, Hall and Co., Lithited, £35; Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Limited, £4O; J. &J. Tinsley, ...C3 12s. a ; total, £B7 ss. Bid. THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON. —For week ending Saturday, Feb. 6th, 1886.—The mean temperature was 34.8 Fahr., and therefore '7 degrees cooler than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 42 Fahrenheit. was recorded on the sth inst., and the minimum temperature. 23 Fahrenheit., on the 6th inst. The rainfall measured 0.39 in. The general direction of the . wind was N.W. During the week, which was the 6th of the current year, 26 births and 26 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 29.1 per 1,000, against 27.46 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 131 the cor- responding week of last year. The deaths included 3 from whooping cough, 1 from rheumatism, 3 from' tubercular disease, 1 from phthisis, 2 from old age, 4 from brain disease, 2 from heart disettse, 6 from lung disease, and 1 from liver disease, 1 case of scarlatina was reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.—JoHN IL GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health
Mr. G. Fleotwoool Wilson has been appointed private soc• rotary to Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., Financial Secretary to the War Office.

The Dublin boat Avoca fouled the steamship Chirnbor- azor, at anchor in the Thames on Friday. The Avoca was cut to the water's edge and returned for repairs. MURDER BY A. MOTHER. - Mrs Harris, of Brunswick Close, St. John's-street,London, Cut her child's threat and her own this morning. The child died but the mother lives

An unqualified denial is given to the story that Mr. Glad- stone has given Lord Kenmare an assurance that he will not introduce a Home Rule Bill, at any rate for six months to come. TEE UNExtPLoYED.—Replying to a deputation of unem- ployed workmen who waited upon the Dudley Board of Guardians yesterday, the chairman regretted that the law would not allow Guardians to give them out-door relief. It was decided to appeal to the Local Government Board to allow a relaxation of the law.

THE RIOT IN THE METROPOLIS.—The Cential News is authorised to state that Mr. Childers proposes to appoint a committee to inquire and report as to the origin and char- acter of the disturbances which took place in the metropolis on Monday, and as to the conduct of the police autihorities in relation thereto. Mr. Childers will himself act as chair- man of the committee.

FATAL RAILW a m Y ACCIDENTaried r AmTanrinEa AmTeocr PatrickN o n Rr sets eOvn, Thursday morning aged 38, whilst engaged in shunting operations on the Lon- don and North-Western Railway at Heaton Norris, was thrown out of a waggon, the wheels of which passed over him. He died from his injuries a few minutes after being admitted to the Stockport Infirmary. AN EXTRAORDINARY' BANICRDPICf.—ArI extraordinary point came before the official receiver at Birmingham on Friday. A bankrupt, after filing a petition, corainitted enenide, and on Friday, when the proceedings came on, it was contended that it would be telly to make a dead man a bmkeupt. The official receiver said it was the first case of the kind that had occurred. He woukl consult the Inspec- tor• General in Bankruptcy. SnociErNei FATALITY AT BOLTON.—About four o'clock on Friday morning an old man named James Holt, an engineer at a steam laundry at Bromley Cross, near Bolton, was pro- ceeding to his work when, on crossing the line at Bromley Cross, he was knocked down by the Hellifield express to Manchester. He was very deaf, and did not hear the warn- ing of the pointsman who called to him. He was imme- diately killed. Both his feet were cut off. KILLED BY A FOOTBALL.-00 Friday, Mr. S. Smelt, deputy city coroner, held an inquest on the body of a boy named Henry Burgess, nine years of age, late of 52, Birch- street, Ardwick, Manchester. On Saturday last the deceased and a companion went to see a football match. They wan- dered behind the goal posts, and one of the players kicked the ball, which struck the deceased on the head. Deceased was a very delicate boy. A doctor was sent for, who pre- scribed for him, bet the unfortunate boy died on Tuesday. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death.
