LORD MACAULAY.—A meeting of the Warrington Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society was held on Wednesday evening, presided. over by the Rev. J. H. Jones,.when a most concise B,nd able essay on 11 the "Life of Lord Macaulay" was read by Mr. Broadhurst. The essayist gave an account of the private and public works of the noble lord, men- tioning several cases of his great liberality, and his abilities as a politician. In the debate which ensued, the following took part :—Messrs. C. Plins- ton, W. Bennett, J. S. Green, J.. Swift, 11. H. Dutton, 1 and the Chairman. . WORK AND WAGES IN WARRINGTON.--The strike ,of a portion of the employes of :.‘Lessrs. Houghton, of the Sankey Wire Mills, still continues without as yet any apparent signs of a speedy agreement be- ing come to. About half-a,dozen men from York- shire have during the present week taken the place .of the strikers, but these, we understand, being dis- satisfied with the wages have either returned or are about to return to their homes. Some precautions have been taken to guard• the mill premises with police, but those who speak on behalf of the work- men Say that they are entirely unnecessary, as the ' men aredetermined to conduct the dispute in a peaceful and orderly fashion. THE HIRE SYSTEM OF PURCHASE.—At the Borough Court, on Monday, a man named John Penny was charged with stealing a quantity of furniture, value. £648 6d, the property of Elijah Cunnington, furni- ture dealer.—Mr. Yearsley, who appeared to prose- cute, said that prisoner hired the furniture from Mr. Cunnington, and agreed to pay periodical sums for the hire of the goods. It was also agreed that he could terminate the hiring at any time by becoming the purchaser, the amount to be paid to be the dif- ference between the rent paid under the agreement and the contract price. It was subsequently learned that prisoner had disposed of the goods. Some people seemed to think that if they obtained goods on the hire system they became the owners of them, and it. was to dispel that idea that the present pro- tredings were taken.—Prisoner, who said that im was out of work, and had been driven to dispose of , the furniture by poverty, was sent to prison for a month.

THE IMPRISONMENT Or A BANRILUPT.—At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, Mr. A. Browne, solicitor,' Warrington, appeared on behalf of Peter Philip Longshaw, bankrupt, to make an application, the terms of which had been placed on the file. The fbrrn of application set forth that the bankrupt was committed to Walton Gaol on the 25th January last, by his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, for contempt of court in not having obeyed a certain order to file accounts; that all the books, documents, &c., were. in the possession of the Official Receiver; that the bankrupt was willing and ready to purge his con- tempt by furnishing, the accounts required; that the governor of the wison had given permission for the documents and books to be admitted into, such prison; and that the Official Reeeiver,on being applied to. had refused to allow them out of his possession. Mr. Browne ilow applied for an order directing the Official Receiver to deliver 'the books, papers, and documents to the bankrupt, or such person as the court might name, necessary to the furnishing of the accounts.—Mr. Worsley (deputy Official Receiver) said that the Official Receiver did not desire to keep the bankrupt in prison, but only wished protection as far as the books were con- cerned.—After a discussion between his Honour, the Deputy Official Receive; and Mr. Brown it was decided that the books should be taken to Brown, in charge of some person appointed by the Official Receiver, the sum of £3 to be deposited on behalf of the bankrupt as a guarantee for the expense in- curred: " THE GREAT D VICE OF WELLINGTON."—The Rev. G. E. Cutting, of Warrington, gave a lecture on.Thursdayr evening to the members of the Padgate Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society, taking for his subject "The Great Duke of Wellington." Mr. Jenkins presided. Mr. Cutting said that within the narrow limits of a single lecture it was impos- sible to do justice to such a Subject, but yet, in a record of greatness, to read a page here and there gave an inspiration of power very helpful in the battle in which they were engaged. The inspira- tion of a noble life, he said, was never fully felt until that life had passed away. The sceptre ,held over them that night was the sword of a warrior, but he need make no apology for that, for the sword of Wellington was never drawn for an unworthy Purpose, and no unhealthy military enthusiasm need be raised. In all his engagements, Welling- ton was a man of peace, although a man of War, and gratitude demanded that a high tribute be paid to one who so nobly defended our national life. The subject of the lecture was born in Ireland in 1769, but his ancestors were of English descent. After being in his early youth at a preparatory school, he, went to Eton, but did not rank high as a scholar, although he developed pugilistic tendencies. From Eton he went , to a military academy in , Prance, where he remained two years. When very young he took a commission in the army, and de- voted himself closely to military studies. In 1794 he commenced his active career. Mr. Cutting then vividly described Wellington's career in the Indian campaign', and referred in graphic language to the engagement at Waterloo. The indomitable persever- ance, thoroughness, patiende, and other distinguish- ing traits of the' character of the duke were ably portrayed by the lecturer, who said that Wellington had left a legacy greater even, than his glory—he had left to us the contemplation of his character. The very humblest and most despairing might profit by his example, wkich was not the case with all great men. Wellington's career was built up by patience, industry, and perseverance, and perhaps he reminded us more than any other that" We may make our lives sublime—A hearty vote of thanks was accorded. to Mr. Cutting, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Is A. .Bennett, and a vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the - proceedings.

MAKING BAD WORSE BY "A WICKED DEFENr...• —On Thursday, at the Liverpool Assizes, hel(3,' Mr. Justice Day, Thomas Marsh (41), labourer,•W:: charged with having stolen, at Wrigtington, on, 4'; 27th ult., a brass rule, the property,. of Jall7 Houghton. Mr. Shea prosecuted. From the elr dence of Police-constable 1,286, upon whose tes_t,s mony the prosecution mainly rested, it appes that whilst this constable was speaking to the Prr soner in the Foresters' Arms beerhouse, at Sheving:% ton, about another case, he dropped from his It" a brass rule, which was afterwards identified re Houghton's. Prisoner asserted that he saw' officer evidently trying to conceal the rule up. sleeve, but that when it fell he at once charged nw* (Marsh) with having let it drop. Prisoner remos, strated with him for making such ,an unfoundr, charge, but all the same the officer took him in:, custody. The landlord of the 'public-house wiwA called, and stated that he heard the rule fall, upon asking asking the •prisoner who let it fall 3farT, answered that it had fallen off the counter. Mar% afterwards said it had come from the policentail: coat sleeve.—Prisoner, in the course of a statemen: to the jury, said the constable had a spite again him, and was constantly in the habit%of searching him.—His Lordship said if the prisoner's accusation •;, were true, the constable had been guilty of the most atrocious offence of scheming to convict all , Innocent person, and also of gross perjury.—The prisoner was foiuid guilty, and admitted a previong conviction.—The learned Judge, in addressing tbe prisoner, said the defence which had been sst IP , was'one of the most wicked conceivable descrir tion. If it had not bean for the courageous manli,er in which the jury had discharged , their duties tuti officer might have been left under the suspicion o having committed an offence which, if it were trio,. would be a thorough disqualification for him getting any employment among peoplawho valued honeSti and propriety of conduct. He, then sentenced the prisoner to six months' imprisonment. •

THE CHAMBER or SHIPPING.—At the ninth annual meet', log of the Ckamber of Shipping, held in London,on Friday Mr. Anderson, representing the port of London, was elected president for the ensuing year, and Mr. Watts, as represent- ing the Tyne ports, vice-president. In the course of the discussion on the load line the question of the necessity of the revision of Lloyd's rule was generally advocated, and muck indignation was expressed at the action taken by the Board of Trade at the instigation of Lloyd's. Resolutions were passed in favour of the revision of quarantine regula- tions, of insertion in the bill of lading of negligence clases, and of the abolition of light dues. , SELeIOUS RTO TING AT LEICESTER.-20 PERSONS ARRESTED. The dainaee caused by the riots at Leicester on Thum- day night is greater than at first reported, and over a dezen large factories have been cleared or their windows. The titers again assembied on Friday morning,several thousands strong, and quickly gathering at particular points, the police were unable to prevent the windows being smashed. The nembers are so great, and the rioters pass so quickly from one part of the town to another, that it is impressible for the police to muster in sufficient force to preeerve order. In- formation has been received at the Central Police -tation that an attack has been made on the largest factory in the town where no dispute existed, and police reinforcements have been telegraphed for from Manchester, Sheffield, Not- tingham, and ether places. Four young men were fined 40s for throwing stones on Thursday. The ringleaders are not apprehended. A later telegram says :—As the aspect of affairs is becom- ing very serioue, the military have been telegraphed for. The rioters are now attackinee factories where no dispute exists, with the object of forcing those werkpeeple to join the strike. The rioters made a determined attack on the warehouse of Messrs. Cooper and Cc., but were driven back by men with powerful hose pipes, aided by the police. The rioters are now smashing factery windows in Friday. street. Telegraphieg at half-pa4t fenr this evening, our Leicester correseoudent states the town has been in a disturbed state all day, and things are now growing worse. Two hundred policemen are on duty, but, although 20 arrests have been Made, the police are powerless to restore order, and tele- grams asking ,for a hundred additional constables have been 1 despatched. , ' At five- -o'clock last evening seventeen prisoners were taken before the magistrates, who were sitting most of the day, and, after formal evidence had been given, they were retnanded for a week, MeantebEe the mob had perambula- ted other parts of the town, but the police and constables from Sheffield and Northampton were better able, to ciintrol then, and kept them moving on. A boy has been conveyed to the infirmary said to be severely injured. FATAL BOILER EXPLOSION IN ITALY.
